stimuli.title: Eight bank officers in a row, with departments
stimuli.content:
Eight officers of a bank, Anmol, Bishakha, Dolly, Gagandeep, Hrithik, Inaaya, Kirtan and Mehr, sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each works in a different department among Accounts, Audit, Credit, Forex, HR, IT, Legal and Treasury. (Facing north, a person's right is towards the east end of the row.)

- Inaaya sits fourth from the left end of the row and works in Credit.
- Bishakha sits second to the right of Inaaya and works in HR.
- The person who works in Accounts sits immediately to the right of Bishakha.
- Gagandeep sits at the extreme right end and works in Treasury.
- Dolly sits at an extreme end of the row, and Anmol sits immediately to the left of Inaaya.
- Mehr sits immediately to the left of Bishakha, and Kirtan is not an immediate neighbour of Bishakha.
- The person who works in IT sits second to the left of the person who works in Accounts.
- The person in Forex sits immediately to the right of the person in Legal, and Anmol does not work in Forex.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the left (west) end.
Step 1: Inaaya = 4 (Credit), Bishakha = 6 (HR), Accounts = 7, Gagandeep = 8 (Treasury).
Step 2: Dolly is at an end; seat 8 is taken, so Dolly = 1. Anmol = 3, Mehr = 5.
Step 3: Seats 2 and 7 remain for Hrithik and Kirtan. Kirtan cannot sit next to Bishakha (6), so Kirtan = 2 and Hrithik = 7 (Accounts).
Step 4: IT is two seats left of Accounts: seat 5, Mehr. Audit, Forex and Legal remain for seats 1, 2 and 3; Forex is immediately right of Legal, and Anmol (3) is not in Forex, so Legal = 1 (Dolly), Forex = 2 (Kirtan) and Audit = 3 (Anmol).

| Seat | Person | Department |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dolly | Legal |
| 2 | Kirtan | Forex |
| 3 | Anmol | Audit |
| 4 | Inaaya | Credit |
| 5 | Mehr | IT |
| 6 | Bishakha | HR |
| 7 | Hrithik | Accounts |
| 8 | Gagandeep | Treasury |

stimuli.title: A row of unknown length and an interchange
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons in the row is not given. Harshit, Tejas, Vrinda and Yamuna are among them.

- Harshit sits tenth from the left end of the row, and Tejas sits somewhere to his right.
- If Harshit and Tejas interchange their seats, Harshit becomes seventeenth from the left end and Tejas becomes fourteenth from the right end.
- Vrinda sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Yamuna sits second to the left of the seat that Tejas occupies before the interchange.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: After the interchange Harshit takes Tejas's seat and becomes 17th from the left, so Tejas sits 17th from the left.
Step 2: Tejas takes Harshit's seat (10th from the left) and becomes 14th from the right, so the row has 10 + 14 − 1 = 23 persons.
Step 3: Vrinda is in the middle: (23 + 1) ÷ 2 = 12th from the left. Yamuna is second to the left of 17th: 15th from the left.

| Person | From the left (before) | From the right (before) |
|---|---|---|
| Harshit | 10th | 14th |
| Vrinda | 12th | 12th |
| Yamuna | 15th | 9th |
| Tejas | 17th | 7th |

stimuli.title: Nine persons from three teams in one row
stimuli.content:
Nine persons Aaradhya, Bodhi, Chinmayi, Divit, Eshna, Falguni, Hridya, Ivaan and Jaanvi sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each belongs to one of three teams, Red, Blue and Green, and each team has exactly three members among them. (Facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Jaanvi sits exactly in the middle of the row, and Falguni sits immediately to her left.
- Ivaan sits third to the right of Falguni, and they are in the same team.
- Divit sits at the extreme left end, and Eshna sits at the extreme right end.
- Aaradhya sits third to the left of Eshna, and Chinmayi sits immediately to the left of Eshna.
- Hridya sits to the left of Bodhi.
- No two members of the same team sit next to each other.
- Divit is in the Red team, and Aaradhya is in the Blue team.
- Jaanvi and Chinmayi are in the same team, and so are Hridya and Eshna.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 9 from the left end.
Step 1: Jaanvi = 5, Falguni = 4, Ivaan = 7, Divit = 1, Eshna = 9, Aaradhya = 6, Chinmayi = 8.
Step 2: Seats 2 and 3 remain for Hridya and Bodhi; Hridya is to the left: Hridya = 2, Bodhi = 3.
Step 3: Divit is Red and Aaradhya Blue. Jaanvi (5) and Ivaan (7) both sit next to Aaradhya, so neither is Blue, and so their team-mates Chinmayi and Falguni are not Blue either. Falguni sits next to Jaanvi, so the pair Falguni–Ivaan and the pair Jaanvi–Chinmayi take Red and Green in some order.
Step 4: If Falguni and Ivaan were Green, Jaanvi, Chinmayi and Divit would fill Red; Hridya and Eshna could not both join Green (it would have four), so they would be Blue and Bodhi Green — but Bodhi (3) sits next to Falguni (4) ✗. So Falguni and Ivaan are Red (Red is now full) and Jaanvi and Chinmayi are Green.
Step 5: Hridya and Eshna share a team; Red is full and Green has room for only one more, so both are Blue with Aaradhya, and Bodhi is the third Green member. No two neighbours share a team.

| Seat | Person | Team |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Divit | Red |
| 2 | Hridya | Blue |
| 3 | Bodhi | Green |
| 4 | Falguni | Red |
| 5 | Jaanvi | Green |
| 6 | Aaradhya | Blue |
| 7 | Ivaan | Red |
| 8 | Chinmayi | Green |
| 9 | Eshna | Blue |

stimuli.title: Seven persons around a round table, with favourite cuisines
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Ayaan, Gunika, Madhur, Parul, Rehaan, Sarika and Tanvir sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Each likes a different cuisine among Bengali, Chinese, Gujarati, Italian, Mexican, Punjabi and Thai. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise and the left is clockwise.)

- Parul sits immediately to the right of Ayaan, and Gunika sits third to the right of Ayaan.
- Madhur sits second to the left of Ayaan.
- Tanvir sits immediately between Parul and Gunika.
- Rehaan is an immediate neighbour of Ayaan.
- Ayaan likes Punjabi food, and the person who likes Thai food sits immediately to his right.
- Gunika likes Bengali food, and the person who likes Chinese food sits immediately to her right.
- The person who likes Mexican food sits immediately to the left of Ayaan.
- Madhur does not like Italian food.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 6 anticlockwise starting from Ayaan.
Step 1: Parul = 1 and Gunika = 3 (right = anticlockwise). Madhur is second to Ayaan's left (clockwise): 5.
Step 2: Tanvir sits between Parul (1) and Gunika (3): seat 2. Rehaan is next to Ayaan: seat 6 (seat 1 is Parul's). Sarika takes seat 4.
Step 3: Ayaan likes Punjabi; Thai is on his right: Parul. Gunika likes Bengali; Chinese is on her right: Sarika (4). Mexican is on Ayaan's left: Rehaan (6).
Step 4: Gujarati and Italian remain for Tanvir and Madhur; Madhur does not like Italian, so Madhur likes Gujarati and Tanvir Italian.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person | Cuisine |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Ayaan | Punjabi |
| 1 | Parul | Thai |
| 2 | Tanvir | Italian |
| 3 | Gunika | Bengali |
| 4 | Sarika | Chinese |
| 5 | Madhur | Gujarati |
| 6 | Rehaan | Mexican |

stimuli.title: Rectangular table: middle seats of the longer sides face outside
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Kshitij, Mahua, Nikunj, Prerak, Rumi, Sudhir, Tvisha and Urmila sit around a rectangular table. Three persons sit along each longer side and one person at each shorter side. The person in the middle seat of each longer side faces away from the centre; the other six face the centre. Each person on a longer side sits directly opposite a person on the other longer side. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Kshitij and Prerak sit at the two shorter sides of the table.
- Rumi sits immediately to the right of Kshitij.
- Mahua sits second to the right of Prerak.
- Urmila sits directly opposite Mahua.
- Nikunj sits immediately to the left of Urmila.
- Sudhir does not sit next to Prerak.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise, starting with Kshitij at one shorter side; Prerak is at the other shorter side, seat 4. Seats 1–3 and 5–7 are the longer sides (2 and 6 are their middle seats, facing outside), and seat s faces seat 8 − s.
Step 1: Kshitij faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: Rumi = 1.
Step 2: Prerak also faces the centre: Mahua = 4 + 2 = 6 (a middle seat, facing outside). Urmila is opposite Mahua: seat 2, also facing outside.
Step 3: Urmila faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Nikunj = 3.
Step 4: Seats 5 and 7 remain for Sudhir and Tvisha; seat 5 is next to Prerak, so Sudhir = 7, Tvisha = 5.

| Seat | Person | Position |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Kshitij | shorter side, facing the centre |
| 1 | Rumi | longer side, facing the centre |
| 2 | Urmila | middle of a longer side, facing outside |
| 3 | Nikunj | longer side, facing the centre |
| 4 | Prerak | shorter side, facing the centre |
| 5 | Tvisha | longer side, facing the centre |
| 6 | Mahua | middle of a longer side, facing outside |
| 7 | Sudhir | longer side, facing the centre |

stimuli.title: Three at an inner table, six at an outer table
stimuli.content:
Nine persons sit around two concentric circular tables. Three of them sit at the smaller inner table, equally spaced and facing outside; the other six sit at the outer table, equally spaced and facing the centre. Each person at the inner table directly faces one person at the outer table, and between any two such outer persons there is exactly one other outer person. The nine persons are Abeer, Deeksha, Faiyaz, Hamsini, Ishant, Kajol, Lakshit, Navin and Ojal. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Abeer, Kajol and Navin sit at the inner table; Abeer faces Hamsini.
- Kajol sits immediately to the left of Abeer.
- Faiyaz faces Kajol, and Deeksha sits immediately to the right of Faiyaz.
- Ishant sits immediately to the left of Hamsini.
- Lakshit sits second to the right of Faiyaz.
stimuli.solution:
Number the outer seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise from Hamsini, the person Abeer faces. The inner persons face outer seats 0, 2 and 4.
Step 1: Abeer faces outside, so his left is anticlockwise: Kajol is at the next inner seat anticlockwise and faces outer seat 2. Navin faces outer seat 4.
Step 2: Faiyaz faces Kajol: outer seat 2. Deeksha, to Faiyaz's right (anticlockwise): 3. Lakshit, second to Faiyaz's right: 4, so Lakshit faces Navin.
Step 3: Ishant is to Hamsini's left (clockwise): seat 5. Ojal takes seat 1.

| Outer seat | Outer person | Faced by (inner) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Hamsini | Abeer |
| 1 | Ojal | – |
| 2 | Faiyaz | Kajol |
| 3 | Deeksha | – |
| 4 | Lakshit | Navin |
| 5 | Ishant | – |

stimuli.title: Five floors and five vehicles
stimuli.content:
Five persons Amrit, Dimpy, Hari, Kanak and Sohan live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 5 the topmost). Each owns a different vehicle among a Bicycle, a Bike, a Car, a Scooter and a Van.

- Sohan lives exactly in the middle floor of the building and owns the Car.
- Amrit lives immediately above Sohan, and Kanak lives somewhere above Amrit.
- Dimpy lives on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who owns the Van lives on the lowermost floor.
- The person who owns the Scooter lives immediately above the person who owns the Bicycle.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Sohan = 3 (Car), Amrit = 4, Kanak = 5.
Step 2: Dimpy is on an even floor: 2 (floor 4 is Amrit's). Hari = 1, so Hari owns the Van.
Step 3: Bicycle, Bike and Scooter remain for floors 2, 4 and 5. The Scooter is immediately above the Bicycle: floors 4 and 5 (floor 3 is the Car). So Amrit has the Bicycle, Kanak the Scooter and Dimpy the Bike.

| Floor | Person | Vehicle |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Kanak | Scooter |
| 4 | Amrit | Bicycle |
| 3 | Sohan | Car |
| 2 | Dimpy | Bike |
| 1 | Hari | Van |

stimuli.title: Seven gift boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, D, F, H, K, M and P are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Each box contains a different gift among a Clock, a Lamp, a Mug, a Pen set, a Scarf, a Toy and a Watch.

- Box P is kept exactly in the middle of the stack, and Box B is kept immediately below Box P.
- Only one box is kept between Box P and Box D, and Box D is kept above Box P.
- Box M is kept at the top of the stack.
- Box H contains the Watch, and it is kept immediately below Box D.
- Box F is kept below Box K, and Box B contains the Clock.
- The box containing the Toy is kept immediately above the box containing the Mug, and below the box containing the Watch.
- The box containing the Scarf is kept two places above the box containing the Lamp.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: P = 4, B = 3, D = 6, M = 7, H = 5 (Watch).
Step 2: Positions 1 and 2 remain for F and K; F is below K: F = 1, K = 2. B holds the Clock.
Step 3: Lamp, Mug, Pen set, Scarf and Toy remain for positions 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7. The Toy is immediately above the Mug and below the Watch (5): positions 1–2, so F has the Mug and K the Toy.
Step 4: The Scarf is two places above the Lamp: positions 4 and 6, so P has the Lamp, D the Scarf and M the Pen set.

| Position | Box | Gift |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | M | Pen set |
| 6 | D | Scarf |
| 5 | H | Watch |
| 4 | P | Lamp |
| 3 | B | Clock |
| 2 | K | Toy |
| 1 | F | Mug |

stimuli.title: Seven coloured boxes in a line on a shelf
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes Q, R, T, V, W, X and Y are placed side by side in a single line on a shelf. Left and right are as seen by a person facing the shelf. Each box is of a different colour among Beige, Blue, Grey, Lemon, Olive, Peach and Teal.

- Box T is placed exactly in the middle of the line, and Box R is placed immediately to the right of Box T.
- Box Q is placed second to the left of Box T, and Box Y is placed immediately to the right of Box Q.
- Box W is placed at the extreme left end, and Box V at the extreme right end.
- Box T is Blue, and the Peach box is placed immediately to the left of the Blue box.
- The Teal box is at the left end and the Beige box at the right end.
- The Grey box is placed between the Teal box and the Peach box.
- The Olive box is placed immediately to the right of the Blue box.
stimuli.solution:
Number the places 1 to 7 from the left.
Step 1: T = 4, R = 5, Q = 2, Y = 3, W = 1, V = 7, so X = 6.
Step 2: T is Blue; Peach is immediately left of it: Y. Teal = 1 (W), Beige = 7 (V).
Step 3: Grey lies between Teal (1) and Peach (3): place 2, Q. Olive is immediately right of Blue: R. Lemon is left for X.

| Place (from left) | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | W | Teal |
| 2 | Q | Grey |
| 3 | Y | Peach |
| 4 | T | Blue |
| 5 | R | Olive |
| 6 | X | Lemon |
| 7 | V | Beige |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in three stacks of different heights
stimuli.content:
Nine boxes B, C, F, J, L, N, R, U and Z are kept in three stacks standing side by side: the Left stack has two boxes, the Middle stack three and the Right stack four. Level 1 is the bottom of every stack; 'directly above/below' means in the same stack, one level higher/lower.

- Box L is at the top of the tallest stack, and Box R is directly below Box L.
- Box U is directly below Box R. Box B is in the middle stack, at the same level as Box U.
- Box N is directly above Box B.
- Box C is at the top of a stack, and Box J is directly below Box C.
- Box Z is not in the same stack as Box L.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: The tallest stack is the Right one: L = Right 4, R = Right 3, U = Right 2.
Step 2: B is in the Middle stack at U's level: Middle 2. N is directly above B: Middle 3, the top of that stack.
Step 3: C is at the top of a stack with J directly below it. Right and Middle tops are taken, so C = Left 2 and J = Left 1.
Step 4: Middle 1 and Right 1 remain for F and Z. Z is not in L's (Right) stack: Z = Middle 1, F = Right 1.

| Level | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | – | – | L |
| 3 | – | N | R |
| 2 | C | B | U |
| 1 | J | Z | F |

stimuli.title: Two stacks, lighter boxes always on top
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes D, E, G, H, K, M, P and T are kept in two stacks, A and B, with four boxes in each stack (level 1 is the bottom of a stack). Their weights are 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 kg, one weight per box. In each stack, every box is lighter than the box directly below it.

- Box T is the heaviest box and is in stack A.
- Box K is at the top of stack B and weighs 7 kg.
- Box M is the lightest box.
- Box H is at the bottom of stack B and weighs 3 kg less than Box T.
- Box G is kept directly below Box D.
- Box P weighs twice as much as Box E.
- Box G is in the same stack as Box T.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Every stack gets lighter upwards, so the heaviest box is at the bottom of its stack: T = A1 (24 kg). K = B4 (7 kg). H = B1 with 24 − 3 = 21 kg.
Step 2: The lightest box M (5 kg) must be at the top of a stack; B4 is K, so M = A4.
Step 3: D, E, G and P take A2, A3, B2 and B3 with 9, 12, 15 and 18 kg. P = 2 × E, so P = 18 and E = 9; G and D share 12 and 15.
Step 4: G is directly below D and in T's stack, so G and D are in stack A (G = A2, D = A3) and P, E are in stack B. In each stack the lower box is heavier: G = 15, D = 12, P = B2 (18), E = B3 (9).

| Level | Stack A | Stack B |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | M (5 kg) | K (7 kg) |
| 3 | D (12 kg) | E (9 kg) |
| 2 | G (15 kg) | P (18 kg) |
| 1 | T (24 kg) | H (21 kg) |

stimuli.title: Five colour words for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, colour words are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A pink B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A blue B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A red B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A grey B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A green B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: pink means >, blue means <, red means ≥, grey means ≤ and green means =. Rewrite every statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain and test each conclusion along it.

stimuli.title: Six exams on the weekdays of March 2027
stimuli.content:
Six exams — Chemistry, Hindi, Physics, Sanskrit, Statistics and Zoology — are held on six different dates in March 2027, one exam per date. No exam is held on a Saturday or a Sunday. 1 March 2027 is a Monday.

- The Statistics exam is on the first Wednesday of the month.
- The Physics exam is exactly 15 days after the Statistics exam.
- The Hindi exam is on the last Friday of the month.
- The Chemistry exam is on the same day of the week as the Physics exam, exactly one week earlier.
- The Zoology exam is on the first Monday after the Chemistry exam.
- The Sanskrit exam is on a date that is a multiple of 10, before the Hindi exam.
stimuli.solution:
Mondays of March 2027: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, so Wednesdays are 3, 10, 17, 24, 31 and Fridays 5, 12, 19, 26. Statistics: first Wednesday, 3rd. Physics: 3 + 15 = 18th (Thursday). Hindi: last Friday, 26th. Chemistry: 18 − 7 = 11th (Thursday). Zoology: first Monday after the 11th, the 15th. Sanskrit: multiples of 10 are 10 (Wednesday), 20 (Saturday, no exams) and 30 (after Hindi), so the 10th.

Order: Statistics 3 (Wed), Sanskrit 10 (Wed), Chemistry 11 (Thu), Zoology 15 (Mon), Physics 18 (Thu), Hindi 26 (Fri).

stimuli.title: Seven book launches from April to October, in three genres
stimuli.content:
Seven authors Amit, Bhanu, Charu, Dhruva, Esha, Firdaus and Gunjan each launch one book in a different month from April to October of the same year. Each book belongs to one of three genres: Poetry, Fiction or Travel.

- No two books launched in consecutive months are of the same genre.
- Three of the books are Poetry, two are Fiction and two are Travel.
- Charu's book, a Poetry book, is launched in July.
- Esha's book is launched in the month immediately before Charu's, and it is not a Fiction book.
- Amit's book is launched in the first of the seven months and Gunjan's in the last, and neither of their books is Poetry.
- Firdaus's book is a Fiction book launched in a month that has 31 days.
- The two Fiction books are launched exactly four months apart.
- Bhanu's book is launched later than Dhruva's.
stimuli.solution:
Charu: July, Poetry. Esha: June; her book is not Fiction, and it cannot be Poetry next to Charu's Poetry July, so it is Travel. Amit: April, Gunjan: October, neither Poetry. Two more Poetry books are needed among May, August and September (April and October are not Poetry); August touches Charu's Poetry July, so May and September are Poetry. Firdaus (Fiction, 31-day month: May or August) therefore takes August, and Dhruva and Bhanu take May and September — Bhanu later, so Dhruva May, Bhanu September. The second Fiction book must be four months from August: April (Amit), since October is only two months away. Gunjan's book is then Travel.

Apr Amit (Fiction), May Dhruva (Poetry), Jun Esha (Travel), Jul Charu (Poetry), Aug Firdaus (Fiction), Sep Bhanu (Poetry), Oct Gunjan (Travel).

stimuli.title: Six bank branches and their opening years
stimuli.content:
A bank opened six branches — Alwar, Bidar, Churu, Dhule, Etah and Gonda — in six different years. The age of a branch in a year is the number of years completed since it opened (a branch opened in 2006 is 20 years old in 2026).

- In 2026, the Churu branch completes exactly 20 years.
- In 2026, the Alwar branch is exactly twice as old as the Churu branch.
- The Gonda branch opened seven years after the Churu branch.
- The Etah branch opened in a leap year, after the Churu branch but before the Gonda branch, and its age in 2026 is a multiple of 7.
- In 2026, the age of the Dhule branch equals the sum of the ages of the Gonda and Etah branches.
- The Bidar branch opened in the year in which the Alwar branch completed 10 years.
stimuli.solution:
Churu: 2026 − 20 = 2006. Alwar: 40 years old, 1986. Gonda: 2013. Etah: a leap year after 2006 and before 2013 is 2008 or 2012; ages 18 and 14, and only 14 is a multiple of 7: 2012. Dhule: 13 + 14 = 27 years, 1999. Bidar: Alwar completed 10 years in 1996.

Oldest to newest: Alwar 1986, Bidar 1996, Dhule 1999, Churu 2006, Etah 2012, Gonda 2013.

stimuli.title: Three rows of numbers with square and prime rules
stimuli.content:
Each row has three numbers. Work from left to right: apply the first rule below that fits the first two numbers, then apply the first rule that fits that result and the third number. The final value is the row's result.

(i) If the first number of the pair is a perfect square, the result is its square root multiplied by the second number.
(ii) Otherwise, if the first number is a prime number, the result is the first number plus twice the second number.
(iii) Otherwise, if the second number is even it is subtracted from the first; if it is odd it is added to the first.

Row 1: 16   5   3
Row 2: 7   6   4
Row 3: 25   3   9
stimuli.solution:
Row 1: 16 is a square → 4 × 5 = 20; 20 is neither a square nor a prime and 3 is odd → 23.
Row 2: 7 is prime → 7 + 12 = 19; 19 is prime → 19 + 8 = 27.
Row 3: 25 is a square → 5 × 3 = 15; 15 is neither, 9 is odd → 24.

When no odd number is left, it takes the smallest even number in the same way. The other numbers keep their order. A step that would not change the line is not counted, and the machine stops when the arrangement is complete.

It adds the number of letters in that word to that number, and places the word followed by the new number at the right end, immediately to the left of the pairs already placed there (in Step I, at the extreme right). All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

stimuli.title: Glasses for working hands
stimuli.content:
Somewhere in their forties, most people notice a small but annoying change. The print in the newspaper seems smaller than it used to be, and they begin to hold their phones further away to read a message. This is presbyopia, the gradual loss of the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects. It is not a disease. It happens to almost everyone with age, because the lens inside the eye slowly becomes less flexible.

For an office worker in a city, the remedy is simple: a visit to an optician and a pair of reading glasses. For many people in villages and small towns, however, the change can quietly damage their livelihood. A tailor who cannot see the eye of a needle, a weaver who can no longer follow a fine pattern, or a farmer who cannot sort seeds may work more slowly and earn less, often in the very years when their skills are at their best.

What makes this loss especially sad is how easily it can be prevented. Simple reading glasses are among the cheapest of all medical aids. In most cases a trained health worker with a basic reading chart can find the right strength in a few minutes.

The difficulty lies in reaching people. Many have never had their eyes tested, and some believe that weak near vision is simply a part of growing old that must be accepted. Others worry that glasses will make their eyes lazy, or feel embarrassed to wear them in front of their neighbours.

Several voluntary groups now hold eye camps at weekly markets and village fairs, where people can try on glasses and take home a pair that suits them. Organisers say the reaction is often the same. A woman threads a needle at the first attempt, or an old shopkeeper reads his account book without squinting, and then laughs in surprise. For a small cost, years of good work are given back.

stimuli.title: Paths that walkers choose
stimuli.content:
Walk through almost any park or college campus and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass, often running at an angle between two paved paths. Nobody planned them. They were made by thousands of people who decided, one step at a time, that the official route was too long. Planners call them 'desire lines' or 'desire paths'.

Such paths appear for a simple reason. Most people, when they are in a hurry, take the shortest route they can see. If a paved path turns a corner at a right angle, walkers will cut the corner. Once a few have done so, the grass wears thin, a faint line becomes visible, and others follow it, so that within weeks the faint track becomes a clear one.

For a long time, the usual response was to fight the walkers. Park managers put up fences, planted hedges or added signs asking people to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A fence would be stepped over or a gap would be pushed through a hedge, and the path would reappear a little further along.

Some planners now take the opposite view. Instead of treating desire paths as damage, they treat them as information. A path worn across a lawn shows exactly where people want to go, which is something no drawing can predict with certainty. Some have even suggested waiting until a new campus has been in use for a few months before laying its walkways, so that the paved paths can follow the tracks that appear.

The idea reaches beyond parks. Designers of websites, offices and public services face the same question: should people be made to follow the route that was planned for them, or should the route be redrawn to follow people? Desire paths suggest that when many people keep ignoring a design, the fault may lie with the design rather than with the people.

stimuli.title: The pot that is auctioned
stimuli.content:
In many Indian towns, long before banks reached every street, families saved and borrowed through the chit fund. The idea is simple. Suppose twenty people agree to pay one thousand rupees each month for twenty months. Every month, the whole pool collected from the members goes to one member, so that by the end, every member has received the pool once.

Who gets the money first? In most chit funds, members who need cash urgently bid for it. The pool goes to the member who is willing to give up the largest amount, called the discount. That discount, after the organiser's fee is deducted, is shared among the other members as a kind of dividend, which reduces what each of them pays that month. A member who takes the pool early therefore receives less than he will eventually pay in, while a member who waits until the end receives the full pool after paying less than his full share in most months.

In effect, the chit fund is both a savings scheme and a loan. Early takers borrow from the group and pay for it through the discount; late takers save and are rewarded for their patience. Because members often know one another, the group can judge who is likely to keep paying, something a distant bank cannot easily do.

The arrangement has obvious risks. A member who takes the pool early may stop paying once he has the money. A dishonest organiser may disappear with the collections. For this reason, chit funds in India are regulated by law, and registered funds must follow rules on how they are run. Unregistered schemes, however, continue to operate in many places, and from time to time some of them collapse, leaving members with heavy losses.

Supporters argue that, when it is run honestly, the chit fund offers something that formal finance often does not: credit that is quick, flexible and decided by people who know the borrower. Critics reply that the same informality that makes it useful also makes it dangerous.

stimuli.title: When a fine becomes a fee
stimuli.content:
A group of day-care centres had a familiar problem: some parents arrived late to collect their children, so that teachers had to stay on after closing time. The solution seemed obvious. Introduce a small fine for every late pick-up, and parents would surely become more punctual.

When economists studied what happened after such a fine was introduced at a number of day-care centres in Israel, they found the opposite. The number of late arrivals rose and settled at a higher level than before. More surprising still, when the fine was later withdrawn, lateness did not fall back to its old level.

The researchers offered an explanation that has since become well known. Before the fine, a parent who came late felt that he was imposing on a teacher's goodwill, and that sense of guilt kept most parents on time. The fine changed how the situation was understood. Lateness was no longer a favour taken from a teacher but a service that could be bought, and a modest price for an extra half-hour seemed reasonable to many parents. Once the moral question had been turned into a commercial one, removing the price did not turn it back.

The lesson is not that penalties never work. A fine large enough to hurt will usually change behaviour, and many rules depend on penalties to be obeyed at all. The point is narrower: when people already behave well out of duty, pride or a sense of fairness, a small payment can weaken those motives instead of adding to them. Psychologists sometimes describe this as money 'crowding out' other reasons for acting.

The same risk may appear elsewhere. A small reward for volunteering, for instance, could make the work feel like a poorly paid job rather than a good deed. Policy makers who reach for fines and rewards, therefore, need to ask not only how large an incentive should be, but also what message it sends about the behaviour it is meant to change.

stimuli.title: Profitable but out of cash
stimuli.content:
Ask a shopkeeper whether his business is doing well, and he will probably answer in terms of profit: how much more he sells his goods for than he paid for them. Yet a surprising number of firms that earn a profit on paper close down because they run out of cash. To understand how, it helps to separate two ideas that are easily confused.

Profit measures whether a sale earns more than it costs. Cash measures whether there is money in the bank today to pay the bills that are due today. The two can drift far apart because they move at different times. A wholesaler may pay his supplier on delivery, store the goods for a month, and then sell them to retailers who are allowed sixty days to pay. For three months, the money he has spent is tied up in stock and in amounts owed to him. The sale may be profitable, but in the meantime he must still pay rent, wages and electricity.

Growth makes the problem worse rather than better. Consider a trader who buys goods for ₹80,000 and sells them for ₹1,00,000 on two months' credit. Each such order earns ₹20,000 of profit, but it also locks up ₹80,000 until the buyer pays. If the trader doubles the number of such orders, his expected profit doubles, but so does the cash he must find in advance. A firm that grows faster than its cash can support may collapse at the very moment its order book looks healthiest.

This is why lenders look closely at the working-capital cycle, the time between paying for inputs and receiving cash from customers. Shortening it, by collecting dues faster, holding less stock or negotiating longer credit from suppliers, frees cash without any change in profit. Banks offer overdrafts and short-term loans to bridge the gap, but these carry interest and are best arranged before a crisis arrives, not after.

An old business saying puts the point bluntly: turnover is vanity, profit is sanity, but cash is king. A business can survive for a while without profit; it cannot survive for long without cash.

stimuli.title: Walls that give
stimuli.content:
On a busy road in some Indian cities, you may come across an unusual wall. Rows of hooks and hangers are fixed to it, and on them hang shirts, sweaters, blankets and children's clothes. A painted sign above them carries a simple (1) ______: 'Leave what you do not need; take what you need.'

These 'walls of kindness' are usually started by a few residents or a local group. The rules are few. Anyone who has clean clothes that they no longer wear can hang them up, and anyone who needs them can take them, without asking (2) ______ and without having to explain why. There is no counter, no form to fill in and no one keeping (3) ______ of who gives and who takes.

Supporters say this is exactly what makes the idea work. Many people who badly need a warm blanket in winter feel (4) ______ to stand in a queue and ask for charity. At the wall, they can choose quietly, like any other passer-by. Donors, for their part, find it easier to give when they can simply stop on their way to work.

The walls are not free of problems. Some fill up with torn or dirty clothes that nobody can use, and in the rainy season, clothes left in the open can be (5) ______ within days. Volunteers who look after the walls often sort the clothes every evening and take the unusable ones away.

Still, the idea has spread, and some groups have added shelves for books, toys and shoes. A wall, after all, is usually built to keep people apart. These walls do the (6) ______: they bring together people who might otherwise never meet.

stimuli.title: The mark that will not wash off
stimuli.content:
At every election in India, a voter who has cast her vote leaves the polling station with a small dark line on her left forefinger. It is drawn by a polling official with a special ink, and fingers are checked before anyone is allowed to vote. The mark is a simple but effective (1) ______ against fraud: anyone who tries to vote a second time can be spotted at once, because a finger that already carries the mark gives the game away.

The ink owes its staying power to silver nitrate. When it is applied to the skin and (2) ______ to light, the chemical reacts with the outer layer of the skin and leaves a stain that cannot be removed with soap, oil or ordinary cleaning liquids. The mark does not wash away; it (3) ______ only slowly, as old skin cells are naturally shed and replaced by new ones, a process that usually takes some weeks.

For decades, the ink used in Indian elections has been made by a public-sector company in Karnataka, which also supplies it to a number of other countries for their elections. The exact formula is closely (4) ______, and each batch is tested for quality before it is (5) ______ to polling stations across the country.

Critics sometimes point out that, in an age of electronic voter lists and photo identity cards, such an old-fashioned method seems (6) ______. Election officials reply that its strength lies precisely in its simplicity. It needs no electricity, no network connection and no special training. A glance at a voter's finger is enough to tell whether she has already voted.

stimuli.title: The money left on the card
stimuli.content:
A gift card seems like the perfect present. The buyer does not have to guess the receiver's taste, and the receiver can choose whatever she likes. For the shops that sell them, however, gift cards have an added (1) ______ that is rarely advertised: part of the money loaded on them is never spent.

Some cards are lost in drawers, some are forgotten, and many are used for a purchase that leaves a balance too (2) ______ to bother with. In the retail trade, this unspent money is known as 'breakage'. Because the shop has already received the full amount when the card was sold, every rupee that is never used is, in effect, pure (3) ______.

Shops also gain in less obvious ways. A customer with a card worth one thousand rupees often spends more than that amount, paying the difference from her own pocket. And the money from cards sold before a festival stays with the seller for weeks or months before any goods are handed over, which amounts to an interest-free loan from the buyer.

Consumer groups argue that expiry dates make the problem worse, since a card that (4) ______ after a year turns forgetfulness into a direct gain for the seller. In several countries, rules now limit how soon a gift card may expire or say how unused balances must be treated. The rules differ widely, however, and they are often (5) ______ by buyers who never read the fine print.

None of this means that gift cards are a bad idea. It does mean that the most useful thing a giver can do, after handing over the card, is to remind the receiver to use it before the money quietly disappears.

stimuli.title: Paying for power in advance
stimuli.content:
For decades, electricity in most Indian homes has been paid for after it is used. A meter reader visits, a bill arrives weeks later, and the household pays, or **(1) delays**, as its finances allow. Prepaid smart meters reverse this order. Like a mobile phone, the meter must be recharged before power can be used, and the balance falls as electricity is consumed.

Distribution companies see clear advantages. A large share of their losses comes from bills that are paid late or never paid at all, and from errors in reading meters by hand. A prepaid meter **(2) widens** both gaps: the money arrives in advance, and readings are sent automatically. Supporters add that customers benefit too, since they can track their daily use on a phone and are no longer **(3) surprised** by a large bill at the end of a hot summer month.

The concerns are mostly about poorer households. A family that runs out of balance late at night may find its power cut before it can recharge, which is a serious matter during a heatwave or when a child is unwell. For this reason, many prepaid systems offer a small emergency credit, send repeated alerts as the balance runs low and avoid **(4) restoring** supply at night or on holidays.

There is also a question of trust. When a new meter shows higher readings than the old one, customers often suspect that it is faulty, even when the old meter was simply **(5) overstating** their use. Utilities that install meters without explaining how they work have faced protests in several places.

The technology itself is neither good nor bad. Whether prepaid meters help or hurt depends on how carefully they are **(6) introduced**: with clear information, a fair grace period and a quick way to settle complaints, or with none of these.

stimuli.title: Logic circuit of a strong-room alarm
stimuli.content:
A bank's strong room has four sensors, each giving 1 (true) or 0 (false):

- D = 1 when the strong-room door is open
- K = 1 when a valid key card has been swiped
- M = 1 when the motion sensor detects movement
- N = 1 when night mode is switched on

The alarm output A is produced by this circuit:

```
A = (D AND (NOT K)) OR (M AND N)
```

The alarm sounds when A = 1.
stimuli.solution: A = 1 for 7 of the 16 input combinations: D = 1, K = 0 (4 combinations) plus M = 1, N = 1 (4 combinations), less the 1 combination counted twice. By De Morgan's laws, the alarm is silent when (NOT D OR K) AND (NOT M OR NOT N).

solution.concept: Powers first, then ÷ and × from left to right, then + and − from left to right

questions.question_text:

solution.concept: 'Of' is worked first; convert the mixed numbers to fractions (1⅔ = 5/3, 3¾ = 15/4)

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2^(x + y) = 64 and 3^(x − y) = 1/9, what is the value of 2x + y?

solution.concept: Write both right sides as powers of the same base and compare exponents: 64 = 2⁶ and 1/9 = 3⁻²
solution.explanation: 2^(x + y) = 2⁶ gives x + y = 6. 3^(x − y) = 3⁻² gives x − y = −2. Adding, 2x = 4, so x = 2 and y = 4. Then 2x + y = 4 + 4 = 8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 drops the minus sign (x − y = 2 gives x = 4, y = 2); 6 is x + y, not 2x + y; 8.5 writes 1/9 as 3⁻¹ (x − y = −1 gives x = 2.5, y = 3.5).

solution.explanation: 6,889 lies between 80² = 6,400 and 90² = 8,100 and ends in 9, so its root is 83 or 87; 83² = 6,889. 19,683 lies between 20³ and 30³ and ends in 3, so its cube root ends in 7: 27³ = 19,683. 83 − 27 = 56.

solution.why_others_wrong: 60 picks 87 as the square root (87² = 7,569); 46 takes the cube root as 37; 110 adds the two roots.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 4ᵃ = 5 and 5ᵇ = 32, what is the value of ab?

solution.concept: Substitute one equation into the other: (4ᵃ)ᵇ = 4^(ab)
solution.explanation: 5ᵇ = 32 and 5 = 4ᵃ, so (4ᵃ)ᵇ = 32, i.e. 4^(ab) = 32. Writing both as powers of 2: 2^(2ab) = 2⁵, so 2ab = 5 and ab = 5/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 treats 4^(ab) as 2^(ab), forgetting that 4 = 2²; 8 divides 32 by 4 as if the exponents were factors; 2/5 inverts the result (it is the value of 1/(ab)).

solution.concept: Rationalise each term: 1/(√k + √(k + 1)) = √(k + 1) − √k, so the sum telescopes
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 forgets to subtract √1; 99 counts the terms instead of adding them; 11 adds √1 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 4, 9, 19, 36, ?

solution.concept: The differences are one more than the perfect squares: 1 + 1, 4 + 1, 9 + 1, 16 + 1, …

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 20x + 99 = 0
II. y² − 25y + 156 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise: find two numbers with the given sum and product
solution.explanation: I: 9 + 11 = 20 and 9 × 11 = 99, so x = 9 or 11. II: 12 + 13 = 25 and 12 × 13 = 156, so y = 12 or 13. The largest x (11) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison: every root of I is smaller than every root of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and decide how x is related to y.
I. x² + 4x − 45 = 0
II. y² − 10y + 25 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Equation II is a perfect square, so it has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: (x + 9)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −9. II: (y − 5)² = 0, so y = 5 only. x = 5 equals y and x = −9 is less than y, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 5 = y; x ≥ y fails for x = −9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the two equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all their roots.
I. 3x² − 8x − 35 = 0
II. 2y² − 13y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.explanation: I: 3x² − 15x + 7x − 35 = (3x + 7)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −7/3. II: 2y² − 7y − 6y + 21 = (2y − 7)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 3.5 or 3. x = 5 is greater than both values of y, but x = −2.33 is smaller than both, so no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y fail for x = −7/3 (a sign slip that reads the root as +7/3 makes them look true); x ≤ y and x < y fail for x = 5.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 5(x − 2) = 2(x + 7)
II. y² − 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation fully before comparing; a shared value makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 5x − 10 = 2x + 14, so 3x = 24 and x = 8. II: (y − 8)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 8 or 9. x = 8 equals one root and is less than the other, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y overlooks that x = 8 equals the root y = 8; x > y reverses the comparison of 8 with 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the linear equation I and the quadratic equation II and state the relation between x and y.
I. x/3 + x/5 = 16
II. y² − 51y + 650 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Clear the fractions in I with the LCM 15
solution.explanation: I: (5x + 3x)/15 = 16, so 8x = 240 and x = 30. II: 25 + 26 = 51 and 25 × 26 = 650, so y = 25 or 26. x = 30 is greater than both, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from clearing the fractions wrongly: 8x = 16 (forgetting to multiply 16 by 15) gives x = 2, below both roots of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains √x (the non-negative square root of x). Find every x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. x − 7√x + 12 = 0
II. y² − 33y + 272 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Treat I as a quadratic in √x: (√x)² − 7√x + 12 = 0
solution.explanation: I: (√x − 3)(√x − 4) = 0, so √x = 3 or 4 and x = 9 or 16. II: 16 + 17 = 33 and 16 × 17 = 272, so y = 16 or 17. x = 16 equals y = 16 and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the shared value 16 (it also follows from stopping at √x = 3, 4 without squaring); x ≥ y fails for x = 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is a cubic. Find all its real roots and the roots of II, then choose the relation between x and y.
I. x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = 0
II. y² − 9y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Try small integers: x = 1 makes the cubic zero, so (x − 1) is a factor
solution.explanation: x = 1 gives 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = (x − 1)(x² − 5x + 6) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3). So x = 1, 2 or 3. II: (y − 4)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 5. The largest x (3) is below the smallest y (4), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison: even the largest root of I (3) is below the smallest root of II (4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has an irrational coefficient (√2 ≈ 1.414). Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all roots.
I. x² + 2√2x − 6 = 0
II. y² − 2y − 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Look for factors of the form (x + a√2)(x − b√2) with ab × 2 = 6 and (a − b)√2 = 2√2
solution.explanation: I: (x + 3√2)(x − √2) = 0, since 3√2 × √2 = 6 and 3√2 − √2 = 2√2. So x = √2 ≈ 1.41 or −3√2 ≈ −4.24. II: (y − 3)(y + 1) = 0, so y = 3 or −1. x = 1.41 is less than 3 but greater than −1, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 1.41, y = −1; x ≥ y fails for x = −4.24; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be added to 7,385 so that the sum is exactly divisible by 12?

solution.concept: Find the remainder on division by 12; the number to add is 12 minus that remainder
solution.explanation: 12 × 615 = 7,380, so 7,385 leaves a remainder of 5. Adding 12 − 5 = 7 gives 7,392 = 12 × 616.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is the remainder, which would have to be subtracted, not added; 3 makes 7,388, divisible by 4 but not by 3 (digit sum 26); 1 makes 7,386, divisible by 3 but not by 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the greatest number that divides 398, 436 and 542 leaving remainders 7, 11 and 15 respectively?

solution.concept: Subtract each remainder first; the required number is the HCF of the results
solution.why_others_wrong: 34 = 2 × 17 does not divide the odd number 425; 51 = 3 × 17 does not divide 425 (digit sum 11); 23 divides 391 but not 425 or 527.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is divided by 12?

solution.concept: From 4! = 24 onwards every factorial is a multiple of 12, so only the first three terms matter
solution.explanation: 4! = 24 and every later factorial contains 24 as a factor, so each leaves remainder 0. The remainder therefore comes from 1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9.
steps: n! is a multiple of 12 for n ≥ 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes every term is a multiple of 12; 3 also drops 3! = 6, which is not a multiple of 12; 1 keeps only 1!.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1¹ + 2² + 3³ + 4⁴ + … + 10¹⁰?

solution.concept: Find the unit digit of each term from the cycle of its last digit, then add the unit digits
solution.explanation: Unit digits: 1¹ → 1, 2² → 4, 3³ → 7, 4⁴ → 6, 5⁵ → 5, 6⁶ → 6, 7⁷ → 3 (cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 7 mod 4 = 3), 8⁸ → 6 (cycle 8, 4, 2, 6; 8 mod 4 = 0), 9⁹ → 9, 10¹⁰ → 0. Sum = 47, so the unit digit is 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 takes the unit digit of 7⁷ as 7 (sum 51); 9 takes the unit digit of 8⁸ as 8 (sum 49); 5 adds the bases 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55, ignoring the powers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest number that divides n⁵ − n exactly for every natural number n?

solution.concept: Factorise n⁵ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1)(n² + 1) and test the smallest case n = 2
solution.explanation: (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 6. By Fermat's little theorem, n⁵ − n is also divisible by 5. So 30 always divides it. For n = 2, n⁵ − n = 30, so no number larger than 30 can always divide it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 and 6 always divide n⁵ − n but are not the largest such number; 60 fails for n = 2, where n⁵ − n = 30.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a number is increased by 15%, it becomes 391. What is the number?

solution.concept: After a 15% increase the number is 115% of the original, so divide by 1.15
solution.why_others_wrong: 332.35 takes 15% off 391 (15% of 391, not of the original); 376 subtracts 15 instead of 15%; 449.65 increases 391 by a further 15%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Amit's monthly salary is ₹36,000. He saves 15% of it and spends 40% of the rest on rent. How much does he pay as rent each month?

solution.concept: The 40% applies to what is left after saving, not to the whole salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,400 takes 40% of the whole salary; ₹18,360 is what remains after rent (60% of 30,600); ₹5,400 is the saving, not the rent.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of 2.5 kg is 375 g?

solution.concept: Convert to the same unit first: 2.5 kg = 2,500 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5% converts 2.5 kg to 25,000 g; 150% converts it to 250 g; 6.67% inverts the ratio (2,500 ÷ 375 = 6.67).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of petrol rises by 10% and then by another 10%. A motorist cuts his consumption so that his spending on petrol rises by only 10% overall. By what percentage did he cut his consumption?

solution.concept: Spending = price × consumption; two 10% rises make the price 1.21 times the original
solution.explanation: Price becomes 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21 times. Spending must be 1.10 times, so consumption = 1.10 ÷ 1.21 = 10/11 of the original. The cut is 1/11 = 9.09%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% simply matches the second 10% price rise; 11% subtracts the 10% target from the 21% price rise and treats the 11-point gap as the cut; 21% cuts consumption by the whole price rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A machine bought for ₹5,00,000 loses 10% of its value every year (on its value at the start of that year). At the end of 2 years it is sold for ₹4,86,000. By what percentage is the sale price above the machine's depreciated value at that time?

solution.why_others_wrong: 21.5% depreciates by a flat 20% of the cost (₹4,00,000) instead of compounding; 8% depreciates for only one year (₹4,50,000); 2.8% compares the sale price with the purchase price (a fall of ₹14,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cricket team won 60% of its first 40 matches. How many of its next 20 matches must it win so that it has won 70% of all its matches?

solution.concept: Work with numbers of wins, not percentages: wins needed = 70% of the 60 matches
solution.explanation: Wins so far = 60% of 40 = 24. For 70% of 60 matches it needs 42 wins, so it must win 42 − 24 = 18 of the next 20.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 wins only 70% of the next 20 matches, which leaves the total at 38/60 = 63.3%; 16 raises the next-20 rate by just 10 points (80%), giving 40/60; 42 is the total number of wins needed, not the further wins.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is first increased by x% and the result is then decreased by x%. The final value is 4% less than the original number. What is x?

solution.concept: An increase of x% followed by a decrease of x% gives a net change of −x²/100 %
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 solves x² = 4, dropping the /100; 4 takes the net loss of 4% to be x itself; 16 squares 4 instead of taking the square root of 400.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A transporter's running cost per trip is 60% fuel, 25% maintenance and 15% insurance. The cost of fuel rises by 20%, maintenance cost falls by 8% and insurance cost rises by 10%. By what percentage does the running cost per trip rise?

solution.concept: Weight each component's change by its share of the total cost
solution.explanation: Take the cost as 100: fuel 60 → 72, maintenance 25 → 23, insurance 15 → 16.5. New cost = 72 + 23 + 16.5 = 111.5, a rise of 11.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22% adds the three changes without weighting them (20 − 8 + 10); 7.33% averages the three changes equally; 12% counts only the fuel component (60% of 20%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An officer's gross salary has three parts: basic pay is 50% of the gross, house rent allowance (HRA) is 40% of the basic pay, and the rest is a special allowance. The basic pay is raised by 10% (HRA stays at 40% of the new basic) and the special allowance is unchanged. By what percentage does the gross salary rise?

solution.concept: Take the gross as 100 and split it into its parts before applying the rise
solution.explanation: Gross 100: basic 50, HRA 40% of 50 = 20, special 30. New basic = 55 and new HRA = 22, special still 30. New gross = 107, a rise of 7%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% assumes the whole gross rises by 10%; 5% raises only the basic and forgets that HRA follows it; 4% counts only the HRA's share of the rise (40% of 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If A : B = 2 : 3, B : C = 4 : 5 and C : D = 6 : 7, what is A : D?

solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 7 takes the first term of the first ratio and the last term of the last; 35 : 16 inverts the answer (D : A); 8 : 15 stops at A : C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x + 4 is the mean proportional between x and x + 10, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: b is the mean proportional between a and c when b² = ac
solution.explanation: (x + 4)² = x(x + 10) gives x² + 8x + 16 = x² + 10x, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check: 12² = 144 = 8 × 18.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 expands (x + 4)² as x² + 16, dropping the 8x (16 = 10x); 2⅔ expands it as x² + 4x + 16 (16 = 6x); 12 is x + 4, the mean proportional itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹5,500 is divided among A, B and C so that, if ₹100, ₹150 and ₹50 are taken away from their shares respectively, the amounts left are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6. What is B's share?

solution.concept: Remove the deductions from the total first; share the rest in the ratio; then add each deduction back
solution.explanation: Total deducted = 100 + 150 + 50 = 300, leaving 5,200 in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6. One part = 5,200 ÷ 13 = 400. B's share = 4 × 400 + 150 = ₹1,750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,600 forgets to add back B's ₹150; ₹1,692.31 divides the whole ₹5,500 in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6; ₹2,450 is C's share (6 × 400 + 50).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In class P the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 2 and in class Q it is 5 : 7. When the two classes are combined, the numbers of boys and girls are equal. What is the ratio of the number of students in P to the number in Q?

solution.concept: Let P have 5a students (3a boys, 2a girls) and Q have 12b (5b boys, 7b girls); equate total boys and girls
solution.explanation: Boys = 3a + 5b and girls = 2a + 7b. Equal totals give a = 2b. So P : Q = 5a : 12b = 10b : 12b = 5 : 6.
solution.shortcut: Alligation on the boys' share: P has 3/5 = 60% boys, Q has 5/12 ≈ 41.7%, target 50%; the gaps 8.3 and 10 give P : Q = 5 : 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 : 5 inverts the answer; 2 : 1 is a : b, the multipliers, not the class sizes; 5 : 12 compares the ratio totals 5 and 12 directly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a mother and her twin sons add up to 55 years. Seven years from now, the mother's age will equal the sum of the twins' ages then. What is the mother's present age?

solution.concept: In 7 years each twin also ages 7 years, so the twins' sum grows by 14
solution.explanation: Let each twin be s years old. In 7 years: M + 7 = 2(s + 7), so M = 2s + 7. Then M + 2s = 4s + 7 = 55, so s = 12 and M = 31.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 years is the twins' present total (2 × 12); 38 years is the mother's age 7 years from now; 12 years is each twin's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years ago, the average age of A and B was 30 years. The average present age of B and C is 40 years. Five years from now, the average age of A and C will be 44 years. What is C's present age?

solution.concept: Convert each average into a present-day sum first: add 5 years per person for the past, subtract for the future
solution.why_others_wrong: 34 years is A's age; 54 years ignores the ±10 adjustments (60 and 88 used as present sums); 49 years is C's age five years from now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi tells his younger cousin Arun: "When I was as old as you are now, you were 6 years old. When you are as old as I am now, I shall be 42." What is Ravi's present age?

solution.concept: The age gap d stays the same: going back d years makes Ravi Arun's age; going forward d years makes Arun Ravi's
solution.explanation: Let the gap be d. d years ago Arun was 6, so Arun = 6 + d. In d years Ravi will be 42, so Ravi = 42 − d. Also Ravi = Arun + d = 6 + 2d. So 42 − d = 6 + 2d, giving d = 12 and Ravi = 30 (Arun = 18).
solution.shortcut: 6, Arun, Ravi, 42 are equally spaced (gap d), so 3d = 42 − 6 = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 years is Arun's age; 24 years takes Ravi's age as the midpoint of 6 and 42 (that is the average of the two ages); 36 years is 42 − 6, three gaps rather than Ravi's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average mark of 40 students in a test is 62. On re-checking, 3 marks are added to the score of each of 30 of these students. What is the new average of the class?

solution.concept: The total rises by 30 × 3 = 90 marks; spread this over all 40 students
solution.explanation: Extra marks = 30 × 3 = 90. The average rises by 90 ÷ 40 = 2.25, so the new average is 62 + 2.25 = 64.25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 adds 3 to the average, as if all 40 students gained 3; 62.75 adds only 30 marks in all; 62.075 adds just 3 marks to the class total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of the first nine of ten numbers is 18. The tenth number is 9 more than the average of all ten numbers. What is the tenth number?

solution.concept: Let the average of all ten be m; write the total in two ways
solution.explanation: Total of ten = 10m. It is also 9 × 18 + x = 162 + x, with x = m + 9. So 10m = 171 + m, giving m = 19 and x = 28.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 adds 9 to the average of the first nine (18) instead of the average of all ten; 19 is the average of all ten; 190 is their total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 12 numbers is 40. Each of the first five numbers is increased by 6 and each of the other seven is decreased by 3. What is the new average?

solution.concept: Find the net change in the total and divide by the count
solution.explanation: Change in total = 5 × 6 − 7 × 3 = 30 − 21 = 9. The average rises by 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75, to 40.75.
solution.why_others_wrong: 43 adds 6 − 3 = 3 to the average, ignoring how many numbers change; 39.25 swaps the signs (−30 + 21); 49 adds the whole net change of 9 to the average without dividing by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a quiz, the scores 10, 20, 30 and 40 were obtained by 3, x, y and 4 participants respectively. There were 20 participants in all and their mean score was 26. What is x?

solution.concept: Two equations: the frequencies add up to 20, and Σ(score × frequency) = 26 × 20
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 is y, the frequency of the score 30; 6.5 splits the 13 missing participants equally; 13 is x + y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Six different three-digit numbers can be formed using each of the digits 2, 5 and 8 exactly once. What is the average of these six numbers?

solution.concept: Each digit appears in each place (hundreds, tens, units) exactly twice among the six numbers
solution.explanation: In each place the digits 2, 5 and 8 appear twice, so the sum of the six numbers is 2 × (2 + 5 + 8) × 111 = 3,330. Average = 3,330 ÷ 6 = 555.
steps: Each digit occurs twice in each place
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,330 is the sum of the six numbers, not their average; 277.5 divides by 6 twice (15 × 111 ÷ 6); 1,665 divides the sum by 2 instead of 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank branch has 10 officers with an average monthly salary of ₹50,000, 40 clerks with an average of ₹24,000 and some sub-staff with an average of ₹15,000. The average salary of all the staff is ₹25,000. How many sub-staff are there?

solution.concept: Compare each group with the overall average: the surplus above ₹25,000 must equal the shortfall below it
solution.explanation: Officers are ₹25,000 above the average: surplus 10 × 25,000 = 2,50,000. Clerks are ₹1,000 below: shortfall 40 × 1,000 = 40,000. Net surplus = 2,10,000, which the sub-staff (₹10,000 below the average each) must offset: 2,10,000 ÷ 10,000 = 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 146 sets the total salary equal to 25,000 × s, forgetting the 50 officers and clerks on the right side; 14 divides the surplus by ₹15,000 (the sub-staff salary) instead of the ₹10,000 shortfall; 42 divides it by ₹5,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer buys a mobile phone for ₹12,500 and pays ₹500 for its transport. At what price must he sell it to make a profit of 20% on his total cost?

solution.concept: Total cost includes transport; the profit percentage is applied to the total cost
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15,000 ignores the transport cost; ₹15,500 adds the transport after taking 20% on the phone alone; ₹2,600 is the profit, not the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tailor's cost for a shirt is ₹300 for cloth and ₹120 for stitching, plus overheads equal to 5% of these two costs. He sells the shirt for ₹529.20. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Full cost = (cloth + stitching) × 1.05; profit % is on this full cost
solution.explanation: Cloth + stitching = ₹420. Overheads = 5% of 420 = ₹21, so the full cost is ₹441. Profit = 529.20 − 441 = 88.20, which is 88.20 ÷ 441 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26% leaves out the overheads (529.20 ÷ 420); 76.4% counts only the cloth as cost; 16.67% takes the profit as a percentage of the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A milk vendor adds 1 litre of water to every 10 litres of milk. His 1-litre measure actually holds only 900 ml. He sells the mixture at the cost price of pure milk per litre. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Find how much pure milk the customer actually gets for the price of 1 litre
solution.explanation: A 'litre' sold is 0.9 litre of mixture, of which 10/11 is milk: 0.9 × 10/11 = 9/11 litre of milk. He is paid for 1 litre, so gain = (1 − 9/11) ÷ 9/11 = 2/9 = 22.22%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% adds the two 10% cheats; 21% compounds 10% and 10% (1.1 × 1.1), but the short measure gives 1/9 more, not 1/10; 11.11% counts only the short measure and ignores the water.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop sells 400 electric irons a week at a profit of ₹50 each. It cuts the price of an iron by ₹10, and weekly sales rise by 50%. What happens to the shop's weekly profit?

solution.concept: Weekly profit = profit per unit × units sold; the price cut comes straight out of the profit per unit
solution.explanation: Before: 400 × 50 = ₹20,000. After: profit per iron = 50 − 10 = ₹40 and sales = 600, so profit = 600 × 40 = ₹24,000. The rise is 4,000 ÷ 20,000 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% subtracts the 20% fall in unit profit from the 50% rise in sales instead of multiplying; 50% counts only the rise in sales; 'falls by 20%' counts only the drop in profit per iron.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An online seller lists a lamp at ₹1,000. The marketplace keeps a commission of 2% of the listed price, and the seller pays ₹40 for shipping each order. If the lamp costs him ₹750, what is his profit percentage on each sale?

solution.concept: Net receipt = listed price − commission − shipping; profit % is on the cost
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% ignores both charges; 30.67% subtracts the commission but forgets the shipping; 28% subtracts the shipping but forgets the commission.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sold an article to B at a loss of 10%. B sold it to C at a profit of x%, and C sold it to D at a profit of x%. D paid 8.9% more than A's cost. What is x?

solution.why_others_wrong: 9.45% adds the percentages (−10 + 2x = 8.9) instead of multiplying the factors; 4.36% ignores A's 10% loss ((1 + x/100)² = 1.089); 21% stops at 1.21 and reads it as a single profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A manufacturer makes 1,000 table lamps. Each lamp costs ₹150 in materials and labour, and the fixed costs for the batch are ₹60,000. He sells 800 lamps at ₹300 each and clears the rest at a single lower price. At what price must the remaining lamps be sold for his overall profit to be 20% of his total cost?

solution.concept: Total cost includes the fixed cost; target revenue = 1.2 × total cost
solution.explanation: Total cost = 1,000 × 150 + 60,000 = ₹2,10,000. Target revenue = 1.2 × 2,10,000 = ₹2,52,000. The 800 lamps bring in ₹2,40,000, so the other 200 must bring ₹12,000: ₹60 each.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹112.50 takes the profit as 20% of revenue (2,10,000 ÷ 0.8); ₹252 is the target revenue per lamp over all 1,000 lamps; ₹15 divides the shortfall of ₹12,000 by 800 instead of 200.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cloth dealer buys cloth X at ₹200 per metre and cloth Y at ₹300 per metre, in the ratio 3 : 2 by length. 10% of X and 5% of Y turn out to be damaged and cannot be sold. He sells all the rest at ₹320 per metre. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Take 3 m of X and 2 m of Y; subtract the damaged lengths before computing revenue
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% ignores the damage (5 m × 320); 28% compares ₹320 with the simple average cost ₹250, ignoring both the 3 : 2 ratio and the damage; 23.33% applies the average damage rate 7.5% to all 5 m.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop gives successive discounts of 25% and 20% on a jacket marked ₹4,000. How much does a customer pay?

solution.concept: Apply the second discount to the already reduced price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,200 adds the discounts (45% off); ₹1,600 is the total discount, not the price paid; ₹3,000 applies only the first discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopping app offers 20% off, subject to a maximum discount of ₹500, and then 5% cashback on the amount paid. What is the effective cost of an item priced at ₹3,000?

solution.concept: 20% of 3,000 = 600 exceeds the cap, so the discount is only ₹500; cashback is on the amount actually paid
solution.explanation: 20% of 3,000 = ₹600, but the cap limits the discount to ₹500, so the buyer pays ₹2,500. Cashback = 5% of 2,500 = ₹125. Effective cost = 2,500 − 125 = ₹2,375.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,280 ignores the cap (2,400 × 0.95); ₹2,500 forgets the cashback; ₹2,400 ignores both the cap and the cashback.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A television marked ₹40,000 is sold at a 12.5% discount. The buyer also hands over his old set, for which the shop allows ₹3,000 off the price; the shop can resell the old set for only ₹1,200. If the new television cost the shop ₹28,000, what is the shop's profit percentage on the deal?

solution.concept: The shop's receipts = cash received + what the old set is really worth to it
solution.explanation: Price after discount = 40,000 × 0.875 = ₹35,000. Cash received = 35,000 − 3,000 = ₹32,000. Adding the old set's real worth, ₹1,200, the shop gets ₹33,200. Profit = 5,200, which is 5,200 ÷ 28,000 = 18.57%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% values the old set at the full ₹3,000 allowed for it (₹35,000 received); 14.29% treats the old set as worthless (₹32,000); 15.66% takes the profit as a percentage of the ₹33,200 received instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Before a sale, a shop raises the marked price of a cooler by 25% and then advertises 'flat 30% off'. Card buyers get a further 10% off the sale price. Selling to a card buyer, the shop still makes a 26% profit on cost. By what percentage above cost was the original marked price?

solution.concept: Chain the factors: card price = original MP × 1.25 × 0.70 × 0.90
solution.explanation: Card price = MP × 1.25 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.7875 MP. This equals 1.26 × cost, so MP = 1.26 ÷ 0.7875 = 1.6 × cost, i.e. 60% above cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48.24% adds and subtracts the percentages (1.25 − 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.85); 100% ignores the 25% price rise (0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63); 44% forgets the card discount (0.875).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the simple interest on ₹6,400 at 7.5% per annum for 2 years 8 months?

solution.concept: Convert the period to years: 2 years 8 months = 2 8/12 = 8/3 years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,344 reads 2 years 8 months as 2.8 years; ₹960 counts only the 2 whole years; ₹7,680 is the amount (principal + interest), not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi deposits ₹2,000 at the start of every month for 12 months in a recurring deposit that pays 6% per annum simple interest. How much interest has he earned at the end of the 12th month?

solution.concept: The first deposit earns interest for 12 months, the second for 11, …, the last for 1 month
solution.explanation: Interest on ₹2,000 for one month = 2,000 × 6% ÷ 12 = ₹10. The deposits earn for 12 + 11 + … + 1 = 78 months in all, so the interest = 78 × 10 = ₹780.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,440 gives every deposit a full year of interest; ₹720 gives each deposit 6 months on average instead of 6.5; ₹660 counts the first deposit for only 11 months (11 + 10 + … + 1 = 66).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum doubles itself in 10 years at simple interest. After the first 5 years the rate is raised to 12% per annum. In how many years in all will the sum become three times itself?

solution.concept: Doubling in 10 years means 100% interest in 10 years, i.e. 10% a year; tripling needs 200% interest
solution.explanation: Rate = 100% ÷ 10 = 10%. In the first 5 years the interest is 50% of the sum. The remaining 150% at 12% a year takes 150 ÷ 12 = 12.5 years. Total = 5 + 12.5 = 17.5 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 years keeps the rate at 10% throughout; 12.5 years gives only the second phase; 16⅔ years applies 12% from the start (200 ÷ 12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹5,000 for 1½ years at 20% per annum, compounded annually? (For the last half year, interest is at half the annual rate on the amount then due.)

solution.concept: Compound for the full year, then add 10% (half of 20%) for the half year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,655 compounds half-yearly for 3 periods (5,000 × 1.1³ − 5,000); ₹1,500 is simple interest for 1½ years; ₹1,000 stops after the first year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On the same sum, what is the ratio of the compound interest (compounded annually) to the simple interest for 2 years at 10% per annum?

solution.concept: For 2 years, CI = P(1.1² − 1) = 0.21P and SI = 0.20P
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 : 10 compares one year's growth factor 1.1 with 1; 1 : 1 forgets the interest on interest in year 2; 121 : 100 compares the CI amount with the principal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹20,000 is invested at compound interest, compounded annually, at 5% for the first year, 10% for the second year and 20% for the third year. What is the compound interest for the three years?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,000 adds the rates as simple interest (35%); ₹27,720 is the amount, not the interest; ₹7,100 compounds the first two years but takes the 20% on the original ₹20,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much must be invested now at 10% per annum compound interest (compounded annually) so that ₹13,310 can be withdrawn at the end of 3 years and a further ₹14,641 at the end of 4 years, leaving nothing?

solution.concept: The investment equals the sum of the present values of the two withdrawals
solution.explanation: Present value of 13,310 due in 3 years = 13,310 ÷ 1.1³ = ₹10,000. Present value of 14,641 due in 4 years = 14,641 ÷ 1.1⁴ = ₹10,000. Investment = ₹20,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,000 discounts the second withdrawal for only 3 years (14,641 ÷ 1.331 = 11,000); ₹10,000 covers only one withdrawal; ₹27,951 adds the withdrawals without discounting.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest for the same period and share the profit in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. A invested ₹45,000. What was the total capital of the three partners?

solution.concept: For the same period, profits are in the ratio of capitals, so one part = 45,000 ÷ 3
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 is B's capital; ₹75,000 is C's capital; ₹1,35,000 multiplies A's capital by 3 instead of dividing by 3 and multiplying by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹60,000 and ₹40,000 in a firm for a year. B also lends ₹20,000 to the firm at 10% per annum interest, which is paid before the profit is shared. The year's profit before this interest is ₹32,000, and the rest is shared in the ratio of capitals. How much does B receive in all?

solution.concept: Pay the loan interest first; only the remainder is shared in the ratio 3 : 2; B gets both
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,800 shares the whole ₹32,000 and ignores the loan; ₹16,000 treats the loan as capital (60 : 60); ₹12,000 forgets to add the interest B earns on his loan.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest ₹1,50,000, ₹90,000 and ₹60,000 in a firm. B manages it and first takes 10% of the profit as a management fee. Of the remaining profit, one-third is shared equally among the three and the rest in the ratio of their capitals. Out of a profit of ₹1,20,000, how much does B receive in all?

solution.concept: Fee first; then split the remainder into an equal part and a capital-ratio part (capitals 5 : 3 : 2)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹44,400 shares all of the ₹1,08,000 in the ratio of capitals, ignoring the equal one-third; ₹36,000 gives B 30% of the whole profit with no fee and no equal part; ₹33,600 leaves out B's ₹12,000 from the equal part.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of water must be added to 15 litres of a 12% salt solution to make it a 9% salt solution?

solution.concept: The amount of salt does not change when water is added
solution.explanation: Salt = 12% of 15 = 1.8 litres. In the new solution 1.8 litres must be 9%, so the total is 1.8 ÷ 0.09 = 20 litres. Water to add = 20 − 15 = 5 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres is the new total volume, not the water added; 3.75 litres takes the 3-point drop as a fraction of 12 (15 × 3/12); 1.8 litres is the amount of salt.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A farm store has two fertilisers: type X contains 40% nitrogen and type Y contains 16% nitrogen. In what ratio must X and Y be mixed to get a fertiliser with 25% nitrogen?

solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 3 puts the differences the wrong way round; 3 : 8 compares 9 with 40 − 16 = 24, the whole gap; 5 : 2 is just the ratio of the two strengths, 40 : 16.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 10 litres of a 30% acid solution, 15 litres of a 20% acid solution and 25 litres of a 10% acid solution are mixed. What is the acid concentration of the mixture?

solution.explanation: Acid = 3 + 3 + 2.5 = 8.5 litres in 50 litres, so the concentration is 8.5 ÷ 50 = 17%.
