questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Hiral was born on the only date that occurs in leap years alone, so she celebrates on that date in 2028. Her brother Inder's birthday in 2028 is exactly 100 days after Hiral's birthday. 1 January 2028 is a Saturday.

On which date and day of the week is Inder's birthday in 2028?

solution.concept: Count days across months; use the leap day
solution.explanation: Hiral's birthday is 29 February. 1 January is a Saturday and 29 February is the 60th day of the year; 59 days later is 59 = 8 × 7 + 3 weekdays on: Saturday + 3 = Tuesday. Adding 100 days: March has 31 (to 31 March: 31 days), April 30 (61), May 31 (92), and 8 more days give 8 June. 100 = 14 × 7 + 2, so the weekday is Tuesday + 2 = Thursday.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 June miscounts the days by one; 8 June, Wednesday takes 100 days as 14 weeks + 1; 9 June, Friday starts counting from 1 March.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six volunteers Arnav, Bulbul, Chandan, Damini, Eklavya and Falguni each run a weekend camp in a different month from January to June 2026. 1 January 2026 is a Thursday, and 2026 is not a leap year.
- Bulbul's month has five Saturdays but only four Sundays.
- Damini's month has five Saturdays and five Sundays.
- Chandan's month has five Sundays.
- Falguni's month begins on the same day of the week as Chandan's month.
- Arnav's month comes after Eklavya's month.

Whose month begins on a Wednesday?

solution.concept: A month has five of a weekday only for the weekdays of its first (days − 28) days
solution.explanation: 1sts of 2026: Jan Thu, Feb Sun, Mar Sun, Apr Wed, May Fri, Jun Mon. A 31-day month has five each of its first three weekdays, a 30-day month of its first two, and February only four of each. January (Thu, Fri, Sat): five Saturdays, four Sundays — Bulbul. May (Fri, Sat, Sun): five Saturdays and Sundays — Damini. March (Sun, Mon, Tue): five Sundays — Chandan. Falguni's month begins on a Sunday like March: February. April and June remain, Eklavya earlier: Eklavya April, Arnav June. April begins on a Wednesday: Eklavya.
steps: 1sts: Jan Thu, Feb Sun, Mar Sun, Apr Wed, May Fri, Jun Mon
Five-of-a-kind days: Jan Thu–Sat, Mar Sun–Tue, Apr Wed–Thu, May Fri–Sun, Jun Mon–Tue
Bulbul Jan, Damini May, Chandan Mar, Falguni Feb
Eklavya Apr, Arnav Jun ⇒ Wednesday start: Eklavya
solution.why_others_wrong: Arnav's June begins on a Monday; Falguni's February and Chandan's March both begin on a Sunday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six participants Nandini, Omesh, Pari, Qamar, Riya and Sahil took a quiz and got different scores (whole numbers).
- Exactly two participants scored more than Pari, who scored 47.
- Omesh scored 6 more than Riya and 4 less than Nandini.
- Qamar had the lowest score, 31, and the average of Qamar's and Riya's scores is 35.5.
- The highest score was 55, and Sahil scored more than Nandini.

Who has the fourth highest score?

solution.concept: Fix the values from the numeric clues, then rank
solution.explanation: Qamar 31 and Riya + Qamar = 71 give Riya 40, so Omesh 46 and Nandini 50. Sahil beats Nandini and the top score is 55, so Sahil 55 (no one else can reach 55). Pari 47 with exactly Sahil and Nandini above her. Order: Sahil 55, Nandini 50, Pari 47, Omesh 46, Riya 40, Qamar 31. Fourth: Omesh.
steps: Order: Sahil, Nandini, Pari, Omesh, Riya, Qamar ⇒ fourth Omesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Pari is third, Riya fifth and Nandini second.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Jyoti is the only daughter of Kamal. Kamal's father is Lakhan, and Lakhan's wife is Mira. How is Jyoti related to Mira?

solution.concept: A son's daughter is a granddaughter
solution.explanation: Mira is Lakhan's wife, so she is Kamal's mother. Jyoti is Kamal's daughter, so she is Mira's granddaughter.
solution.why_others_wrong: Daughter skips a generation; Niece would need Jyoti's parent to be Mira's sibling; Daughter-in-law would need Jyoti to be married to Mira's son.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Check whether every gender needed is given
solution.explanation: A is B's child and B is C's husband, so C is A's mother. C is D's sister, so D is a sibling of A's mother. D's gender is not given, so D may be A's maternal uncle or maternal aunt: the exact relation cannot be determined.
steps: A # B, B @ C ⇒ C is A's mother
C $ D ⇒ D is a sibling of A's mother
D's gender unknown ⇒ uncle or aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Uncle and Aunt each assume a gender the code never states; a cousin would be a child of D.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ojas and Pallavi are a married couple with exactly two children, Qadir and Radha. Qadir is unmarried. Sameer is Qadir's only brother-in-law. How is Sameer related to Pallavi?

solution.concept: An unmarried man's brother-in-law is his sister's husband
solution.explanation: Qadir is unmarried, so his brother-in-law can only be the husband of his sister. His only sibling is Radha, so Sameer is Radha's husband. The husband of Pallavi's daughter is Pallavi's son-in-law.
solution.why_others_wrong: Pallavi's only son is Qadir; Sameer is not the child of Pallavi's sibling; he is Qadir's brother-in-law, not Pallavi's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ruchi is the daughter-in-law of Lata, who has only one son. Nandita is Lata's only daughter. Om is the son-in-law of Lata's husband, and Parth is the son of Om and Nandita. Ishaan is Ruchi's son. Every person mentioned has only one spouse. How is Parth related to Ruchi?

solution.concept: Find both couples, then link through Lata's children
solution.explanation: Ruchi is the wife of Lata's only son. Om, the son-in-law of Lata's husband, is the husband of Lata's only daughter Nandita. Parth is Nandita's son, i.e. the son of Ruchi's husband's sister: Ruchi's nephew (and Ishaan's cousin).
steps: Ruchi = wife of Lata's only son
Nandita = Lata's only daughter = sister of Ruchi's husband
solution.why_others_wrong: Ruchi's son is Ishaan; Parth is Ishaan's cousin, not Ruchi's; he is a generation below Ruchi, so not her brother-in-law.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between benches A and C, and in which direction is C from A?

solution.explanation: C is 20 m east and 15 m north of A: √(400 + 225) = 25 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '25 m, North-West' mixes up east and west; '25 m, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '35 m, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is bench E with respect to bench B?

solution.explanation: E (10, 0) − B (0, 15) = (10, −15): east and south, so E is south-east of B.
solution.why_others_wrong: North-West is B's direction from E; South-West takes E as west of A; East ignores the 15 m north–south gap.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which bench is nearest to bench A?

solution.explanation: Distances from A: B 15 m, C 25 m, D 20 m, E 10 m. E is nearest.
solution.why_others_wrong: B is 15 m, D 20 m and C 25 m from A.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One evening before sunset, Arjun walked straight towards his own shadow. In which direction was he walking?

solution.concept: Evening sun is in the west
solution.explanation: Before sunset the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Walking towards his shadow, Arjun was walking east.
steps: Shadow points away from the sun ⇒ east
solution.why_others_wrong: West is towards the sun; North and South are at right angles to the shadow.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pooja walks 9 km towards the south, then turns left and walks 12 km. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.explanation: Facing south, a left turn makes her face east. She ends 12 km east and 9 km south of the start: √(144 + 81) = 15 km, south-east.
steps: Turn left from south ⇒ east: 12 km → (12, -9)
solution.why_others_wrong: '15 km, South-West' mixes up east and west; '15 km, North-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '21 km, South-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Where is the robot, with respect to O, at the end of the program 'F6 R F8 L F4 B F2'?

solution.concept: Equal east and north parts give a diagonal
solution.explanation: North 6 → (0, 6); right ⇒ east 8 → (8, 6); left ⇒ north 4 → (8, 10); about turn ⇒ south 2 → (8, 8). It is 8 m east and 8 m north of O: 8√2 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '8√2 m, North-West' mixes up east and west; '8√2 m, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '16 m, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which direction is the robot facing at the end of the program 'F4 L F7 B F3 R R F2'?

solution.concept: Only the turns change the facing
solution.explanation: Facing: north → L ⇒ west → B ⇒ east → R ⇒ south → R ⇒ west. The moves do not change the facing, so it ends facing west.
solution.why_others_wrong: East is the facing before the last two right turns; South is after only one of them; North ignores the about-turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: The program 'F10 R F6 R F10 R' is to be completed with one more step so that the robot ends exactly at O. Which step should be added?

solution.concept: Find the position and the facing first
solution.explanation: North 10 → (0, 10); right ⇒ east 6 → (6, 10); right ⇒ south 10 → (6, 0); right ⇒ facing west. O is 6 m to its west, so 'F6' brings it back.
solution.why_others_wrong: F10 overshoots by 4 m; 'B F6' moves it east, away from O; 'L F6' moves it south.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between P and R, and in which direction is R from P?

solution.explanation: Q is 4 m east and 4 m north of P; R is 7 m south of Q, so R = (4, −3): 4 m east and 3 m south of P, 5 m away, south-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '5 m, South-West' mixes up east and west; '5 m, North-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '7 m, South-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which point lies exactly midway between R and S?

solution.explanation: R (4, −3) and S (−4, −3) are on the same east–west line; their midpoint is (0, −3), which is V (3 m south of P).
steps: Midpoint of R and S = (0, −3) = V
solution.why_others_wrong: P is 3 m north of that midpoint, U 5 m north, and T is far to the west.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is T with respect to Q?

solution.explanation: T (−4, 6) − Q (4, 4) = (−8, 2): 8 m west and 2 m north, so T is north-west of Q.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West misreads T as below Q; South-East is the direction of Q from T; West ignores the 2 m north component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the shortest distance between U and V, and in which direction is U from V?

solution.explanation: U = T + (4, −4) = (0, 2), so U is 2 m north of P; V is 3 m south of P. Both lie on the north–south line through P, and U is 2 + 3 = 5 m north of V.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m, South is V's direction from U; 4√2 m treats U as a diagonal step from V; 9 m adds T's north step instead of U's position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Just before sunset, Ravi stood facing his own shadow. He then turned 135° clockwise and walked 6√2 m, and then turned 135° anticlockwise and walked 14 m. How far is he now from where he stood, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Fix the first facing from the shadow
solution.explanation: Before sunset the sun is in the west and the shadow points east, so Ravi faced east. 135° clockwise from east is south-west: 6√2 m moves him 6 m west and 6 m south → (−6, −6). 135° anticlockwise from south-west is east: 14 m → (8, −6). He is 8 m east and 6 m south of the start: 10 m, south-east.
steps: Facing the shadow at sunset ⇒ facing east
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 m, South-West' mixes up east and west; '10 m, North-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '14 m, South-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Town X is 30 km east of town Y. Town Z is due north of X and is 50 km from Y in a straight line. A car drives from Z straight towards Y and stops exactly halfway, at W. How far is W from X, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Find Z first, then the midpoint
solution.explanation: Z is north of X with YZ = 50 and YX = 30, so XZ = √(50² − 30²) = 40 km: Z = (30, 40) with Y at (0, 0). The midpoint W of ZY is (15, 20). From X (30, 0), W is 15 km west and 20 km north: √(225 + 400) = 25 km, north-west.
steps: W = midpoint of Z and Y = (15, 20)
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East forgets that W is west of X; 20 km is only the north part; 35 km adds the two parts.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PLANET is written as PAELNT. How is GARDEN written in that code?

solution.concept: Odd places first, then even places
solution.explanation: PLANET: the letters in the 1st, 3rd and 5th places (P, A, E) are written first, followed by those in the 2nd, 4th and 6th places (L, N, T): PAELNT. GARDEN: G, R, E then A, D, N = GREADN.
steps: Odd places: P A E; even places: L N T
GARDEN ⇒ G R E + A D N
solution.why_others_wrong: GAREDN only swaps two middle letters; NEDRAG reverses the word; AGDRNE swaps neighbouring letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BED is written as 40 and DOG is written as 420. How is HEN written in that code?

solution.why_others_wrong: 27 adds the positions; 112 multiplies only the first and last letters; 520 takes N as 13.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'SPRINT'?

solution.explanation: SPRINT has one vowel (I), so only I is coded as ◎; the rest follow the table: S ©, P $, R 8, N 7, T 5 ⇒ ©$8◎75.
steps: S © P $ R 8 I ◎ N 7 T 5
solution.why_others_wrong: ©$8175 ignores the condition; 5$8◎7© also swaps the end codes (condition (ii)); ©$8◇75 uses the symbol of condition (iii).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'MANGO'?

solution.explanation: MANGO has two vowels (A, O), so the codes of the first and last letters are interchanged: table codes @ 6 7 % 2 become 2 6 7 % @.
solution.why_others_wrong: @67%2 ignores the condition; @◎7%◎ applies condition (i); 2@7%6 swaps the wrong codes.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'TOMATO'?

solution.explanation: TOMATO has three vowels (O, A, O). Each consonant followed by a vowel — T, M and T — becomes ◇; the vowels keep their codes (O 2, A 6): ◇2◇6◇2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52@652 ignores the condition; ◇2◇6◇◇ wrongly changes the last vowel; 256@25 reverses the plain code.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words is coded as '◇1◇★◇9'?

solution.explanation: MINUTE (3 vowels): M, N and T are each followed by a vowel ⇒ ◇1◇★◇9. MINUET → ◇1◇★95, MANURE → ◇6◇★◇9, IMPUTE → 1@◇★◇9.
steps: All four words have three vowels ⇒ condition (iii)
solution.why_others_wrong: MINUET ends in T after a vowel, MANURE has A (6) as its 2nd letter, and IMPUTE starts with the vowel I.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'BOARD'?

solution.explanation: BOARD has two vowels (O, A), so the first and last codes are interchanged: table codes # 2 6 8 3 become 3 2 6 8 #.
solution.why_others_wrong: #2683 ignores the condition; #◎◎83 applies condition (i) to both vowels; 3◇683 mixes in condition (iii).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is 'WHITE' written in this code?

solution.explanation: W is in row 5, column 3 (53); H row 3, column 2 (32); I 33; T row 2, column 1 (21); E row 1, column 5 (15).
solution.why_others_wrong: 35 23 33 12 51 reads column before row; the third option reverses only E; the fourth swaps H and I.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is written as '22 42 12 24' in this code?

solution.explanation: 22 = row 2, column 2 = B; 42 = O; 12 = L; 24 = D: BOLD.
solution.why_others_wrong: BALD would be 22 13 12 24, BOND 22 42 14 24 and BOLT 22 42 12 21.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the digits in the code for 'GRAPE'?

solution.concept: Code first, then add the digits
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 drops a digit of R's code; 26 takes A as 33; 29 takes E as 55.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BANKER is written as BCLOSF and TICKET is written as JULDUF. How is MIRROR written in that code?

solution.explanation: BANKER → swap each pair: AB KN RE → each letter one place forward: BC LO SF. TICKET → IT KC TE → JU LD UF. MIRROR → IM RR RO → JN SS SP.
steps: Swap pairs: MI RR OR → IM RR RO
solution.why_others_wrong: NJSSPS shifts without swapping; HLQQQN moves the letters back; JNSSSQ shifts the last letter twice.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PLANET is written as LH1J2P and CABIN is written as Y1X3J. How is MOUSE written in that code?

solution.concept: Vowels and consonants follow different rules
solution.explanation: Consonants move 4 places back (P→L, L→H, N→J, T→P; C→Y, B→X, N→J). Vowels become their place among the vowels A 1, E 2, I 3, O 4, U 5 (A→1, E→2; A→1, I→3). MOUSE: M→I, O→4, U→5, S→O, E→2 = I45O2.
steps: Vowels: A1 E2 I3 O4 U5
M I, O 4, U 5, S O, E 2
solution.why_others_wrong: I1521O5 uses alphabetical positions for the vowels; I54O2 swaps O and U; Q45W2 moves the consonants forward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which term should replace the question mark in the series?

1A, 4D, 9I, 16P, ?

solution.concept: Squares and the letters at those places
solution.explanation: The numbers are 1², 2², 3², 4², so the next is 5² = 25. Each letter is the letter at that place in the alphabet (A 1, D 4, I 9, P 16), so the 25th letter Y goes with 25: 25Y.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25X takes the 24th letter; 24Y breaks the square pattern; 36Y skips a square.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which letter is 6th to the left of the 10th letter from the right end of the English alphabet?

solution.explanation: The 10th letter from the right is the 26 − 10 + 1 = 17th from the left, Q. Six places to its left is the 11th letter: K.
solution.why_others_wrong: J and L are one place off; W is 6 places to the right of Q.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters of the English alphabet are there between the letter that is 4th to the right of H and the letter that is 3rd to the left of W?

solution.explanation: 4th to the right of H (8) is the 12th letter, L. 3rd to the left of W (23) is the 20th letter, T. Between L and T lie M, N, O, P, Q, R, S: 20 − 12 − 1 = 7 letters.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 is the difference of the positions; 6 subtracts one too many; 9 counts both end letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words CANNOT be formed using the letters of the word 'PERSONALITY', each letter used no more often than it appears in PERSONALITY?

solution.explanation: PERSONALITY has eleven different letters, each only once: P, E, R, S, O, N, A, L, I, T, Y. TERRAIN needs two R's, so it cannot be formed. PAINTER, SENATOR and PLASTER use each of their letters only once, and all of them are available.
steps: Each letter of PERSONALITY occurs once
solution.why_others_wrong: PAINTER, SENATOR and PLASTER can all be formed.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Count the letter pairs in 'HOSTEL' whose gap in the word (the number of letters between them) equals their gap in the English alphabet, in either direction. How many such pairs are there?

solution.concept: Compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet
solution.explanation: Pairs found: ST — 1 in all.
steps: Alphabet positions: H 8, O 15, S 19, T 20, E 5, L 12
A pair qualifies when |word gap| = |alphabet gap|

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the words RELIABLE, RELATION, RELEASE and RELIEF are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary, which word will be third?

solution.concept: Compare the first letter that differs
solution.explanation: All begin with REL. The 4th letters are A (RELATION), E (RELEASE) and I (RELIABLE, RELIEF). Between RELIABLE and RELIEF the 5th letters are A and E, so RELIABLE comes first. Order: RELATION, RELEASE, RELIABLE, RELIEF.
solution.why_others_wrong: RELATION is first, RELEASE second and RELIEF fourth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the new arrangement, which letter is 8th to the right of the 12th letter from the left end?

solution.concept: Count in the new arrangement, not the usual alphabet
solution.explanation: The 12th letter is Y. Eight places to its right is the 20th letter of the new arrangement: G.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the new arrangement, how many letters are there between G and S?

solution.explanation: S is 6th and G is 20th in the new arrangement; letters between them: 20 − 6 − 1 = 13.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 counts the gap in the usual alphabet (S − G − 1); 12 and 14 miscount by one at an end.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the new arrangement, which letter lies exactly midway between Q and C?

solution.concept: Midway = average of the two new positions
solution.explanation: Q is 4th and C is 24th; (4 + 24) ÷ 2 = 14th: M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every 4th letter of the new arrangement (the 4th, 8th, 12th, … letters) is removed, which letter will be 10th from the right end of what remains?

solution.explanation: Removed: Q, U, Y, K, G, C. Remaining (20 letters): N O P R S T V W X Z M L J I H F E D B A. The 10th from the right is M.
steps: Remaining: N O P R S T V W X Z M L J I H F E D B A

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In how many of the numbers is the sum of the first and the last digits equal to the middle digit?

steps: Check first + last = middle for each

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the digits within each number are arranged in descending order, and the new numbers are then arranged in ascending order, which original number will be in the middle?

solution.why_others_wrong: 473 gives 743 (2nd), 852 stays 852 (4th) and 619 gives 961 (5th).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the difference between the product of the digits of the largest number and the product of the digits of the smallest number?

solution.concept: Find the extremes, then multiply digits
solution.explanation: Largest 852: 8 × 5 × 2 = 80. Smallest 352: 3 × 5 × 2 = 30. Difference 80 − 30 = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 and 80 are the two products themselves; 54 uses 473 (84) instead of 852.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the result of Row 2?

solution.concept: Check the rules in order for each step
solution.explanation: 7 is prime, so rule (ii): 7 + 2 × 6 = 19. 19 is also prime, so rule (ii) again: 19 + 2 × 4 = 27.
solution.why_others_wrong: 19 stops after the first step; 23 adds 4 instead of 8; 15 applies rule (iii) to 19.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the sum of the results of Row 1 and Row 3?

solution.why_others_wrong: 35 adds only the first-step values (20 + 15); 50 adds Rows 1 and 2; 51 adds Rows 2 and 3.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the 6 in Row 2 is replaced by 9, what will be the result of Row 2?

solution.concept: A new first-step result can change which rule applies next
solution.explanation: 7 is prime: 7 + 2 × 9 = 25. Now 25 is a perfect square, so rule (i) applies: √25 × 4 = 20.
solution.why_others_wrong: 29 adds 4 to 25 (rule iii) and 33 adds 2 × 4 (rule ii), both ignoring that 25 is a square; 100 multiplies 25 by 4 without taking the square root.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is Step II?

solution.concept: Odd numbers are arranged before even numbers
solution.why_others_wrong: The first two wrong lines are Steps I and III; the last puts all the numbers in plain ascending order.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: The machine stops once the seven numbers stand in their final order. How many steps does it need for this input?

solution.concept: Stop when the line is final
solution.explanation: Step I: 17 42 68 33 91 24 55. Step II: 17 33 42 68 91 24 55. Step III: 17 33 55 42 68 91 24. Step IV: 17 33 55 91 42 68 24. Step V: 17 33 55 91 24 42 68. After Step V, 42 and 68 are already in their places, so no further step is needed.

questions.question_text: In Step III, which number is 4th from the right end?

solution.explanation: Step III: 17 33 55 42 68 91 24. The 4th from the right is 42.

questions.question_text: In which step does 91 first stand immediately to the right of 55?

solution.concept: Track two numbers through the steps

questions.question_text: In the last step, what is the position of 24 from the left end?

solution.explanation: Last step: 17 33 55 91 24 42 68. There are four odd numbers, so 24 is 5th from the left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A word machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word whose first letter comes latest in the alphabet, replaces that first letter by the letter just before it in the alphabet (for example, 'nest' becomes 'mest'), and places the new word immediately to the right of the words already arranged at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other words keep their order.

Input: tide hall rope moss vane cork

Which of the following is Step IV?

options.text: uane side qope hall moss cork
vane tide rope moss hall cork
uane side qope loss hall cork
uane side qope loss gall cork

solution.concept: Selection by the first letter, then a one-letter change
solution.explanation: Step I: uane tide hall rope moss cork. Step II: uane side hall rope moss cork. Step III: uane side qope hall moss cork. Step IV: uane side qope loss hall cork.
steps: Step I: uane tide hall rope moss cork
Step II: uane side hall rope moss cork
Step III: uane side qope hall moss cork
Step IV: uane side qope loss hall cork
solution.why_others_wrong: The first two wrong lines are Steps III and V; the last forgets to change the first letters.
solution.final_answer: Option C: uane side qope loss hall cork

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is Step III?

steps: Step I: violet 28 73 coral 46 indigo olive 59 amber 20
Step II: violet 73 46 indigo olive 59 coral 33 amber 20
Step III: violet 73 olive 59 indigo 52 coral 33 amber 20

questions.question_text: In Step II, which element is 3rd to the left of 'amber'?

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the numbers in the last step?

steps: Last step: violet 79 olive 64 indigo 52 coral 33 amber 20

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following is Step II?

solution.concept: Select by the middle digit, then swap the end digits
solution.why_others_wrong: The first two wrong lines are Steps I and III; the last forgets to interchange the digits.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In Step IV, what is the difference between the 2nd number from the left and the 2nd number from the right?

solution.explanation: Step IV: 916 137 452 569 482 873. 2nd from the left = 137, 2nd from the right = 482; difference = 345.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the last step, how many of the six three-digit numbers are odd?

solution.concept: Swapping the end digits can change a number from odd to even
solution.explanation: Last step: 916 137 452 569 378 284. Only 137 and 569 are odd, so there are two odd numbers (the input had four).
solution.why_others_wrong: Four counts the odd numbers of the input; Three and One miscount the new numbers.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: How much money does Asha have?

I. Asha and Bela together have ₹500.
II. Asha has ₹100 more than Bela.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Two unknowns need two independent facts
solution.explanation: I alone allows many splits of ₹500, and II alone gives only the difference. Together: A + B = 500 and A − B = 100, so A = ₹300.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'alone' option relies on one equation in two unknowns; 'together not sufficient' ignores that the two equations fix A.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Is the whole number x even?

I. x + 3 is odd.
II. 5x is even.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.explanation: I: odd − 3 is even, so x is even — sufficient. II: 5 is odd, so 5x is even only when x is even — sufficient. Each statement alone answers 'yes'.
steps: II: odd × x even ⇒ x even
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'alone' option overlooks that the other statement also settles the question; 'both together necessary' needs both when one is enough.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: In a certain code, every letter of a word is replaced by the letter a fixed number of places after it in the alphabet (the same number for every letter, counting on from A after Z). What is the code for 'MAP'?

I. The fixed number of places is an odd number less than 6.
II. 'GO' is written as 'JR'.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: A shift code is fixed once the shift is known
solution.explanation: I allows a shift of 1, 3 or 5 — not sufficient. II: G → J and O → R are shifts of 3, so 'MAP' is 'PDS' — sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' trusts a statement that leaves three shifts; the 'together' options ignore that II alone fixes the shift.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: How many years older than Chetan is Amit?

I. Amit is 6 years older than Bhanu.
II. Chetan is younger than Bhanu.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: An inequality cannot fix a difference
solution.explanation: I gives Amit − Bhanu = 6. II says only that Chetan is younger than Bhanu, not by how much. So Amit − Chetan is more than 6, but could be 7, 8, 9, … — not fixed even with both statements.
steps: Together: A − C > 6 but not fixed ⇒ not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: The 'alone' options use one statement; 'both together necessary' treats 'younger' as if it gave the size of the gap.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statements I and II together are not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Five persons J, K, L, M and N stand in a queue, one behind another. Who stands at the back of the queue?

I. K is third from the front, and J stands immediately behind K.
II. M stands somewhere in front of L, and N stands somewhere in front of M.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Fill the free places using the order
solution.explanation: I leaves places 1, 2 and 5 for L, M and N in any order — not sufficient. II gives N before M before L, but not their places — not sufficient. Together, N, M and L take places 1, 2 and 5 in that order, so L is at the back.
steps: II: N ahead of M ahead of L
solution.why_others_wrong: Each statement alone leaves more than one person for the last place; 'together not sufficient' ignores that the order fills the three free places uniquely.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Five subjects — Maths, Physics, Chemistry, Biology and English — are taught in five periods (1 to 5) on Monday, one subject per period. Which subject is taught in period 4?

I. Biology is taught in period 2, and Physics is taught in the period immediately after Maths.
II. Chemistry, Biology and English are taught in periods 1, 2 and 3 in some order, and Physics is taught in the period immediately after Maths.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.explanation: I: with Biology in period 2, Maths and Physics can be in periods 3–4 or 4–5, so period 4 has Physics or Maths — not sufficient. II: periods 4 and 5 are left for Maths and Physics, and Physics comes right after Maths, so Maths is in period 4 — sufficient.
steps: I: Maths–Physics in 3–4 or 4–5 ⇒ not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' trusts a statement that leaves two subjects for period 4; the 'together' options ignore that II alone is enough.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Ravi's roll number is a two-digit number. What is it?

I. It is a prime number, its digits add up to 10, and its tens digit is greater than its units digit.
II. Its units digit is 3.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: List the numbers each statement allows
solution.explanation: I: the two-digit numbers whose digits add up to 10 and whose tens digit is larger are 64, 73, 82 and 91; of these only 73 is prime — sufficient. II allows 13, 23, …, 93 — not sufficient.
steps: II: nine numbers end in 3 ⇒ not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'II alone' trusts a statement that allows nine numbers; the 'together' options add a statement that is not needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: In a class with no tied ranks, how many students rank between Gauri and Hema?

I. Gauri is 8th from the top, and Hema is 15th from the top.
II. There are 40 students in the class, and Hema is 26th from the bottom.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Ranks between two persons need both ranks from the same end
solution.explanation: I: 15 − 8 − 1 = 6 students rank between them — sufficient. II gives only Hema's rank (15th from the top) and nothing about Gauri — not sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'II alone' trusts a statement that never mentions Gauri; the 'together' options add a statement that is not needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: What is the weight of box R?

I. Boxes P and Q together weigh 30 kg, and boxes P, Q and R together weigh 48 kg.
II. Box Q weighs 12 kg, and box R weighs 6 kg more than box Q.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.explanation: I: R = 48 − 30 = 18 kg — sufficient. II: R = 12 + 6 = 18 kg — sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'alone' option ignores that the other statement also gives R; 'both together necessary' needs both when either works.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Is A greater than D?

I. A ≥ B.
II. B > C.
III. C ≥ D.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
Even all three statements together are not sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

solution.explanation: All three give A ≥ B > C ≥ D, so A > D: 'yes'. Any two statements leave a gap in the chain: I + II says nothing about D, II + III says nothing about A, and I + III does not connect B with C. So all three are needed.
steps: I + II + III: A ≥ B > C ≥ D ⇒ A > D
Any pair leaves A or D unconnected
solution.why_others_wrong: Each pair misses one link of the chain, and with all three the answer is fixed, so 'not sufficient' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: What is the value of x + y?

I. x − y = 4.
II. xy = 21.
III. x and y are both positive integers.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements I and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.explanation: I + II: x = 7, y = 3 or x = −3, y = −7, so x + y = 10 or −10 — not sufficient. II + III: (1, 21), (3, 7), (7, 3), (21, 1) give sums 22 or 10. I + III: infinitely many pairs. All three: x = 7, y = 3, so x + y = 10.
solution.why_others_wrong: I + II forgets the negative pair; I + III gives a whole family; with all three the sum is fixed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Arun, Bina, Chirag and Dev each own one car, and the four cars are red, blue, green and white, one of each colour. What is the colour of Arun's car?

I. Bina's car is not blue.
II. Chirag's car is white.
III. Dev's car is blue, and Bina's car is not green.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Pair the statements and test each pair
solution.explanation: II + III: Chirag white, Dev blue, Bina not green ⇒ Bina red, so Arun green — sufficient. I + II: Chirag white, Bina red or green, Arun could be red, blue or green. I + III: Dev blue, Bina red or white, Arun could be red, green or white. No single statement is enough.
steps: II + III: Chirag white, Dev blue, Bina red ⇒ Arun green
I + II and I + III leave Arun open
solution.why_others_wrong: I + II leaves several colours for Arun; II + III already fixes it, so all three are not necessary.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only statements II and III together are sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The municipal corporation has asked every restaurant in the city to display its food-hygiene rating at the entrance.

Assumptions:
I. Customers may use the hygiene rating when deciding where to eat.
II. Every restaurant in the city has the highest hygiene rating.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Ratings are displayed at the entrance so that customers can see them before choosing a restaurant, so I is implicit. If every restaurant had the top rating, displaying it would tell customers nothing; II is not assumed and goes against the purpose of the order.
steps: Display at the entrance ⇒ customers can use it to choose: I
Ratings must differ to be useful ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept a claim that makes the display pointless; Neither ignores why it is displayed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Meena's birthday is on 12 August. Today is 5 August of the same year.

Conclusions:
I. Meena's birthday is 7 days from today.
II. Meena's birthday has already passed this year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: From 5 August to 12 August is 12 − 5 = 7 days, so I follows. The birthday is still a week away, so it has not passed; II is false.
steps: Birthday is still to come ⇒ II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept a conclusion the dates contradict; Neither ignores the simple count.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Rita is taller than Sita, and Sita is taller than Gita.

Conclusions:
I. Rita is taller than Gita.
II. Gita is the shortest of the three.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Rita > Sita > Gita, so Rita is taller than Gita (I), and Gita is shorter than both the others, so she is the shortest of the three (II).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two direct consequences of the same chain.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A shop offered a 10% discount on all shirts last Sunday.

Conclusions:
I. The shop sold more shirts last Sunday than on the Saturday before it.
II. The shop had no trousers for sale last Sunday.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The statement tells us only about the discount. It gives no sales figures for either day (I does not follow), and a discount on shirts says nothing about whether trousers were on sale (II does not follow).
steps: No sales figures ⇒ I does not follow
Shirts only mentioned ⇒ nothing about trousers ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option accepts an outcome or a fact that the statement does not give.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The train to Jaipur left the station on time at 4:15 pm. Ravi reached the station at 4:25 pm.

Conclusions:
I. Ravi will travel to Jaipur by bus.
II. Ravi could not board that train at the station.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The train had left ten minutes before Ravi reached the station, so he could not board it there (II). How he will travel now, or whether he was going to Jaipur at all, is not stated, so I does not follow.
steps: Train left 4:15; Ravi arrived 4:25 ⇒ could not board it: II
His further plans are unknown ⇒ I does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both guess Ravi's next step; Neither misses the direct timing.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: On Monday, every one of the 40 passenger seats on a school bus was occupied by a student, and 5 more students travelled standing. Apart from the driver, there was no one else on the bus.

Conclusions:
I. The bus carries more than 40 students every day.
II. 45 students travelled on the bus on Monday.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: On Monday, 40 seated and 5 standing students travelled: 45 in all (II). The statement is about Monday only, so nothing follows about other days (I).
steps: Other days are not described ⇒ I does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both turn a single day into a daily pattern; Neither ignores the direct count.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: In a company, only employees who have completed five years of service are eligible for the long-service award, and every eligible employee who has no disciplinary record receives it. Leela has completed seven years of service and has no disciplinary record.

Conclusions:
I. Leela receives the long-service award.
II. Every employee who receives the long-service award has completed five years of service.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: 'Only employees with five years of service are eligible' makes five years necessary for eligibility, not enough for it; other conditions may apply. So we cannot say that Leela is eligible, and I does not follow. Every award-winner must be eligible, and every eligible employee has five years of service, so II follows.
steps: 'Only X are eligible' ⇒ eligible ⇒ X (not X ⇒ eligible)
Leela's eligibility not established ⇒ I does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both read 'only those with five years' as 'all those with five years'; Neither misses that every award-winner must be eligible.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A test has 50 questions. Each correct answer earns 2 marks, each wrong answer costs 1 mark, and an unanswered question earns nothing. Tarun answered all 50 questions and scored 73 marks.

Conclusions:
I. Tarun answered 41 questions correctly.
II. Tarun got more than 10 questions wrong.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: If c answers are correct, 50 − c are wrong: 2c − (50 − c) = 73, so 3c = 123 and c = 41 (I). Then 9 answers were wrong, which is not more than 10, so II is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept a count the arithmetic rules out; Neither ignores the direct calculation.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A building has 10 floors with 4 flats on each floor. Every flat on floors 1 to 5 has exactly one balcony, and every flat on floors 6 to 10 has exactly two balconies.

Conclusions:
I. The flats of the building have 60 balconies in all.
II. More than half of the flats' balconies are on floors 6 to 10.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Floors 1–5: 5 × 4 × 1 = 20 balconies; floors 6–10: 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 balconies. Total 60 (I), and 40 of the 60 are on floors 6 to 10, which is more than half (II).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two direct calculations.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The average monthly salary of the 10 employees of a firm is ₹30,000.

Conclusions:
I. At least one employee of the firm earns ₹30,000 or more a month.
II. Every employee of the firm earns at least ₹25,000 a month.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: If every employee earned less than ₹30,000, the average would also be less than ₹30,000. So at least one earns ₹30,000 or more (I). An average says nothing about the lowest salary — one employee could earn ₹10,000 while others earn more — so II does not follow.
steps: Not everyone can be below the average ⇒ I
The minimum is not fixed by the average ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both treat the average as a floor; Neither misses that some value must reach the average.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: This year, the number of cars sold by a company fell by 10%, while the number of two-wheelers it sold rose by 10%.

Conclusions:
I. The total number of vehicles the company sold this year was the same as last year.
II. The company sold more two-wheelers than cars this year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Percentage changes depend on last year's numbers, which are not given. If the company sold more cars than two-wheelers last year, the total fell; if fewer, it rose — so I does not follow. Whether two-wheelers now outnumber cars also depends on the starting numbers, so II does not follow.
steps: Equal percentages on unequal bases ⇒ totals unknown ⇒ I does not follow
Last year's numbers unknown ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option treats equal percentage changes as if the bases were known.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The college raised the fees for its hostel by 40% this year.
II. Many students of the college moved out of the hostel this year into cheaper shared flats nearby.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: A steep rise in hostel fees makes the hostel costlier than shared flats, so students move out to save money. I explains II.
steps: II: students move to cheaper flats
solution.why_others_wrong: Students moving out cannot have caused a fee rise announced for the year, so B fails; one statement explains the other, so neither independent nor common causes fit.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. A new metro station opened next to the Sector 18 market last month.
II. The number of shoppers visiting the Sector 18 market rose sharply this month.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: A metro station next to the market makes it much easier for people to reach it, so more shoppers come. The station (I) came first and explains the rise (II).
steps: I: easier access to the market
solution.why_others_wrong: More shoppers this month cannot have caused a station that opened last month (B); no third event is needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The company recalled 20,000 of its new pressure cookers from the market.
II. Tests found that the safety valve of the company's new pressure cooker could fail under high pressure.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: A product is recalled when it is found to be unsafe. The faulty safety valve (II) is the reason for the recall (I).
solution.why_others_wrong: A recall does not create a fault in a valve, so A fails; the fault directly explains the recall.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The price of gold in the country rose to a record high this week.
II. The city's municipal corporation began a drive to clear encroachments from footpaths this week.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Gold prices depend on world markets and demand for gold; clearing footpaths is a civic decision. Neither explains the other, and no single event explains both.
solution.why_others_wrong: A or B would need gold prices and footpath drives to affect each other; E would need one event behind both.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. Petrol pumps across the state ran out of fuel this week because fuel tankers did not reach them.
II. Deliveries of cooking-gas cylinders across the state were badly delayed this week because the trucks carrying them did not run.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Empty petrol pumps do not delay gas cylinders, and delayed cylinders do not empty petrol pumps. Both are what one event would produce — for example, a statewide strike by the tanker and truck operators who carry fuel and gas.
steps: I and II: both depend on fuel transport
Shared trigger: disruption of fuel transport (e.g., a strike)
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B would need one shortage to cause the other; D would need two unrelated reasons in the same week, while one transport disruption explains both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Every evening, vegetable vendors in a town market throw their unsold and rotting vegetables on the road, and the heaps attract stray cattle that block traffic.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ban the sale of vegetables in the town
Ask the traffic police to stop vehicles from using the market road
Place covered waste bins in the market, collect the market's waste every evening, and fine vendors who dump waste on the road

solution.concept: Remove the cause with a practical, enforceable step
solution.explanation: The problem starts with waste dumped on the road. Bins, daily collection and fines stop the dumping, which removes the heaps, the cattle and the traffic blocks.
steps: Cause: dumping of waste on the road
solution.why_others_wrong: Closing the market or banning vegetable sales is extreme; stopping traffic leaves the waste where it is.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Place covered waste bins in the market, collect the market's waste every evening, and fine vendors who dump waste on the road

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: An online poll on a bank's website found that 85% of the people who responded prefer mobile banking to visiting a branch. So the bank can close most of its rural branches without inconveniencing its customers.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Running a rural branch costs the bank less than running a city branch
Most of the bank's rural customers do not use the internet, and very few of them took part in the online poll
The poll received more than 10,000 responses
Some city customers also visit branches

solution.concept: Weaken: show that the sample does not represent the people affected
solution.explanation: The decision affects rural customers, but the poll mostly reached internet users. If rural customers hardly took part and mostly do not use the internet, the poll says nothing about their needs.
steps: Weakener: they were missing from the poll
solution.why_others_wrong: A large number of responses does not fix a biased sample; branch costs and city customers' habits do not show how rural customers would be affected.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Most of the bank's rural customers do not use the internet, and very few of them took part in the online poll

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city should set up more public charging points for electric cars, because the lack of charging points is what is holding back the purchase of electric cars in the city.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: In a survey, most car buyers in the city who had considered an electric car said they did not buy one because they had nowhere to charge it
Electric cars are cheaper to run than petrol cars
Charging points can be installed in parking lots
The city has more than five lakh registered cars

solution.concept: Strengthen: confirm the cause the argument names
solution.explanation: The argument says the shortage of charging points is the obstacle. The survey shows that buyers who considered electric cars were put off for exactly that reason.
steps: Claim: lack of charging points blocks purchases
Strengthener: buyers say so in a survey
solution.why_others_wrong: Running costs and the number of cars do not show what stops buyers; that charging points can be installed shows the plan is possible, not that it would help.
solution.final_answer: Option A: In a survey, most car buyers in the city who had considered an electric car said they did not buy one because they had nowhere to charge it

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A theatre sells balcony tickets at ₹300 each and stall tickets at ₹200 each. On Saturday it sold 150 tickets in all and collected ₹38,000 from them.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: The theatre sold more stall tickets than balcony tickets on Saturday
The theatre collected ₹16,000 from stall tickets on Saturday
The theatre sold 80 balcony tickets on Saturday
The theatre sold 70 balcony tickets on Saturday

solution.explanation: If b balcony tickets were sold, 300b + 200(150 − b) = 38,000, so 100b = 8,000 and b = 80. Then 70 stall tickets were sold, bringing in ₹14,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 is the number of stall tickets; stall tickets (70) were fewer than balcony tickets (80); stall income was ₹14,000, not ₹16,000.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The theatre sold 80 balcony tickets on Saturday

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: After a new highway opened near a district hospital, the number of patients in its emergency ward has doubled, and many of them wait for hours before a doctor sees them.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Reduce the working hours of the emergency ward
Refuse to treat patients from other districts
Add doctors and beds to the emergency ward and set up a trauma-care unit to treat highway accident cases

solution.concept: Match capacity to the new demand
solution.explanation: Demand has doubled, mainly from the highway. More doctors and beds, plus a trauma unit, add the capacity the ward now needs.
steps: Remedy: more staff, beds and a trauma unit
solution.why_others_wrong: Closing the highway is impractical; refusing patients and cutting hours make the problem worse.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Add doctors and beds to the emergency ward and set up a trauma-care unit to treat highway accident cases

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Shops on Gandhi Road that put up bright LED signboards last year reported higher sales this year than the shops on the road that did not. So bright signboards increase a shop's sales.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Gandhi Road is one of the busiest roads in the town
Some shops on Gandhi Road stay open until 10 pm
The shops that put up LED signboards were the same shops that also enlarged their premises and stocked more goods last year
LED signboards use less electricity than older signboards

solution.concept: Weaken: point to another difference between the two groups
solution.explanation: If the shops with new signboards also expanded and added stock, their higher sales could come from the expansion, not the signboards.
steps: Weakener: those shops also expanded ⇒ another cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Electricity use, opening hours of some shops and the road's traffic apply to both groups and do not explain the difference.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The shops that put up LED signboards were the same shops that also enlarged their premises and stocked more goods last year

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: In a quiz tournament, each of five teams played every other team exactly once. Each match had a winner and a loser; the winner got 2 points and the loser 0.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: At least one team won all its matches
The five teams together got 20 points
Each team won exactly two matches
The five teams together got 10 points

solution.explanation: Five teams playing each other once make 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 matches, and each match gives out exactly 2 points, so the teams together got 20 points.
solution.why_others_wrong: The results of individual teams are not given, so 'two wins each' and 'one unbeaten team' need not be true; 10 is the number of matches, not points.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The five teams together got 20 points

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city's decision to make the first hour of parking free in the old market area will bring more shoppers to the old market.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: Some shoppers in the old market come on foot
Parking charges in the city were last revised five years ago
Shopkeepers in the old market say that many of their former customers now shop at the new mall mainly because parking there is free
The old market has more than 200 shops

solution.concept: Strengthen: show that parking cost is what keeps shoppers away
solution.explanation: If shoppers left the old market mainly because they had to pay for parking, free parking removes that reason and is likely to bring some of them back.
steps: Strengthener: paid parking is why shoppers left
solution.why_others_wrong: The number of shops and when charges were last revised do not link parking to shoppers; shoppers on foot are unaffected by parking.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Shopkeepers in the old market say that many of their former customers now shop at the new mall mainly because parking there is free

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A bank has found that many people who took small business loans under a government scheme did not know that the loans had to be repaid, and defaults on these loans are rising.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Explain the repayment terms clearly to every borrower when the loan is given, and send reminders before each instalment falls due
Take legal action against every borrower at once
Stop giving loans under the scheme
Write off all the loans given under the scheme

solution.concept: Remove the misunderstanding that causes the problem
solution.explanation: Defaults are rising because borrowers did not know they had to repay. Clear explanation at the start and reminders later remove that gap without ending the scheme.
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping the scheme or writing off loans is extreme; suing every borrower punishes people for a misunderstanding that the bank can correct.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Explain the repayment terms clearly to every borrower when the loan is given, and send reminders before each instalment falls due

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Since the city introduced a ₹2,000 fine for driving without a seat belt, the number of drivers caught without a seat belt has fallen by 60%. So many more drivers in the city now wear seat belts.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Most new cars warn drivers who have not fastened their seat belts
During the same period, the traffic police cut the number of seat-belt checkpoints in the city by about two-thirds
Many drivers support the higher fine
The fine for not wearing a helmet was also raised during the same period

solution.concept: Weaken: show that the measure itself changed
solution.explanation: The number of drivers caught depends on how many checks are made. If checkpoints fell by two-thirds, far fewer drivers would be caught even if just as many drove without seat belts.
steps: Weakener: far fewer checks ⇒ catches no longer measure behaviour
solution.why_others_wrong: The helmet fine concerns two-wheelers; seat-belt warnings in new cars would, if anything, support the argument; drivers' support for the fine does not show what they do.
solution.final_answer: Option B: During the same period, the traffic police cut the number of seat-belt checkpoints in the city by about two-thirds

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what causes presbyopia?

options.text: The lens inside the eye becoming less flexible with age
Reading on mobile phones for many hours a day
An infection that spreads in crowded villages
A poor diet in the years before middle age

solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: presbyopia 'happens to almost everyone with age, because the lens inside the eye slowly becomes less flexible.'
steps: The lens becomes less flexible with age
solution.why_others_wrong: Holding a phone further away is a sign of presbyopia, not its cause. The passage says it 'is not a disease', so an infection is wrong. Diet is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The lens inside the eye becoming less flexible with age

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following workers is NOT mentioned in the passage as being affected by weak near vision?

options.text: A weaver following a fine pattern

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 names a tailor, a weaver and a farmer who sorts seeds. A driver is never mentioned; reading distant road signs is not even a near-vision task.
solution.why_others_wrong: The tailor, the weaver and the farmer are all named in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A driver reading road signs

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, which of the following is one reason why some people do not get reading glasses?

options.text: Reading glasses are among the costliest medical aids available.
Only doctors in large cities are allowed to test eyesight.
They believe weak near vision must simply be accepted in old age.
Glasses cannot be worn by people who work outdoors.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'some believe that weak near vision is simply a part of growing old that must be accepted.' Others fear lazy eyes or feel embarrassed.
steps: Find 'The difficulty lies in reaching people'
Belief that it must be accepted
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 3 calls glasses 'among the cheapest of all medical aids', the opposite of costliest. It says a trained health worker can test eyes, so doctors are not required. Outdoor work is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They believe weak near vision must simply be accepted in old age.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'remedy' as used in the passage ('For an office worker in a city, the remedy is simple')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: remedy = a way of putting a problem right
solution.explanation: The sentence goes on to name what fixes the problem: a visit to an optician and reading glasses. A remedy is a cure or solution.
steps: Context: a visit to an optician and a pair of glasses
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Danger' and 'habit' do not describe a fix. 'Price' is about cost; the sentence names what to do, not what it costs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by the closing words 'years of good work are given back'?

options.text: Workers can go on using their skills well for many more years.
Glasses make people feel younger than they really are.
People get back the money they spent on eye camps.
Old people are given back the jobs they had lost.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a summing-up phrase
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says weak near vision makes skilled workers slow down 'in the very years when their skills are at their best'. Cheap glasses let them see well again, so they can keep working well for years.
steps: Problem: skilled people lose working years
solution.why_others_wrong: No refund of money is mentioned. Nobody is said to have lost a job and got it back. Feeling younger is not suggested; the phrase is about work.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Workers can go on using their skills well for many more years.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage explains a normal change in near vision, shows how it harms the work of village craftspeople and farmers, and describes how cheap glasses restore their working lives.
steps: Para 1: near vision weakens with age
Paras 2-4: the effect on work and why people go without glasses
Para 5: glasses give working years back
solution.why_others_wrong: Presbyopia is 'not a disease'. The passage says glasses are cheap, not costly. City opticians appear in one sentence only.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Seeing Clearly, Working Longer

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do desire paths appear?

options.text: Grass does not grow well near paved paths.
Park managers mark them out for walkers in a hurry.
Children are told to play away from the paved paths.
People in a hurry take the shortest route they can see.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Most people, when they are in a hurry, take the shortest route they can see.' Cutting corners wears the grass into a path.
steps: Find 'Such paths appear for a simple reason'
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 1 says 'Nobody planned them', so managers did not mark them. Poor grass and children's play are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: People in a hurry take the shortest route they can see.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'faint' as used in the passage ('a faint line becomes visible')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: faint = weak, only just able to be seen
solution.explanation: The line is faint at first and 'within weeks the faint track becomes a clear one'. The contrast with 'clear' shows that faint means only just visible.
solution.why_others_wrong: A path worn by feet is not 'freshly paved' or 'carefully planned' (nobody planned it). 'Very wide' contradicts the narrow strips described in paragraph 1.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a way in which park managers tried to stop walkers?

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists fences, hedges and signs asking people to keep off the grass. Guards and fines are never mentioned.
steps: Guards and fines: not in the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: Fences, hedges and signs are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Posting guards to fine walkers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do the planners mentioned in paragraph 4 mean when they treat desire paths 'as information'?
