solution.explanation: Protests are pressure to change the decision. The management refused to give way: it would not 'back down' on its decision.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Back up' means support or make a copy. 'Back in' and 'back onto' describe moving a vehicle backwards. None means give way under pressure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
His ______ handwriting made the amount on the cheque impossible to read.

solution.concept: Confusable words: legible / illegible (readable / unreadable) vs eligible / ineligible (qualified / not qualified)
solution.explanation: Handwriting that cannot be read is 'illegible'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Legible' means readable, the opposite. 'Eligible' and 'ineligible' are about meeting conditions, not about writing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Once a bustling port, the town is now ______, its warehouses empty and its streets silent.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'Once ... now' contrast, with the description after the comma
solution.explanation: Empty warehouses and silent streets describe a lonely, abandoned place: the town is now 'desolate'.
steps: Contrast: once bustling → now the opposite
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Teeming' (crowded) and 'burgeoning' (growing fast) describe a busy town. 'Opulent' (rich and lavish) does not fit empty warehouses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
Far from ______ the dispute, the chairman's ______ remarks only made both sides more bitter.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'Far from X, ... only Y' means the opposite of X happened
solution.explanation: Making both sides more bitter is the opposite of settling a dispute, so blank 1 is 'settling'. Remarks that make people bitter are harsh and unrestrained: 'intemperate'.
steps: Blank 1: the opposite of the result → settling
Blank 2: remarks that cause bitterness → intemperate
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Conciliatory' and 'soothing' remarks would not make both sides more bitter. 'Far from inflaming' contradicts a result that is itself inflaming.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) letter** posted the **(B) clerk** in the **(C) red** box near the **(D) branch**.

solution.concept: Word swap: check who can perform each action
solution.explanation: A letter cannot post anything. Swapping A and B gives: 'The clerk posted the letter in the red box near the branch.'
steps: The clerk is the one who posts
solution.why_others_wrong: C-D gives 'the branch box near the red', which is meaningless. B-D leaves the letter as the one posting. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'complement' used correctly?

options.text: Every customer received a complement calendar at the new year.
The spicy chutney is a perfect complement to the plain rice.
The manager paid her a complement on her neat handwriting.
He complemented the cashier on her quick service.

solution.concept: Complement (something that completes or goes well with) vs compliment (praise; complimentary = free)
solution.explanation: A chutney that goes well with plain rice completes the meal: it is a 'complement' to it.
steps: Chutney that goes well with rice → 'complement': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are about praise or something given free, which needs 'compliment' or 'complimentary'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The spicy chutney is a perfect complement to the plain rice.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'precede' used correctly?

options.text: After the speech, the guests will precede to the dining hall.
A short prayer will precede the opening of the new branch.
The case cannot precede until all the documents are filed.
Please precede with your complaint; I am listening.

solution.concept: Precede (come before) vs proceed (go forward, continue)
solution.explanation: 'Precede' means come before. A prayer that comes before the opening 'precedes' it.
steps: Guests going on to the hall → 'proceed'
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three describe going forward or continuing, which needs 'proceed'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A short prayer will precede the opening of the new branch.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
When **(A) demand** for onions fell short of **(B) supply**, their **(C) prices** rose sharply and **(D) traders** began to hoard them.

solution.concept: Word swap: test the sentence against the law of demand and supply
solution.explanation: Prices rise when supply falls short of demand, not the other way round. Swapping A and B gives: 'When supply of onions fell short of demand, their prices rose sharply and traders began to hoard them.'
steps: Demand below supply → prices would fall
solution.why_others_wrong: C-D makes the traders rise and the prices hoard. A-C gives 'When prices for onions fell short of supply, their demand rose', which no longer explains the hoarding. The original reverses the economics, so a swap is needed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'noisome' used correctly?

options.text: The noisome crowd cheered loudly when the result was announced.
The noisome children in the next room kept the clerk awake.
A noisome smell rose from the blocked drain behind the market.
The festival was noisome, full of music and drums.

solution.concept: Noisome = very unpleasant or offensive, especially in smell (not 'noisy')
solution.explanation: 'Noisome' has nothing to do with noise; it means foul or offensive. A smell from a blocked drain is noisome.
steps: Foul smell from a drain → 'noisome': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three use 'noisome' as if it meant noisy, which is a common mistake.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A noisome smell rose from the blocked drain behind the market.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'streamlined' as used in the sentence:
'The new software has streamlined the loan approval process, cutting the time taken from two weeks to three days.'

solution.concept: Streamline = make a process simpler and more efficient
solution.explanation: The process now takes three days instead of two weeks. Making a process quicker by removing unnecessary steps is 'streamlining' it.
steps: Clue: two weeks cut to three days
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Made longer and stricter' contradicts the shorter time. Cost and stopping the process are not suggested.
solution.final_answer: Option D: made simpler and more efficient

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Diligent' and 'industrious' both mean hard-working and careful. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'specious' as used in the sentence:
'The auditor rejected the manager's specious argument that the missing cash had simply been miscounted.'

solution.concept: Specious = appearing right or reasonable on the surface but actually wrong
solution.explanation: The manager's claim sounded possible (a miscount), but the auditor saw through it and rejected it. An argument that looks plausible but is false is 'specious'.
steps: The auditor rejected it as false
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Detailed and well supported' would not be rejected. 'Angry and abusive' and 'honest but confused' do not mean specious.
solution.final_answer: Option A: seemingly reasonable but actually false

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Garrulous' means excessively talkative; 'taciturn' means saying very little. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Rani was **delighted** to hear that she had passed the clerk's examination.

solution.explanation: Passing an examination is good news, and 'delighted' means very pleased.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Worried' and 'tired' do not describe joy. 'Surprised' describes an unexpected event, not happiness.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
At the press meeting, the minister **reiterated** his promise to repair the flood-damaged roads before the monsoon.

solution.explanation: A promise that is 'reiterated' is made again, usually for emphasis: it is repeated.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Withdrew' and 'forgot' are the opposite of stating a promise again. 'Doubted' does not describe what the minister did with his own promise.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
A **perspicacious** investor, she sold her shares months before the market crashed.

solution.concept: Perspicacious = quick to notice and understand things; shrewd
solution.explanation: Selling months before a crash shows that she saw the danger clearly before others did. 'Perspicacious' means having sharp insight: shrewd.
steps: Context: sold well before the crash
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Reckless' is the opposite. 'Wealthy' describes money, not judgement. 'Lucky' implies chance, whereas the word describes insight.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **recalcitrant** borrower ignored every notice and refused to meet the recovery officer.

solution.concept: Recalcitrant = stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate
solution.explanation: Ignoring every notice and refusing to meet the officer shows a stubborn refusal to cooperate: the borrower is uncooperative.
steps: Context: ignored notices, refused to meet
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Bankrupt' describes finances, not attitude. 'Forgetful' suggests accident, not refusal. 'Apologetic' is the opposite of his behaviour.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Thanks to a **munificent** donation from a former student, the village school built a new library.

solution.concept: Munificent = very generous, especially with money
solution.explanation: A donation large enough to build a library is very generous: 'munificent'.
steps: Context: a donation that built a library
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Modest' suggests a small gift, the opposite. 'Secret' and 'late' do not describe the size or spirit of a gift.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **obsequious** clerk agreed with everything the visiting director said and laughed at all his jokes.

solution.concept: Obsequious = too eager to please or obey; servile
solution.explanation: Agreeing with everything a senior person says and laughing at all his jokes shows excessive eagerness to please: the clerk is servile.
steps: Context: agrees with everything, laughs at every joke
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rude' is the opposite. 'Honest' and 'sleepy' do not describe flattering a superior.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The water in the village pond is so **shallow** in summer that children can walk across it.

solution.explanation: Water that children can walk across is not deep. The opposite of 'shallow' is 'deep'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Muddy', 'cold' and 'clean' describe the water's condition or temperature, not its depth.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Snow is **rare** in this coastal town, so the children have never built a snowman.

solution.concept: Rare = not happening often; antonym: common
solution.explanation: Something that seldom happens is 'rare'; the opposite is 'common' (happening often).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Heavy', 'cold' and 'late' describe amount, temperature and timing, not how often snow falls.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The bank has put up a **conspicuous** sign at the gate so that no one can miss the new timings.

solution.concept: Conspicuous = easily seen, attracting notice; antonym: unobtrusive
solution.explanation: A sign that 'no one can miss' is conspicuous. The opposite is 'unobtrusive' (not easily noticed).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Prominent' and 'striking' are close in meaning to 'conspicuous'. 'Official' describes who put the sign up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **intrepid** reporter travelled alone into the flood zone to file her story.

solution.explanation: Going alone into a flood zone shows courage. 'Intrepid' means fearless; its opposite is 'timid' (easily frightened).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fearless' is a synonym. 'Careless' and 'famous' do not describe the lack of courage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to see eye to eye'.

options.text: to meet someone face to face

solution.concept: Idiom: see eye to eye = agree, have the same opinion
solution.explanation: People who 'see eye to eye' share the same view. For example: 'The two partners rarely see eye to eye on how to spend the profits.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Staring angrily, meeting face to face and an eye test read the words literally; none means agreeing.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to agree fully with someone

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The contractor finished painting the new branch **at the eleventh hour**, just before the opening ceremony began.

options.text: after a delay of eleven days

solution.concept: Idiom: at the eleventh hour = at the latest possible time
solution.explanation: Finishing 'just before the opening ceremony began' means finishing at the very last moment.
steps: Very late, but still in time
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Eleven o'clock' and 'eleven days' read the idiom literally. 'Much earlier than planned' contradicts 'just before'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: at the last possible moment

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Searching the old record room for the missing file turned out to be **a wild goose chase**; it had been sent to the head office years earlier.

options.text: a pointless search for something that is not there
a pleasant trip away from work

solution.concept: Idiom: a wild goose chase = a hopeless search or pursuit
solution.explanation: The file was never in the record room, so searching there could not succeed. Such a hopeless search is a wild goose chase.
steps: Clue: the file had been sent elsewhere
solution.why_others_wrong: The search was neither exciting, successful nor pleasant; the sentence stresses that it was useless.
solution.final_answer: Option B: a pointless search for something that is not there

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to add fuel to the fire'.

options.text: to waste money on unnecessary things
to make a bad situation worse

solution.concept: Idiom: add fuel to the fire = make an angry or difficult situation worse
solution.explanation: Fuel makes a fire burn more fiercely; doing something that inflames an already tense situation 'adds fuel to the fire'. For example: 'His rude reply only added fuel to the fire.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Giving energy, settling a quarrel and wasting money are not what the idiom means; settling a quarrel is nearly the opposite.
solution.final_answer: Option D: to make a bad situation worse

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The two largest shareholders took **the lion's share** of the profits, leaving little for the rest.

solution.concept: Idiom: the lion's share = the largest part of something
solution.explanation: 'Leaving little for the rest' shows that the two shareholders took most of the profits: the lion's share.
steps: Clue: little left for the others
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A fair part' and 'the smallest part' contradict 'leaving little for the rest'. Nothing suggests the share was hidden.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person authorised to act or vote on behalf of another

solution.explanation: A 'proxy' is a person given authority to act or vote for someone else, as at a company meeting.
steps: Key idea: acts or votes for another person
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'mentor' is an experienced adviser, a 'rival' a competitor and an 'heir' a person who inherits property.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who pretends to be ill in order to avoid work or duty

solution.explanation: A 'malingerer' pretends to be ill, or exaggerates an illness, to escape work or duty.
steps: Key idea: pretends to be ill
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'hypochondriac' truly believes he is ill without cause; he is not pretending. An 'invalid' is a person who really is ill or disabled. A 'sluggard' is lazy but does not pretend to be ill.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The children did not break the window.

options.text: The window was not broken by the children.
The window is not broken by the children.
The window had not been broken by the children.
The window was not break by the children.

solution.concept: Simple past negative active (did not + verb) → was/were not + past participle
solution.explanation: The object 'the window' becomes the subject. 'Did not break' (simple past) becomes 'was not broken'.
steps: Simple past passive negative: was not + broken
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is not broken' changes the tense to the present. 'Was not break' uses the base form instead of the participle. 'Had not been broken' is past perfect.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The window was not broken by the children.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The guard made the visitors wait outside the strongroom.

options.text: The visitors were made wait outside the strongroom by the guard.
The visitors were made to wait outside the strongroom by the guard.
The visitors were making to wait outside the strongroom by the guard.
The visitors had been made to wait outside the strongroom by the guard.

solution.concept: 'Make + object + bare infinitive' in the active becomes 'be made + to-infinitive' in the passive
solution.explanation: In the active, 'make' takes a bare infinitive (made the visitors wait). In the passive, 'to' comes back: 'The visitors were made to wait outside the strongroom by the guard.'
steps: 'to' returns in the passive: made to wait
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Were made wait' leaves out the 'to' that the passive needs. 'Had been made' changes the tense. 'Were making to wait' is not a passive form.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The visitors were made to wait outside the strongroom by the guard.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
I remember my father taking me to the bank for the first time.

options.text: I remember being taken to the bank for the first time by my father.
I remember my father being taken to the bank for the first time.
I remember having taken to the bank for the first time by my father.
I am remembered being taken to the bank for the first time by my father.

solution.explanation: The gerund clause 'my father taking me' is made passive: 'me' becomes the understood subject and the gerund becomes 'being taken': 'I remember being taken to the bank for the first time by my father.' The main verb 'remember' stays active.
steps: Main clause 'I remember' stays the same
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Having taken' is an active perfect gerund. 'I am remembered' wrongly makes the main verb passive. 'My father being taken' reverses who took whom.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I remember being taken to the bank for the first time by my father.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
Ravi said, "I am going to the market."

options.text: Ravi told that he was going to the market.
Ravi said that he had been going to the market.
Ravi said that he was going to the market.
Ravi said that I was going to the market.

solution.concept: Past reporting verb: present continuous → past continuous; 'I' → 'he'
solution.explanation: With 'said', 'am going' becomes 'was going', and 'I' becomes 'he': 'Ravi said that he was going to the market.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Said that I' keeps the first person. 'Told that' needs an object ('told me that'). 'Had been going' backshifts too far.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Ravi said that he was going to the market.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
The manager said to the staff, "Good morning!"

options.text: The manager told the staff that it was a good morning.
The manager wished the staff good morning.
The manager exclaimed to the staff that good morning.
The manager said to the staff that good morning.

solution.concept: Greetings are reported with a suitable verb such as 'wish' or 'greet', not with 'that'
solution.explanation: A greeting is not a statement, so it cannot follow 'that'. It is reported as 'The manager wished the staff good morning.'
steps: Reporting verb for greetings: wished / greeted
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Said ... that good morning' and 'exclaimed ... that good morning' put a greeting in a 'that' clause with no verb. 'That it was a good morning' turns the greeting into a remark about the weather.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The manager wished the staff good morning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
She said, "If I had known about the strike, I would have taken a taxi."

options.text: She said that if she had known about the strike, she will have taken a taxi.
She said that if she had had known about the strike, she would have had taken a taxi.
She said that if she knew about the strike, she would take a taxi.
She said that if she had known about the strike, she would have taken a taxi.

solution.concept: Past perfect and 'would have + past participle' (third conditional) do not change in reported speech
solution.explanation: The past perfect cannot be shifted further back, and 'would have taken' stays the same. Only the pronoun changes: 'She said that if she had known about the strike, she would have taken a taxi.'
steps: Third conditional: had known / would have taken
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Had had known' and 'would have had taken' are not English verb forms. 'Knew ... would take' changes the meaning to a present unreal condition. 'Will have taken' wrongly changes 'would' to 'will'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: She said that if she had known about the strike, she would have taken a taxi.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Here ______ the files you asked for.

solution.concept: After 'Here' or 'There' at the start, the verb agrees with the noun subject that follows it
solution.explanation: The real subject is 'the files', which is plural, so the verb is plural: 'Here are the files you asked for.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is', 'was' and 'has' are singular and do not agree with 'the files'; 'has' also gives no meaning here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
A series of thefts from the lockers ______ forced the bank to install new cameras.

solution.concept: 'A series of + plural noun' takes a singular verb, because the head noun is 'series'
solution.explanation: The head of the subject is 'a series' (one sequence), so the verb is singular: 'A series of thefts ... has forced the bank to install new cameras.'
steps: 'of thefts' does not change the number
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have' agrees wrongly with 'thefts'. 'Were' and 'are' cannot be followed by 'forced' to give an active verb and are plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
This cake ______ wonderful; may I have the recipe?

solution.concept: State verbs of the senses (taste, smell, look, sound) used with an adjective take simple tenses, not continuous
solution.explanation: 'Taste' here describes a quality of the cake (a state), followed by the adjective 'wonderful', so the simple present is used: 'This cake tastes wonderful.'
steps: 'taste' + adjective = a state, not an action
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is tasting' and 'has been tasting' wrongly use continuous forms for a state. 'Was tasting' is past and also continuous, which clashes with 'may I have the recipe?' now.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
I ______ leave the office when the manager called me back for an urgent meeting.

solution.concept: 'Was about to + verb ... when + past simple' = an action on the point of happening when something interrupted it
solution.explanation: The interruption ('the manager called me back') is in the past, so the planned action just before it is expressed by 'was about to': 'I was about to leave the office when the manager called me back ...'.
steps: Action on the point of happening at that moment
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Am about to' and 'will be about to' are present and future and clash with 'called'. 'Have been about to' is not used for a single past moment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ Taj Mahal was built by ______ Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

solution.concept: 'The' with the names of certain famous buildings, and with a title + name when the title identifies the person
solution.explanation: 'The Taj Mahal' is the fixed name of the monument. 'The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan' refers to one particular, identified emperor, so it also takes 'the'.
steps: Identified person with a descriptive title: the Mughal emperor
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A Taj Mahal' would suggest one of many. 'Taj Mahal' without 'the' drops the article that is part of the name. 'A Mughal emperor Shah Jahan' uses 'a' for a person who is already named and identified.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Known for his plays and poems, Ravi is often called ______ Kalidasa of our district.

solution.concept: A proper noun used as a common noun (one who is like a famous person) takes 'the' when a phrase identifies the one meant
solution.explanation: Ravi is being compared with Kalidasa, the great poet. 'Of our district' makes the reference unique: the one person in the district who is like Kalidasa. So it is 'the Kalidasa of our district'.
steps: Kalidasa used as a common noun: a great poet like Kalidasa
'of our district' identifies the unique one
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A Kalidasa of our district' clashes with the identifying phrase, which marks one particular person. 'An' does not fit the consonant sound /k/. With no article, the sentence would call Ravi the actual poet Kalidasa.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The little boy is afraid ______ the dark.

solution.explanation: The adjective 'afraid' takes 'of': 'The little boy is afraid of the dark.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Afraid from', 'afraid with' and 'afraid at' are not used.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The branch is closed ______ Sundays and public holidays.

solution.concept: Prepositions of time: 'on' with days and dates
solution.explanation: Days of the week take 'on': 'The branch is closed on Sundays and public holidays.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In' is used with months, years and parts of the day, 'at' with clock times, and 'by' means no later than. None is used with days in this sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The management finally acceded ______ the union's demand for a five-day week.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: accede to (a request or demand) = agree to it
solution.explanation: To accept a demand after resisting it is to 'accede to' it: 'The management finally acceded to the union's demand ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accede with', 'accede for' and 'accede on' are not used.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
He was very tired, ______ he kept working until the last customer had left.

solution.concept: 'Yet' = but still; it joins two facts that contrast
solution.explanation: Being tired would make one stop, but he kept working. The contrast is shown by 'yet'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'So' would make tiredness the reason he kept working. 'Because' makes keeping on working the reason for being tired, which reverses the logic. 'Or' offers an alternative.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ he was ill, he could not attend the meeting.

solution.explanation: His illness is the reason he could not attend. 'Since' introduces a reason: 'Since he was ill, he could not attend the meeting.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Although' signals a contrast that is not there. 'Unless' makes illness a condition for attending. 'Until' is about time and does not fit 'could not attend'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The rural branches cut their staff costs last year; ______, the urban branches brought down their rent bills.

solution.concept: 'Similarly' links two actions of the same kind
solution.explanation: Both groups of branches reduced a cost: one cut staff costs, the other rent. Parallel actions are linked by 'similarly'.
steps: Action 2: urban branches cut costs too
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Nevertheless' signals a contrast that is not there. 'Otherwise' means 'if not'. 'Consequently' would make the urban rent cuts a result of the rural staff cuts, which the sentence does not suggest.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Combine the two sentences into one without changing the meaning, and choose the correct combined sentence.
He is very rich. He is not happy.

options.text: In addition to his wealth, he is not happy.
For all his wealth, he is not happy.
Owing to his wealth, he is not happy.
Because of his wealth, he is not happy.

solution.concept: 'For all' (= in spite of) introduces a concession
solution.explanation: The two sentences contrast: he is rich, but still not happy. 'For all his wealth' means 'in spite of his wealth', keeping the contrast.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Because of' and 'Owing to' make his wealth the cause of his unhappiness, which changes the meaning. 'In addition to' adds rather than contrasts.
solution.final_answer: Option B: For all his wealth, he is not happy.

questions.subject: General Awareness and Current Affairs
questions.question_text: Along with extending the Jal Jeevan Mission, the Union Cabinet on 10 March 2026 approved declaring which airport in Tamil Nadu an international airport?

solution.explanation: At the Cabinet meeting reported on 10 March 2026, Madurai Airport in Tamil Nadu was declared an international airport. The same set of decisions extended the Jal Jeevan Mission to December 2028 and cleared a greenfield connectivity corridor for Jewar Airport.
solution.why_others_wrong: The source names Madurai Airport; the other airports are not mentioned in the decision.

fact_checks.claim: AIR report of 10 March 2026: Cabinet declared Madurai Airport, Tamil Nadu, an international airport; same briefing extended JJM to December 2028

questions.subject: General Awareness and Current Affairs
questions.question_text: After the Prime Minister's Office moved to Seva Teerth, the Union Cabinet in February 2026 approved integrating the historic North and South Blocks into which proposed museum?

solution.explanation: The Union Cabinet approved the transition of the North and South Blocks into the proposed Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum. Cabinet meetings will no longer be held in South Block, which had nearly 95 years of continuous administrative use; the new PMO complex, Seva Teerth, was dedicated on 13 February 2026.
steps: North and South Blocks -> Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum
South Block: ~95 years of administrative use
solution.why_others_wrong: The source names the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum; the other names are not used for this project.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum

fact_checks.claim: Cabinet approved transition of North and South Blocks into the proposed Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum; Cabinet meetings no longer to be held in South Block (DD News, 14 Feb 2026)

questions.subject: General Awareness and Current Affairs
questions.question_text: Which State was declared the country's first paperless judiciary state by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant in May 2026?

solution.explanation: At a conclave in Gangtok, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant declared Sikkim the country's first paperless judiciary state. Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang Golay welcomed it, saying e-filing and digital case management would make justice delivery faster and more transparent.
steps: Declared by CJI Surya Kant at Gangtok
solution.why_others_wrong: The source names Sikkim; Kerala, Goa and Tripura were not declared.

fact_checks.claim: Sikkim declared the country's first paperless judiciary state by CJI Surya Kant at a conclave in Gangtok (AIR, 1 May 2026)

questions.subject: General Awareness and Current Affairs
questions.question_text: Under Karnataka's Menstrual Leave Policy, 2025, notified by the State labour department on 12 November 2025, how many days of paid menstrual leave can an eligible woman employee get in a year?

solution.explanation: The Karnataka labour department notified the Menstrual Leave Policy, 2025 on 12 November 2025. It gives one day of paid leave a month, or 12 days a year, to permanent, contract and outsourced women employees; no medical certificate is needed and unused leave cannot be carried forward. The Cabinet had approved the policy on 9 October 2025; a six-day proposal had been floated earlier.
steps: 1 day per month = 12 days per year
Notified 12 Nov 2025; no medical certificate; no carry-forward

solution.explanation: Banks are required to provide both the cheque drop box facility and the acknowledgement facility at collection counters, and no branch can refuse an acknowledgement if the customer asks for it while tendering a cheque at the counter.

solution.why_others_wrong: There is no value threshold, the drop box does not replace the acknowledgement, and RBI does not mention a fee.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank runs a term deposit scheme for resident Indian senior citizens offering higher, fixed rates. Under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, which of the following deposits is NOT eligible for it?

options.text: A term deposit in the name of an HUF whose Karta is a resident senior citizen
A term deposit of a resident Indian aged 62 held singly
A term deposit of a resident Indian aged 70 held jointly with his spouse
A term deposit of a retired staff member of the bank who is a resident senior citizen

solution.explanation: Banks may at their discretion run term deposit schemes for resident Indian senior citizens, but the facility is not offered on a term deposit in the name of an HUF or its Karta (as Karta), even if the Karta is a resident senior citizen. Retired staff who are senior citizens may even get the senior-citizen rate over and above their staff benefit.
steps: Senior citizen scheme → individuals, not HUF/Karta
solution.why_others_wrong: Individual resident senior citizens (single or joint) qualify, and retired staff senior citizens may get both benefits.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A term deposit in the name of an HUF whose Karta is a resident senior citizen

fact_checks.claim: A bank may, at its discretion, formulate term deposit schemes specifically for resident Indian senior citizens ... Provided that this facility is not offered on the term deposit standing in the name of an HUF or the Karta of the HUF, even if the Karta is a resident Indian senior citizen

A bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staffs, who are senior citizens, the benefit of additional interest rates as admissible to senior citizens over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of their being retired members of the bank's staff

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Banks may offer term deposits without a premature withdrawal option. Under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, which deposits must nevertheless carry a premature withdrawal facility?

options.text: Only term deposits of senior citizens
All term deposits of ₹3 crore and above (bulk deposits)
All term deposits from individuals (single or joint) of ₹1 crore and below
All term deposits of companies and trusts, whatever the amount

solution.explanation: Banks are free to offer term deposits without a premature withdrawal option, but every term deposit accepted from individuals, held singly or jointly, for ₹1 crore and below must have the premature withdrawal facility.
steps: Exception: individuals' deposits ≤ ₹1 crore must be callable
solution.why_others_wrong: Bulk deposits (₹3 crore+) and deposits of companies can be non-callable; the protection is not limited to senior citizens.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All term deposits from individuals (single or joint) of ₹1 crore and below

fact_checks.claim: A bank shall have the freedom to offer term deposits without premature withdrawal option. Provided that all term deposits accepted by a bank from individuals (held singly or jointly) for amount of ₹1 crore and below shall have premature withdrawal facility

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Banks must enable the Positive Pay System for account holders issuing cheques of ₹50,000 and above. According to RBI's FAQs, for cheques of what value may banks consider making Positive Pay mandatory?

solution.explanation: Under Positive Pay, the drawer sends key cheque details to the bank in advance, and CTS cross-checks them. Availing it is at the account holder's discretion, but banks may consider making it mandatory for cheques of ₹5,00,000 and above.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1 lakh is the free-collection limit for savings accounts; ₹2 lakh and ₹10 lakh are not RBI's thresholds here.

State Co-operative Banks were brought under DICGC deposit insurance
All State Co-operative Banks were converted into Regional Rural Banks
State Co-operative Banks were merged with NABARD

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that co-operative banks came under RBI's regulatory ambit on 1 March 1966, and on 2 July 1966, 12 State Co-operative Banks were included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act.
steps: 1 Mar 1966 → co-op banks under RBI regulation
solution.why_others_wrong: RRBs came only in 1975; deposit insurance reached co-operative banks in 1971; NABARD was set up in 1982.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 12 State Co-operative Banks were included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, by what time on each business day must a bank disclose on its website the interest rates it pays on bulk deposits?

options.text: 12:00 noon, with a grace time up to 12:30 pm
At the close of business of the previous day
10:00 am, with a grace time up to 10:10 am

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank sets fixed rates for FCNR(B) US dollar deposits for December 2026. The overnight Alternative Reference Rate for USD on the last working day of November is 4.30% (assume). Under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, what are the maximum rates it can offer on a 2-year and on a 4-year deposit?

solution.concept: Interest rate ceilings on FCNR(B) deposits
solution.explanation: Fixed-rate FCNR(B) deposits are capped with reference to the overnight ARR for the currency as on the last working day of the preceding month: ARR + 250 bps for 1 year to less than 3 years and ARR + 350 bps for 3 to 5 years. 4.30 + 2.50 = 6.80%; 4.30 + 3.50 = 7.80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.80% for both ignores the higher ceiling for 3–5 years; 7.30%/8.30% and 5.30%/6.30% use wrong spreads.

fact_checks.claim: One year to less than three years: Overnight ARR for the respective currency / Swap plus 250 basis points; Three years and above upto and including five years: Overnight ARR for the respective currency / Swap plus 350 basis points

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A depositor's unclaimed deposit of ₹7.5 lakh (with interest) had been moved to the DEA Fund when it was insured by DICGC (cover ₹5 lakh). The bank is now in liquidation and she claims the money. Under RBI's Miscellaneous Directions, how is the claim settled?

options.text: The Fund pays ₹5 lakh to the liquidator, who pays her; the liquidator pays the remaining ₹2.5 lakh first and then seeks reimbursement from the Fund
DICGC pays her ₹5 lakh directly and the remaining ₹2.5 lakh is forfeited
The Fund pays the entire ₹7.5 lakh to the liquidator in advance
She must claim from the bank's assets only, since the money is no longer in the bank

solution.concept: DEA Fund claims when a bank is in liquidation
solution.explanation: If the deposit was DICGC-insured when transferred, the liquidator claims from the Fund an amount equal to what could have been claimed from DICGC (₹5 lakh) and pays the depositor. The excess (₹2.5 lakh) is paid by the liquidator first and claimed from the Fund only by way of reimbursement.
steps: Insured part: min(7.5, 5) = ₹5 lakh paid by Fund upfront
Excess ₹2.5 lakh: liquidator pays, then is reimbursed
solution.why_others_wrong: The Fund does not prefund the excess; the amount is not forfeited; the claim is routed through the liquidator and the Fund, not the bank's assets alone.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Fund pays ₹5 lakh to the liquidator, who pays her; the liquidator pays the remaining ₹2.5 lakh first and then seeks reimbursement from the Fund

fact_checks.claim: If the deposits of a customer / depositor were covered by DICGC insurance at the time of transfer to the DEA Fund, then the Liquidator can claim an amount equivalent to what could have been claimed from DICGC ... If the above deposit amount is more than the insurance cover of DICGC, then the Liquidator shall claim the amount in excess of DICGC insurance cover only on reimbursement basis

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Anu's term deposit of ₹2,00,000 at 7.00% matured, but she collected the proceeds only 73 days later. The bank's savings deposit rate is 2.50%. Under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, what interest (simple, 365-day year) is due for the 73 days after maturity?

solution.concept: Interest on matured but unclaimed term deposits
solution.explanation: A matured, unpaid term deposit attracts the savings account rate or the contracted rate, whichever is lower. min(2.50%, 7.00%) = 2.50%: 2,00,000 × 2.5% × 73/365 = ₹1,000.
steps: Rate = lower of SB rate and contracted rate = 2.50%
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,800 uses the contracted 7%; interest is not nil; ₹1,900 uses neither rate.

fact_checks.claim: If a Term Deposit (TD) matures and proceeds are unpaid, the amount left unclaimed with a bank, shall attract rate of interest as applicable to savings account or the contracted rate of interest on the matured TD, whichever is lower

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In a USD/INR buy/sell swap auction conducted by RBI (such as the USD 5 billion, three-year swap of May 2026), what does a participating bank do?

options.text: Lends rupees to RBI against government securities
Borrows dollars from RBI to repay external loans
Buys US dollars from RBI now and sells them back later, absorbing rupee liquidity
Sells US dollars to RBI now and agrees to buy the same amount back at the end of the swap, so rupee liquidity is injected for the tenor

solution.concept: FX swaps as a liquidity tool
solution.explanation: In a buy/sell swap from RBI's side, a bank sells US dollars to RBI and simultaneously agrees to buy the same amount back at the end of the swap period. RBI pays rupees in the near leg, injecting durable rupee liquidity for the swap's tenor; banks bid the premium they will pay to RBI.
steps: Near leg: bank sells USD, gets ₹ → liquidity injected
Far leg: bank buys back USD
solution.why_others_wrong: The second option describes a sell/buy (absorbing) swap; the others are not swaps.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Sells US dollars to RBI now and agrees to buy the same amount back at the end of the swap, so rupee liquidity is injected for the tenor

fact_checks.claim: The swap is in the nature of a simple buy/sell foreign exchange swap from the Reserve Bank side. A bank shall sell US dollars to the Reserve Bank and simultaneously agree to buy the same amount of US dollars at the end of the swap period

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rates on Advances Directions, 2025, which floating rate loans must be linked to an external benchmark, and what restriction applies to the choice of benchmark?

options.text: All loans of all borrowers; the benchmark must be the bank's own MCLR
All floating rate personal or retail loans and floating rate loans to MSMEs; a bank must use one uniform external benchmark within a loan category
Only floating rate home loans; a bank may use different benchmarks for different borrowers in a category
Only loans to micro enterprises; the benchmark must be the 91-day T-bill yield

solution.explanation: The Directions require all floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.) and floating rate loans to MSMEs to be benchmarked to an external benchmark. To ensure transparency and standardisation, a bank must adopt a uniform external benchmark within a loan category; multiple benchmarks within a category are not allowed.
steps: One external benchmark per loan category
solution.why_others_wrong: Coverage is wider than home loans and narrower than all loans; MCLR is internal; there is no single mandated benchmark such as the 91-day T-bill.
solution.final_answer: Option B: All floating rate personal or retail loans and floating rate loans to MSMEs; a bank must use one uniform external benchmark within a loan category

fact_checks.claim: All floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, etc.), and floating rate loans extended by banks to Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) shall be benchmarked to an External Benchmark Rate
a bank must adopt a uniform external benchmark within a loan category; in other words, the adoption of multiple benchmarks by the same bank is not allowed within a loan category

OMO purchases of ₹1,00,000 crore in two tranches and a USD 5 billion swap

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the RBI MPC and Monetary Policy Process Regulations, 2016, at what time are the minutes of an MPC meeting released?

At noon on the day of the policy announcement
At 5 pm on the last working day of the month
At 5 pm on the 14th day from the policy day (or the next working day if it is a holiday in Mumbai)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank's funds (other than equity) for computing MCLR are spread, from the longest maturity bucket down, as 15.1%, 11.8%, 9.3%, 16.9%, 24.3% and 10.5%. No single bucket exceeds 30%. Under RBI's Interest Rates on Advances Directions, 2025, to what tenor must its MCLR correspond?

options.text: The weighted average tenor of the first three maturity buckets, which together first exceed 30% (36.2%)
The tenor of the first two buckets (26.9%)
The weighted average tenor of all six buckets
The tenor of the largest bucket (24.3%)

solution.explanation: MCLR corresponds to the tenor of the single largest maturity bucket if it exceeds 30% of funds; otherwise to the weighted average tenor of two or more buckets that together account for more than 30%, taken cumulatively in descending order of maturity. Cumulative: 15.1, 26.9, 36.2 → the first three buckets.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24.3% is below 30%; all six buckets are not needed; two buckets give only 26.9%.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After peaking at 15% in July 1989, when was the CRR first reduced, according to RBI's table of CRR changes?

solution.explanation: RBI's table shows CRR at 15% from 1 July 1989 (with additional incremental requirements) until it was cut to 14.5% on 17 April 1993, and 14% on 15 May 1993.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 July 1991 was a Bank Rate change; 25 October 1997 and 1 July 1974 are other CRR changes.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to a footnote in RBI's table of CRR changes, what special relief was given to banks for the 'millennium change' (Y2K)?

options.text: Cash in hand could be counted for CRR from 1 December 1999 to 31 January 2000, but not simultaneously for SLR
CRR was reduced to zero for one fortnight
Banks could count their SLR securities towards CRR

solution.explanation: To help banks tide over the millennium change, cash in hand maintained for CRR was treated as eligible for CRR for two months (1 December 1999–31 January 2000); that cash could not simultaneously count as an SLR asset. Normally CRR is a balance with RBI.
steps: Y2K: cash in hand counted for 2 months, not double-counted for SLR
solution.why_others_wrong: CRR was not suspended or cut to zero, and SLR securities never count for CRR.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Cash in hand could be counted for CRR from 1 December 1999 to 31 January 2000, but not simultaneously for SLR

fact_checks.claim: to facilitate banks to tide over the contingency during the millennium change, it has been decided to treat cash in hand maintained by banks for compliance of CRR for a limited period of two months commencing from December 1,1999 to January 31, 2000. The cash in hand which will be counted for CRR purpose, during the above period cannot be treatrd as eligible asset for SLR purpose simulataneously

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's table of CRR changes shows a series of increases in 1981–82. What was the highest CRR reached in that phase, before cuts later in 1982?

solution.explanation: CRR rose from 6.5% (July 1981) through 7%, 7.25% and 7.5% to 7.75% on 29 January 1982, and was then cut to 7.25% (April 1982) and 7% (June 1982).
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5% was the preceding step; 8.5% (1983) and 15% (1989) belong to later phases.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's table shows the CRR raised in 1973 from 3% to 5% (29 June), 6% (8 September) and 7% (22 September). For a bank with net demand and time liabilities of ₹1,000 crore, how much additional cash had to be kept with RBI by the end of September 1973 compared with June 1973?

solution.explanation: CRR went from 3% to 7%, an increase of 4 percentage points: 4% × ₹1,000 crore = ₹40 crore of additional impounded cash.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹20 crore counts only the first step; ₹70 crore is the total CRR, not the increase; ₹10 crore one 1% step.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's table of reserve requirement changes, at what level was the Statutory Liquidity Ratio first prescribed, from 16 March 1949?

solution.explanation: SLR was introduced with the Banking Companies Act, 1949, which came into force on 16 March 1949; RBI's table shows the first SLR at 20% from that date.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% came later; 38.5% was the 1990 peak; 18% is today's level.

fact_checks.claim: Statutory Liquidity Ratio: 20 16-03-1949

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's table, the SLR was raised to 30% in which year?

solution.explanation: RBI's table shows SLR at 29% from 4 August 1972 and 30% from 17 November 1972, then 32% (December 1973) and 33% (July 1974).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's chronology, by mid-1985 the statutory pre-emption of banks' resources through SLR and CRR together had exceeded:

solution.explanation: RBI's chronology records that by mid-1985 the combined SLR and CRR pre-emption exceeded 45%; after the CRR was raised to 15% in July 1989, it went above 53%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 53% was the 1989 level; 25% and 60% are not in the chronology.

fact_checks.claim: By mid-1985, the statutory preemption on banks' resources in the form of the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) exceeded 45%

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In 1992 SLR was 38.5% of net DTL as on 3 April 1992, plus 30% on any increase in net DTL over that level. A bank's net DTL was ₹1,000 crore on 3 April 1992 and ₹1,200 crore later in the year. What SLR assets did it need?

solution.explanation: Base: 38.5% × 1,000 = ₹385 crore. Increment: 30% × (1,200 − 1,000) = ₹60 crore. Total ₹445 crore — less than 38.5% on the whole ₹1,200 crore (₹462 crore), easing the burden on new liabilities.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹462 crore applies 38.5% to all liabilities; ₹360 crore applies 30% to all; ₹385 crore ignores the increase.

fact_checks.claim: 38.5 + # (29-02-1992); + : SLR on net DTL as on April 3, 1992. # : In addition there was 30% SLR on the increase in net DTL over April 3, 1992 level

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's first Bank Rate (5 July 1935) was 3.5%. According to RBI's table, to what was it cut on 28 November 1935, a level that lasted until November 1951?

solution.explanation: The Bank Rate was cut to 3% on 28 November 1935 and raised back to 3.5% only on 15 November 1951.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other levels do not appear for that period.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Amid the inflation of the oil-shock years, RBI's table shows the Bank Rate raised from 7% (31 May 1973) to what level on 23 July 1974?

solution.explanation: The Bank Rate went from 7% (31 May 1973) to 9% (23 July 1974) and stayed there until it was raised to 10% in July 1981.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% came in 1981 and 12% in 1991; 8% is not the 1974 level.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's table shows the Bank Rate at 12% from 9 October 1991, then 11% (16 April 1997), 10% (26 June 1997) and 9% (22 October 1997). What was the total cut in 1997, and what happened next?

options.text: 100 bps; it was raised to 12% in 1998
300 bps; it was raised by 200 bps to 11% in January 1998
300 bps; it was cut further to 8% in January 1998

solution.explanation: 12% → 9% in 1997 = 300 bps of cuts. On 17 January 1998, amid the Asian crisis, it was raised to 11%.
solution.why_others_wrong: The January 1998 move was an increase; the 1997 cut was 300 bps.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 300 bps; it was raised by 200 bps to 11% in January 1998

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to MoSPI's CPI (base 2024=100) release for September 2026, from how many markets are real-time prices collected?

options.text: 1,407 urban markets (including online markets) and 1,465 villages

solution.explanation: Prices are collected from 1,407 urban markets (including online markets) and 1,465 villages covering all States/UTs, by NSO field staff on a weekly roster; the response rate in September 2026 was 100%.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other numbers are not in the release.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1,407 urban markets (including online markets) and 1,465 villages
