Direct interface with customers is not permitted

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following can a scheduled commercial bank engage as a Business Correspondent under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025?

solution.explanation: Eligible BCs include specified individuals, NGOs/MFIs under Societies/Trust Acts and Section 8 companies, co-operative societies, post offices, payments banks, companies (other than NBFCs) with large and widespread retail outlets, and non-deposit-taking NBFCs subject to safeguards.
steps: Listed: payments banks, post offices, co-operatives, NGOs/MFIs, retail companies, NBFC-ND
Not listed: deposit-taking NBFCs, ARCs, chit funds
solution.why_others_wrong: Only non-deposit-taking NBFCs are allowed; ARCs and chit fund companies are not in the list.

fact_checks.claim: A bank may engage the following individuals / entities as BCs: ... (4) Post Offices (5) Payments Bank; and (6) Companies [other than Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)] ... (7) Non-deposit taking NBFCs (NBFCs-ND)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A person holds two savings accounts, each with a RuPay debit card, and both are PMJDY-type accounts. According to SBI's FAQs on PMJDY, how does the free accidental insurance cover attached to RuPay cards apply?

options.text: It is available separately on each card
It doubles to ₹4 lakh because of the two cards
It is available in only one account
It is lost on both cards because of the duplication

solution.concept: RuPay card accident insurance under PMJDY
solution.explanation: SBI's FAQs say that where a person has two or more accounts and RuPay debit cards, the accidental insurance cover is available only in one account.
steps: Multiple RuPay cards → cover in one account only
solution.why_others_wrong: The cover is neither multiplied nor forfeited; it is limited to one account.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It is available in only one account

fact_checks.claim: If someone has two or more accounts and two or more RuPay Debit Cards, whether accidental insurance cove is available in each account / each card? ANS : Accidental insurance cover is available only in one account

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Before engaging a Business Correspondent, a bank must carry out due diligence. Which of the following is NOT one of the aspects RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025 say this may cover?

options.text: The BC's holding of a licence from the State Government as a moneylender
Ability to implement technology solutions in rendering financial services

solution.explanation: The due diligence may cover reputation/market standing, financial soundness, management and corporate governance, cash handling ability and ability to implement technology solutions. A moneylender licence is not among them.
steps: Listed: reputation, financial soundness, governance, cash handling, technology
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are named in the Directions.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The BC's holding of a licence from the State Government as a moneylender

fact_checks.claim: The due diligence exercise may, inter alia, cover aspects such as (i) reputation / market standing, (ii) financial soundness, (iii) management and corporate governance, (iv) cash handling ability and (v) ability to implement technology solutions in rendering financial services

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: During a year a bank opens 120 full-time Banking Outlets, 26 of them in Unbanked Rural Centres (URCs). It also opens three part-time outlets in URCs, each working 5 hours a day on 4 days a week. Applying the pro-rata method in RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025, does the bank meet the norm for URCs?

options.text: Yes; URC outlets are 29 of 123 (about 23.6%), which rounds up to the norm
Yes; URC outlets are 29 of 120 (about 24.2%), and the norm is 20%
No; URC outlets are 26 of 120 (about 21.7%), as part-time outlets are ignored
No; URC outlets are 28.4 of 122.4 (about 23.2%), against the required 25% (30.6)

solution.concept: 25% Unbanked Rural Centre norm with part-time outlets
solution.explanation: At least 25% of the Banking Outlets opened in a year must be in URCs. Part-time outlets count pro rata against a 20-hour week (4 hours × 5 days), with at most 4 hours a day counted, in both the numerator (if in a URC) and the denominator. Each part-time outlet = 4 × 4 ÷ 20 = 0.8. Denominator = 120 + 2.4 = 122.4; numerator = 26 + 2.4 = 28.4, about 23.2%, below 25% (which would need 30.6).
solution.why_others_wrong: Part-time outlets count pro rata, not as whole outlets; they are not ignored; the norm is 25%, not 20%.
solution.final_answer: Option D: No; URC outlets are 28.4 of 122.4 (about 23.2%), against the required 25% (30.6)

fact_checks.claim: At least 25 percent of the total number of 'Banking Outlets' opened during a financial year shall be opened in Unbanked Rural Centres (URCs) ... A 'Part-time Banking Outlet', opened in any Centre, will be counted and added to the denominator as well as numerator on pro rata basis
The prescribed period for Banking Outlet is 4 hours per day for 5 days (minimum of 20 hours spread over 5 days) this will remain constant denominator ... a maximum of 4 hours per day will be counted

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements based on SBI's FAQs on Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, which describe the basic savings bank deposit (BSBD) account under RBI guidelines:
I. The holder of a BSBD account is not eligible to open another BSBD account in the same or any other bank.
II. There is no upper limit on the balance in the account, and no initial deposit is required.
III. A cheque book cannot be issued in a PMJDY account.
Which of the above are correct?

solution.explanation: A BSBD holder cannot open another BSBD account in any bank and must declare this. There is no minimum or maximum balance and no initial deposit. Cheque books are available: 25 leaves a year free for branch-channel accounts, and on request for accounts opened at CSP outlets.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: The holder of a BSBD account shall not be eligible to open another BSBD account in the same bank or any other bank
Maximum balance amount ANS : No upper limit ... Whether initial deposit is required? ANS : No
Cheque book with 25 cheque leaves can be issued free of cost per year for accounts opened at branches. Accounts opened at CSP outlets would also be issued cheque book on request

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) framework, how are Level 1 assets counted in the stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA)?

options.text: Without any limit and without any haircut, at no more than their current market value
Up to 40% of the stock of HQLA, without a haircut
Without any limit, but after a uniform 50% haircut
Up to 60% of the stock of HQLA, after a 15% haircut

solution.explanation: RBI's Asset Liability Management Directions say Level 1 assets can be included in the stock of HQLA without any limit and without applying any haircut, valued at no more than current market value. (From 1 April 2026, Level 1 government securities attract the LAF/MSF haircuts.) Caps of 40% and 15% and haircuts of 15% and 50% apply to Level 2A and Level 2B assets.
steps: Level 2 → 40% cap; Level 2A 15% haircut; Level 2B 50% haircut and 15% cap
solution.why_others_wrong: The 15% and 50% haircuts and the 40% cap belong to Level 2 assets, not Level 1.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Without any limit and without any haircut, at no more than their current market value

fact_checks.claim: Level 1 assets can be included in the stock of HQLA without any limit as also without applying any haircut and shall be valued at an amount not greater than their current market value

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Within its mandatory SLR holding, up to what share of its NDTL may a bank count government securities as Level 1 HQLA for the LCR, taking the MSF window and the Facility to Avail Liquidity for LCR (FALLCR) together?

options.text: 15% of NDTL (3% under MSF and 12% under FALLCR)
18% of NDTL (2% under MSF and 16% under FALLCR)

solution.explanation: Level 1 assets include government securities within the mandatory SLR to the extent allowed by RBI under MSF, currently 2% of NDTL, and under FALLCR, currently 16% of NDTL, i.e. 18% of NDTL in all, besides securities held in excess of the SLR.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16% and 2% are only one of the two windows; 3%/12% are not RBI's figures.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 18% of NDTL (2% under MSF and 16% under FALLCR)

fact_checks.claim: Within the mandatory SLR requirement, Government securities to the extent allowed by RBI under (a) MSF currently 2 per cent of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL), and (b) Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio (FALLCR) currently 16 per cent of a bank's NDTL

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A plain-vanilla bond of a non-financial company, rated 'A' by an eligible credit rating agency, trades in a deep and active market and meets RBI's price-stability test. How is it treated in a bank's stock of HQLA for the LCR?

options.text: As a Level 2A asset, with a minimum haircut of 15%
It cannot be included in HQLA at all
As a Level 2B asset, with a minimum haircut of 50%
As a Level 1 asset, with no haircut

solution.concept: Rating bands for corporate bonds in HQLA
solution.explanation: Corporate bonds rated AA- or above (not issued by a bank, FI or NBFC) are Level 2A assets with a 15% haircut. Corporate debt rated between A+ and BBB- that meets the market conditions is a Level 2B asset with a 50% haircut. An 'A' rated bond therefore falls in Level 2B.
solution.why_others_wrong: Level 2A needs AA- or better; corporate bonds are never Level 1; an A-rated non-financial bond meeting the conditions is eligible.
solution.final_answer: Option C: As a Level 2B asset, with a minimum haircut of 50%

fact_checks.claim: Level 2A: Corporate bonds rated AA- or above by an Eligible Credit Rating Agency (ECRA), and not issued by a bank / financial institution / NBFC; minimum 15 per cent haircut
Level 2B: Corporate debt securities, including commercial paper, subject to a 50 per cent haircut ... have a long-term credit rating from an ECRA between A+ and BBB-

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In computing the LCR denominator (total net cash outflows over the next 30 days), up to what limit can a bank count its expected cash inflows?

options.text: Up to 50% of its total expected cash outflows
Up to 100% of its total expected cash outflows
Up to 25% of its stock of HQLA
Up to 75% of its total expected cash outflows

solution.explanation: Total net cash outflows = total expected cash outflows − Min(total expected cash inflows; 75% of total expected cash outflows). The cap ensures that a bank always holds HQLA of at least 25% of its outflows and does not rely only on expected inflows.
solution.why_others_wrong: The cap is 75% of outflows, not 50% or 100%, and it is not linked to HQLA.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Up to 75% of its total expected cash outflows

fact_checks.claim: Total Net Cash Outflows in the next 30 calendar days = total expected cash outflows - Min (total expected cash inflows; 75 per cent of total expected cash outflows)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank holds Level 1 assets of ₹400 crore (already at their HQLA value), Level 2A assets with a market value of ₹200 crore and Level 2B assets with a market value of ₹300 crore, with no short-term repo or reverse repo to unwind. Applying RBI's minimum haircuts and the 15% (Level 2B) and 40% (Level 2) caps, what is its stock of HQLA (approximately)?

solution.concept: Stock of HQLA with haircuts and caps
solution.explanation: Adjusted Level 2A = 85% × 200 = 170; adjusted Level 2B = 50% × 300 = 150. Adjustment for the 15% cap = max[150 − 15/85 × (400 + 170), 150 − 15/60 × 400, 0] = max[49.4, 50, 0] = 50. Adjustment for the 40% cap = max[(170 + 150 − 50) − 2/3 × 400, 0] = 270 − 266.7 = 3.3. Stock of HQLA = 400 + 170 + 150 − 50 − 3.3 ≈ ₹666.7 crore. Check: Level 2 is then exactly 40% and Level 2B exactly 15% of the stock.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹720 crore ignores both caps; ₹670 crore applies only the 15% cap; ₹900 crore ignores haircuts and caps.

fact_checks.claim: Stock of HQLA = Level 1 + Level 2A + Level 2B - Adjustment for 15 per cent cap - Adjustment for 40 per cent cap; Adjustment for 15 per cent cap = Max [{Adjusted Level 2B - 15/85 * (Adjusted Level 1 + Adjusted Level 2A)}, {Adjusted Level 2B - 15/60 * Adjusted Level 1}, 0]; Adjustment for 40 per cent cap = Max {(Adjusted Level 2A + Adjusted Level 2B - Adjustment for 15 per cent cap) - 2/3 * (Adjusted Level 1 assets), 0}
A minimum 15 per cent haircut shall be applied to the current market value of each Level 2A asset; A minimum haircut of 50 per cent shall be applied to the current market value of each Level 2B asset

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following assets of a bank, each meeting RBI's market-liquidity tests:
I. Commercial paper issued by an NBFC, rated equivalent to AA+.
II. Equity shares of a non-financial company included in the Nifty 50 index.
III. A bond of a non-financial company rated BBB-.
Which of them can be counted as Level 2B HQLA under RBI's LCR framework?

solution.explanation: Level 2B includes common equity shares in the Nifty or Sensex not issued by a bank, FI or NBFC, and corporate debt rated between A+ and BBB- not issued by a bank, FI, PD or NBFC. Paper issued by an NBFC is excluded from both Level 2A and Level 2B, however highly rated, because of its wrong-way risk.
steps: II: Nifty share of non-financial firm → Level 2B
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I fails because instruments issued by NBFCs and other financial entities are excluded; II and III both qualify.
solution.final_answer: Option C: II and III only

fact_checks.claim: Common Equity Shares which satisfy all of the following conditions: (a) not issued by a bank / financial institution / NBFC or any of its affiliated entities; (b) included in NSE CNX Nifty index and / or S&P BSE Sensex index

Commercial Papers, with a short-term rating equivalent to the long-term rating of AA- or above by an ECRA, and not issued by a bank / PD / financial institution or any of its affiliated entities; Corporate debt securities ... not issued by a bank / financial institution / primary dealer / NBFC ... long-term credit rating from an ECRA between A+ and BBB-

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: How does RBI describe the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026 (RB-IOS, 2026)?

options.text: A cost-free, expeditious and non-adversarial alternate grievance redress mechanism
A fee-based fast-track tribunal under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
A statutory consumer court set up under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
An arbitration mechanism under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs describe RB-IOS, 2026 as a cost-free, expeditious and non-adversarial alternate grievance redress mechanism for customer complaints involving deficiency in service by the regulated entities it covers. It is not a court, tribunal or arbitration.
steps: RB-IOS → free, quick, non-adversarial alternate grievance redress
solution.why_others_wrong: It is not a consumer court, an arbitration under the 1996 Act, or a fee-based tribunal.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A cost-free, expeditious and non-adversarial alternate grievance redress mechanism

fact_checks.claim: The Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026 (RB-IOS, 2026 / the Scheme) is a cost-free, expeditious and non-adversarial alternate grievance redress mechanism for customer complaints involving deficiency in service by Regulated Entities covered under the Scheme

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Ritu complained to her bank on 1 September 2026. The bank rejected her complaint by a reply dated 12 September 2026, and she is not satisfied. Under RB-IOS, 2026, when can she approach the RBI Ombudsman?

options.text: Only after 30 days from her complaint, and by 11 December 2026
Immediately, and no later than 90 days from the bank's reply, i.e. by 11 December 2026
Immediately, and by 12 March 2027 (six months from the reply)
Only after 30 days from her complaint, i.e. from 1 October 2026, and by 30 December 2026

solution.concept: When a complaint can be filed
solution.explanation: The 30-day wait applies only when the regulated entity has not replied. A complainant who has received a reply and is dissatisfied may approach the Ombudsman at once. The complaint must be made within 90 days from the expiry of the reply period or from the RE's last communication, whichever is later; here the last communication is 12 September, so the limit is 12 September + 90 days = 11 December 2026.
steps: Reply received and not satisfied → no need to wait 30 days
solution.why_others_wrong: Waiting 30 days is needed only when there is no reply; six months is not the limit.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Immediately, and no later than 90 days from the bank's reply, i.e. by 11 December 2026

fact_checks.claim: A complaint can be filed before the RBI Ombudsman if the complainant has not received any reply within 30 days ... or if the complainant is not satisfied with the reply/resolution provided by the Regulated Entity. The complaint must be made to the RBI Ombudsman within 90 days from the date on which the above timeline expires or the date of the last communication from the concerned Regulated Entity, whichever is later

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RB-IOS, 2026, what must happen before the RBI Ombudsman passes an Award against a regulated entity?

options.text: The complainant must deposit 10% of the disputed amount
Both the complainant and the regulated entity must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, orally or in writing
The Appellate Authority must approve the draft Award
The regulated entity's Board must consent to the Award

solution.explanation: If a complaint is not settled and not liable to rejection, the Ombudsman examines the record and may pass an Award directing remedial action or compensation. Before passing it, both parties are given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either orally or in writing.
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no deposit, no prior approval by the Appellate Authority and no Board consent requirement.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both the complainant and the regulated entity must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, orally or in writing

fact_checks.claim: Before passing an Award, both the complainant and the Regulated Entity are given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either orally or in writing

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements based on RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25 (released 1 December 2025):
I. Complaints received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman per lakh accounts fell from 8.9 in 2023-24 to 7.7 in 2024-25.
II. 91.22 per cent of complaints received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman were lodged digitally, through the CMS portal or e-mail.
III. Complaints from individuals made up less than half of the complaints received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The report records that complaints per lakh accounts (deposit and credit) fell from 8.9 to 7.7 and that 91.22% of complaints at the ORBIOs were lodged digitally. Individuals accounted for 87.19% of complaints, so statement III is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing III are wrong; 'II only' omits the correct statement I.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Complaints received at ORBIOs per lakh accounts decreased from 8.9 complaints in F.Y.2023-24 to 7.7 complaints in F.Y.2024-25

Out of the total complaints received at the ORBIOs, 91.22 per cent of the complaints were lodged through digital mode using CMS portal or email. The share of complaints from individuals in the total complaints was the highest at 2,58,365 (87.19 per cent)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In 2024-25 the Offices of RBI Ombudsman disposed of 2,90,567 complaints, of which 62.16 per cent (1,80,621) were maintainable. Of the maintainable complaints, 51.91 per cent were resolved in the complainant's favour through mutual settlement, conciliation or mediation, and 43.36 per cent were rejected. About how many complaints were resolved through settlement, conciliation or mediation?

solution.explanation: The 51.91% share applies to maintainable complaints only: 1,80,621 × 0.5191 ≈ 93,760 (the report gives 93,752). Applying 51.91% to all 2,90,567 disposals gives about 1,50,830, which is wrong; about 78,320 is the rejected share (43.36%).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,50,830 uses the wrong base; 78,320 is the number rejected; 1,12,330 has no basis in the data.

fact_checks.claim: Of these maintainable complaints 93,752 complaints (51.91 per cent) were resolved in favour of the complainant through mutual settlement, conciliation or mediation; 78,323 (43.36 per cent) complaints were rejected by RBI Ombudsmen
Out of the 2,90,567 complaints disposed by the ORBIOs during F.Y.2024-25, 62.16 per cent (1,80,621 complaints) were disposed as maintainable complaints

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Customers file complaints against four NBFCs registered with RBI, none of them an excluded type (figures as per the audited balance sheet of the previous year):
P. A deposit-taking NBFC with assets of ₹60 crore.
Q. A non-deposit-taking NBFC with customer interface and assets of ₹150 crore.
R. A deposit-taking NBFC with assets of ₹20 crore.
S. A non-deposit-taking NBFC with customer interface and assets of ₹90 crore.
Against which of them can a complaint be filed under RB-IOS, 2026?

solution.explanation: RB-IOS, 2026 covers NBFCs (other than the excluded types) that either are authorised to accept deposits or have customer interface with assets of ₹100 crore and above. The ₹100 crore threshold applies only to the customer-interface limb, so every deposit-taking NBFC (P and R) is covered whatever its size; Q (₹150 crore) is covered; S (₹90 crore, non-deposit) is not.
steps: Deposit-taking → covered regardless of size (P, R)
Customer interface → needs ≥ ₹100 crore (Q yes, S no)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'P and Q only' wrongly applies the ₹100 crore test to deposit-taking R; 'Q only' does the same to P and R; S is below the threshold.
solution.final_answer: Option A: P, Q and R only

fact_checks.claim: NBFCs: all NBFCs registered with RBI, excluding Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies, IDF-NBFCs, NBFC-IFCs, NOFHCs, Primary Dealers and Mortgage Guarantee Companies, which either are authorized to accept deposits or have customer interface with asset size of Rs 100 crore and above as on the date of the audited balance sheet of the previous financial year

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Assuming every procedural condition is met, which of the following grievances is maintainable before the RBI Ombudsman under RB-IOS, 2026?

options.text: A borrower's complaint that the bank has not returned his title deeds after he closed his home loan
A bank officer's grievance that he was denied promotion
An IT vendor's dispute with a bank over unpaid software licence fees
A customer's grievance against the personal conduct of a bank's executive director

solution.explanation: RB-IOS, 2026 deals with deficiency in service to customers. Disputes between a vendor and a regulated entity, disputes involving the employee-employer relationship, and grievances against the management or executives of the RE are expressly non-maintainable. Failure to return property documents after loan closure is a deficiency in service to a customer.
solution.why_others_wrong: The vendor, employee and management grievances fall under the excluded categories.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A borrower's complaint that the bank has not returned his title deeds after he closed his home loan

fact_checks.claim: Disputes between a vendor and a Regulated Entity. Grievances against Management or Executives of a Regulated Entity ... Disputes involving employee-employer relationship of a Regulated Entity
Any customer aggrieved by an act or omission of a Regulated Entity resulting in deficiency in service may file a complaint under the Scheme

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, besides the Information Technology Act, 2000, which data-protection law must banks continuously adhere to in their digital banking operations?

options.text: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 only

solution.explanation: The general guidelines require banks offering digital banking to adhere continuously to the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and other legal requirements, with legal jurisdiction within India, along with FEMA, KYC/AML and DPSS instructions.
steps: Digital banking → IT Act, 2000 + DPDP Act, 2023
solution.why_others_wrong: The RTI Act and CICRA are not the data-protection law named; the PSS Act is relevant but is not a data-protection law.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

fact_checks.claim: The provisions (as amended from time to time) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements. The jurisdiction of legal settlement would be within India

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank offers only a 'view only' digital banking facility. Under RBI's Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, which of the following can it offer through this facility?

options.text: A personal loan sanctioned and disbursed online
A bill payment from the savings account
Downloadable application forms for a loan
An IMPS transfer to another bank

solution.explanation: A view-only facility allows only services that do not alter the customer's assets or liabilities, such as balance enquiry, balance viewing and statement download. Loans, fund transfers and other facilities that create a liability or move funds cannot be provided, though downloadable forms for them can.
steps: View only → no change in assets/liabilities
Loans, transfers, payments → transactional facility needed
solution.why_others_wrong: Loans, IMPS transfers and bill payments move funds or create liabilities, so they need a transactional facility.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Downloadable application forms for a loan

fact_checks.claim: View Only Banking Facility – A feature of digital banking channels which only allows banking services that do not alter the asset or liability of the customer viz. balance enquiry, balance viewing, account statement download, etc. Note: Loans, funds transfers, and other such facilities ... cannot be provided by banks having view only facility over digital channels. However, banks providing view only facility can provide downloadable forms for such facilities

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, what must a bank ensure when it offers mobile banking through USSD or SMS rather than a mobile app?

options.text: The service must be restricted to balance enquiry only
The service must be network independent, usable by customers of all mobile network operators
The service must be limited to customers of a single partner telecom operator
The service must be offered only to customers with smartphones

solution.explanation: The Directions define mobile banking to include mobile applications, USSD and SMS. A bank offering mobile banking other than through apps must ensure that customers across mobile network operators can use it, i.e. the service must be network independent.
solution.why_others_wrong: Tying the service to one operator, to balance enquiry or to smartphones contradicts the rule and the purpose of USSD/SMS banking.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The service must be network independent, usable by customers of all mobile network operators

fact_checks.claim: Banks offering mobile banking service (other than through mobile applications) must ensure that customers across mobile network operators can avail of the service, i.e., the service shall be network independent

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Digital Rupee FAQs (updated October 2026), how many participants, banks and non-banks, were in the wholesale e₹ (e₹-W) pilot?

solution.explanation: The FAQs say there are currently 16 participants in the e₹-W pilot, including banks and non-banks. Separately, 19 banks offer retail CBDC wallets, and e₹-W has four use cases.
solution.why_others_wrong: 19 is the number of banks offering retail wallets; 4 is the number of e₹-W use cases; 9 has no basis.

fact_checks.claim: Currently, there are 16 participants in the e₹-W pilot, which includes banks and non-banks

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: When a bank releases a new version of its mobile banking app, RBI's Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026 require it to deactivate older versions within what time?

options.text: Only when customers voluntarily update the app
Within 30 days of the release of the newer version
Within one year of the release of the newer version
In a phased, time-bound manner not exceeding six months from the release of the newer version

solution.explanation: Banks must deactivate older application versions in a phased but time-bound manner, not exceeding six months from the date of release of a newer version, so that only one version (apart from the overlap period) is maintained on each platform.
steps: New version released → old one deactivated within 6 months
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 days and one year are not the prescribed limit, and leaving it to customers defeats the control.
solution.final_answer: Option D: In a phased, time-bound manner not exceeding six months from the release of the newer version

fact_checks.claim: deactivating older application versions in a phased but time-bound manner (not exceeding six months from the date of release of newer version) i.e., maintaining only one version (excluding the overlap period while phasing out older version) of the mobile application on a platform / operating system

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026, when must a bank's mobile application require the user to re-authenticate?

options.text: Each time the user launches the app, and whenever the device or app remains unused for a designated period
Only once, at the time of first registration on the device
Only when the user changes the mobile handset

solution.explanation: The mobile application shall require re-authentication whenever the device or application remains unused for a designated period and each time the user launches it. It must also not store passwords or keys on the device and must wipe sensitive data from memory when the user exits.
solution.why_others_wrong: One-time authentication, amount thresholds or handset change alone do not meet the requirement.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Each time the user launches the app, and whenever the device or app remains unused for a designated period

fact_checks.claim: The mobile application shall require re-authentication whenever the device or application remains unused for a designated period and each time the user launches the application

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the eligibility criteria for a commercial bank to launch a transactional digital banking facility under RBI's Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025:
I. The bank's 'Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy' (GAICA) report must be certified by CERT-In empanelled third-party auditor(s).
II. The bank must meet the minimum paid-up capital or net worth under its licensing requirement as on 31 March of the immediately preceding financial year.
III. A bank that has implemented Core Banking Solution is exempt from the minimum CRAR requirement for this purpose.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: Besides CBS with IPv6-enabled public-facing IT, the bank must comply with the minimum regulatory CRAR, meet the minimum paid-up capital/net worth, show adequate financial and technical capability, and have a satisfactory compliance record, assessed through a GAICA report certified by CERT-In empanelled auditor(s) and the IS audit reports. The paid-up capital/net worth is tested as on 31 March of the immediately preceding financial year. CBS does not exempt a bank from the CRAR condition.
steps: III: wrong – CRAR compliance is a separate condition
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement III is false; 'II only' omits the correct statement I.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: b) Compliance with minimum regulatory CRAR requirement. c) Minimum paid up capital/Net worth as per the applicable licensing requirement (as amended from time to time), as on March 31st of the immediately preceding financial year ... GAICA Report with respect to the technological controls prescribed in para 8 of these Directions. The report shall be certified by (third party) CERT-In empaneled auditor(s)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's Authentication Directions, 2025 require at least two factors of authentication for digital payments, with listed exemptions. Which of the following card transactions still requires two-factor authentication?

options.text: The first transaction under a new recurring e-mandate on a credit card
A payment made from a gift PPI
The third monthly debit under an e-mandate already registered on a credit card
A small-value contactless card payment at a shop

solution.explanation: Annex 1 of the Directions lists exemptions in force, including small-value contactless card transactions, recurring transactions other than the first under the e-mandate framework, NETC transactions, select PPIs (PPI-MTS, gift PPIs) and small-value offline payments. The first transaction of an e-mandate is not exempt.
steps: Recurring e-mandate debits after the first → exempt
First e-mandate transaction → needs two factors
Gift PPIs and small-value contactless → exempt
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are on RBI's list of exemptions.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The first transaction under a new recurring e-mandate on a credit card

fact_checks.claim: Existing exemptions from the requirement of at least two factors of authentication: 1. Small-value Contactless Card transactions 2. Recurring transactions (other than the first) under the e-mandate framework 3. Select Prepaid Instruments such as PPI-MTS and Gift PPIs

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's Digital Rupee FAQs list four present use cases of the wholesale e₹ (e₹-W). Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.text: Tokenised issuance and settlement of corporate bonds
Tokenised issuance and settlement of Certificates of Deposit
Settlement of inter-bank lending and borrowing in the call money market

solution.explanation: The four e₹-W use cases are funds settlement of secondary-market government securities transactions, settlement of call money market lending and borrowing, tokenised issuance and settlement of CDs, and tokenised issuance and settlement of corporate bonds. UPI settlement is not among them.
steps: e₹-W: G-sec settlement, call money, tokenised CDs, tokenised corporate bonds
solution.why_others_wrong: Call money, tokenised CDs and tokenised corporate bonds are all listed use cases.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Inter-bank settlement of UPI transactions

fact_checks.claim: Presently, there are four use cases of e₹-W – (i) funds settlement of secondary market transactions in Government Securities, (ii) settlement of inter-bank lending and borrowing in call money market, (iii) tokenised issuances and settlements of Certificates of Deposit, and (iv) tokenised issuance and settlement of Corporate Bonds

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: From which date have banks been advised not to levy any charges on their savings bank account holders for NEFT transfers initiated online?

solution.concept: NEFT charges for savings account holders
solution.explanation: RBI's NEFT FAQs say that, to give impetus to digital retail payments, banks were advised not to levy any charges from savings bank account holders for NEFT transfers initiated online with effect from 1 January 2020. Separately, RBI stopped levying its own processing charges on member banks from 1 July 2019.
steps: Online NEFT by savings account holders → free from 1 January 2020
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 July 2019 is when RBI stopped charging member banks; 16 December 2019 is when NEFT became 24x7; 1 April 2020 is not a date RBI gives.

fact_checks.claim: banks have been advised to not levy any charges from their savings bank account holders for NEFT funds transfers initiated online with effect from January 01, 2020

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility (INRF) Scheme, which uses the NEFT system to send money from India to Nepal, was launched by RBI in:

solution.explanation: RBI's INRF FAQs say the scheme was launched in May 2008 to give migrant Nepalese workers in India a safe and cost-efficient way to send money home. It was enhanced in August 2021.
solution.why_others_wrong: November 2005 is when NEFT itself started; August 2021 is the enhancement; December 2019 is NEFT going 24x7.

fact_checks.claim: The scheme was launched by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in May 2008 to provide a safe and cost-efficient avenue to migrant Nepalese workers in India to remit money back to their families in Nepal

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility Scheme, a beneficiary in Nepal without a Nepal SBI Ltd account is to collect cash from the money transfer company's outlet. What happens if the beneficiary does not approach the company within a week from the date of the transaction?

options.text: The amount is credited to a suspense account of Nepal SBI Ltd until claimed
The money transfer company arranges to return the remittance to the originator in India
The remittance is forfeited and transferred to a depositor education fund
The amount is converted into a fixed deposit in the beneficiary's name

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say that if the beneficiary does not approach the money transfer company within a week, the company arranges for the return of the remittance to the originator. The money flows back through NEFT to the originating branch, which credits the remitter's account (or refunds a walk-in remitter against the counterfoil).
steps: Remittance returned to the originator through NEFT
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no suspense parking, conversion into a deposit or forfeiture in the scheme.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The money transfer company arranges to return the remittance to the originator in India

fact_checks.claim: If the beneficiary does not approach the money transfer company within a week from the date of the transaction, the money transfer company would make arrangements for return of the remittance to the originator

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A walk-in customer sends two remittances to Nepal under the Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility: ₹4,000 to his mother and ₹20,000 to his brother. Neither beneficiary has an account with Nepal SBI Ltd. Using the charges in RBI's INRF FAQs for remittances up to ₹50,000 (taking the originating bank's maximum), what are the total charges for the two remittances?

solution.explanation: For each remittance up to ₹50,000 the originating bank may charge at most ₹5 and SBI charges ₹20 (shared ₹10 each with Nepal SBI Ltd). If the beneficiary has no NSBL account, a further ₹50 applies for remittances up to ₹5,000 and ₹75 above ₹5,000. So ₹4,000 → 5 + 20 + 50 = ₹75 and ₹20,000 → 5 + 20 + 75 = ₹100; total ₹175.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹150 applies the ₹50 slab to both; ₹50 ignores the cash-delivery charge; ₹200 applies ₹75 to both.

fact_checks.claim: Originating bank – Maximum ₹5/- per transaction. State Bank of India – ₹20/- per transaction ... In case the beneficiary does not maintain an account with NSBL then, an additional amount would be charged- ₹50/- for remittances up to ₹5,000/- and ₹75/- for remittance above ₹5,000/-

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A remitter wants to send money by RTGS but does not know the IFSC of the beneficiary's branch. Besides asking his own branch or checking RBI's website, where do RBI's RTGS FAQs say the IFSC is available?

options.text: On the cheque leaf of the beneficiary

solution.explanation: RBI's RTGS FAQs say the IFSC can be obtained from the remitter's bank branch, is available on the beneficiary's cheque leaf (and can be communicated by the beneficiary), and is listed on RBI's website.
steps: IFSC sources: own branch, beneficiary's cheque leaf, RBI website
solution.why_others_wrong: PAN and Aadhaar documents do not carry the IFSC; NPCI does not run RTGS.
solution.final_answer: Option C: On the cheque leaf of the beneficiary

fact_checks.claim: The IFSC number can be obtained by the remitter (customer) from his / her bank branch. Alternatively, it is available on the cheque leaf of the beneficiary

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Sunil has a dispute about an RTGS transaction. According to RBI's RTGS FAQs (updated October 2026), what is the correct route for his grievance?

options.text: First the bank's grievance redressal cell; if not resolved satisfactorily within the prescribed timeline, a complaint under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026
Directly to RBI's RTGS Help Desk, which decides the dispute
A complaint to NPCI's dispute resolution system
Only a civil suit, since RTGS payments are final and irrevocable

solution.explanation: The FAQs say a customer should approach the bank's grievance redressal cell with the details; if the grievance is not resolved satisfactorily within the timeline prescribed in RB-IOS 2026, a complaint may be lodged under that Scheme, which is a single reference point for complaints against RBI-regulated entities.
solution.why_others_wrong: The Help Desk is a contact point, not an adjudicator; finality of settlement does not bar complaints; NPCI does not operate RTGS.
solution.final_answer: Option A: First the bank's grievance redressal cell; if not resolved satisfactorily within the prescribed timeline, a complaint under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026

fact_checks.claim: You may approach grievance redressal cell of your bank with details of the disputed transaction. In case your grievance is not resolved satisfactorily as per the timeline prescribed in 'The Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS 2026)', you may lodge a complaint under the said Scheme

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Payment Systems Report (December 2025), RTGS handled 20 crore transactions worth ₹1,246 lakh crore in CY 2021 and 33 crore transactions worth ₹2,206 lakh crore in CY 2025. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Volume grew faster than value, so the average transaction fell from about ₹67 lakh to about ₹62 lakh
The average transaction rose from about ₹6.2 lakh to about ₹6.7 lakh
The average transaction stayed unchanged at about ₹65 lakh
Value grew faster than volume, so the average RTGS transaction rose from about ₹62 lakh to about ₹67 lakh

solution.explanation: Average size = value ÷ volume. CY 2021: ₹1,246 lakh crore ÷ 20 crore = ₹62.3 lakh; CY 2025: ₹2,206 lakh crore ÷ 33 crore ≈ ₹66.8 lakh. RBI reports CAGRs of 13.5% in volume and 15.3% in value, consistent with a rising average.
solution.why_others_wrong: The average rose, not fell; ₹6.2–6.7 lakh is off by a factor of ten; it did not stay unchanged.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Value grew faster than volume, so the average RTGS transaction rose from about ₹62 lakh to about ₹67 lakh

fact_checks.claim: RTGS transactions volume grew from 20 crore in CY 2021 to 33 crore in CY 2025, while transactions value increased from ₹1,246 lakh crore to ₹2,206 lakh crore during this period ... a CAGR of 13.5% in transaction volume and 15.3% in transaction value

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: An IMPS credit could not be made to the beneficiary because the remitter gave incomplete beneficiary details. Is this a 'failed transaction' under RBI's harmonised turn-around time (TAT) framework?

options.text: No; only failures caused by technical faults such as link failures are covered
No; any failure involving the customer's own input is excluded altogether
Only if the amount exceeds ₹2 lakh
Yes; failed transactions include credits not effected for lack of full or proper information, and delay in initiating a reversal

solution.explanation: The framework defines a failed transaction as one not fully completed for reasons not attributable to the customer, such as communication failures, ATM cash outages or session time-outs, and expressly includes credits that could not be effected to the beneficiary account for lack of full or proper information and delay in initiating a reversal transaction.
steps: Also covers non-credit for lack of full/proper information
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI's definition expressly covers non-credit for lack of information; there is no amount threshold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Yes; failed transactions include credits not effected for lack of full or proper information, and delay in initiating a reversal

fact_checks.claim: Failed transactions shall also include the credits which could not be effected to the beneficiary account on account of lack of full information or lack of proper information and delay in initiating a reversal transaction

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer uses her bank-issued PPI wallet to send money to a bank account of another bank, and the transfer rides on IMPS (an 'off-us' PPI transaction). It fails after the wallet is debited. Under RBI's TAT framework for failed transactions, which turn-around time and compensation rules apply?

options.text: The rules for ATM transactions, as wallets are treated like cards
No TAT applies, since PPIs are outside the framework
A special PPI rule of reversal within T + 5 days with no compensation
Those of IMPS, the system on which the transaction rides

solution.explanation: For PPI off-us transactions, the framework says the transaction rides on UPI, a card network, IMPS, etc., and the TAT and compensation rules of that system apply. So here the IMPS rule (reversal by T + 1, ₹100 per day thereafter) applies. Separate T + 1 rules cover on-us PPI transactions.
steps: Off-us PPI → follows the underlying system
Here IMPS → IMPS TAT and compensation
solution.why_others_wrong: PPIs are covered; there is no separate T + 5 no-compensation rule; ATM rules are unrelated.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Those of IMPS, the system on which the transaction rides

fact_checks.claim: Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs) – Cards / Wallets ... Off-Us transaction: The transaction will ride on UPI, card network, IMPS, etc., as the case may be. The TAT and compensation rule of respective system shall apply

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Ravi's IMPS transfer fails after his account is debited, and the beneficiary bank sends the money back. Consider the following statements about how RBI's harmonised turn-around time (TAT) framework treats such IMPS failures:
I. 'R', the reversal day, is the day on which the reversal is concluded and the funds are received by the originator, and Ravi's bank must credit him on the same day it receives the funds.
II. The term 'bank' in the framework also covers non-banks wherever they are authorised to operate.
III. 'T', the day of the transaction, means the next working day after Ravi initiated the transfer.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The framework defines R as the day the reversal is concluded and the funds are received by the issuer/originator, and requires the reversal to be effected at the originator's end on the same day the funds are received (I correct). The term bank includes non-banks wherever they are authorised to operate (II correct). T is the day of the transaction and refers to the calendar date, not the next working day (III wrong).
steps: III → wrong (T = calendar date of the transaction)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with III are wrong; 'I only' misses II.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: R is the day on which the reversal is concluded and the funds are received by the issuer / originator. Reversal should be effected at the issuer / originator end on the same day when the funds are received from the beneficiary end
The term bank includes non-banks also and applies to them wherever they are authorised to operate
T is the day of transaction and refers to the calendar date

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's framework for small value digital payments in offline mode (as updated in December 2024), what is the total limit on a UPI Lite balance at any point in time?

solution.explanation: RBI's offline payments framework sets a general limit of ₹500 per transaction and ₹2,000 in total, but for UPI Lite the enhanced limits are ₹1,000 per transaction with ₹5,000 as the total limit.
steps: UPI Lite: ₹5,000 total at any time
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,000 is the general offline total; ₹1,000 is the per-transaction UPI Lite cap; ₹10,000 is not an offline limit.

fact_checks.claim: For UPI Lite, the enhanced limits shall be ₹1,000 per transaction with ₹5,000 being the total limit

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework, 2026, which also covers UPI AutoPay mandates, how far in advance must the issuer send a pre-transaction notification before the actual debit?

solution.explanation: The framework (21 April 2026) consolidates RBI's e-mandate circulars for recurring transactions using cards, PPIs and UPI. The issuer must send a pre-transaction notification at least 24 hours before the charge, giving the merchant's name, amount, date/time of debit, mandate reference and reason for debit, and must let the customer opt out (validated with AFA).
steps: E-mandate debit → notify customer ≥ 24 hours before
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 hours, 7 days and 2 hours are not the period prescribed.

fact_checks.claim: An issuer shall send a pre-transaction notification to the customer, at least 24 hours prior to the actual charge / debit
applicable to all Payment System Providers and Payment System Participants in respect of processing of recurring transactions, domestic or cross-border, using cards / PPI / UPI

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: To reduce the load on the UPI system, NPCI limited balance enquiries from 1 August 2025. What is the limit?

options.text: 50 balance enquiries per day across all UPI apps together
10 balance enquiries per day on each UPI app
50 balance enquiries per day on each UPI app
One balance enquiry after every UPI transaction only

solution.explanation: Under NPCI's changes effective 1 August 2025, a user can make at most 50 balance enquiries a day on each UPI app, and only 25 requests a day for the list of bank accounts linked to the mobile number.
solution.why_others_wrong: The cap applies per app, not across apps, and is 50, not 10.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 50 balance enquiries per day on each UPI app

fact_checks.claim: For balance enquiries, the maximum limit is 50 per day on each UPI app

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Master Direction on Prepaid Payment Instruments, which PPIs may a PPI issuer enable for UPI payments by linking them to its UPI handle?

options.text: Only gift PPIs, through a sponsor bank's handle
All its PPIs, including small PPIs without full KYC
Only its full-KYC PPIs; the issuer acts as a PSP in UPI with a handle issued by NPCI
Only PPIs issued by banks; non-bank PPI issuers cannot participate in UPI

solution.explanation: A PPI issuer acts as a Payment System Provider (PSP) in UPI, and NPCI issues it a handle. It may enable only its full-KYC PPIs to make UPI payments by linking them to its handle; such transactions on the issuer's app are authenticated with the customer's PPI credentials.
steps: PPI issuer = PSP in UPI; NPCI issues handle
Only full-KYC PPIs can be linked
solution.why_others_wrong: Small PPIs are excluded; gift PPIs are not the category named; non-bank PPI issuers can participate.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Only its full-KYC PPIs; the issuer acts as a PSP in UPI with a handle issued by NPCI

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Master Direction on PPIs, banks and non-banks may issue INR-denominated full-KYC PPIs to foreign nationals and NRIs visiting India in the form of wallets linked to UPI. For what can these wallets be used?

options.text: Both P2P and P2M payments, and cash withdrawal at ATMs
Only for paying visa and airport fees

solution.explanation: The PPI Master Direction allows full-KYC INR PPIs for foreign nationals/NRIs visiting India (to start with, travellers from G-20 countries at select international airports). They may be issued as wallets linked to UPI and used for merchant payments (P2M) only.
solution.why_others_wrong: P2P transfers and cash withdrawal are not allowed; the use is not limited to fees.

fact_checks.claim: The PPIs can be issued in the form of wallets linked to UPI and can be used for merchant payments (P2M) only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A non-bank PPI issuer participates in UPI as a Payment System Provider so that its full-KYC wallet holders can make UPI payments. Under RBI's Master Direction on PPIs, how does it settle its UPI transactions?

options.text: Through a sponsor bank, meeting NPCI's requirements for the sponsor bank arrangement
In cash with each beneficiary bank at the end of the day
Directly in its own current account with RBI
Through CCIL as a central counterparty

solution.concept: Settlement of non-bank PPI issuers in UPI
solution.explanation: The PPI Master Direction says that for settlement a non-bank PPI issuer shall participate in UPI through a sponsor bank and meet the sponsor bank arrangement requirements of UPI and all NPCI requirements. Payments to and from the sponsor bank towards settlement obligations are permitted in its escrow account.
steps: Non-bank PPI issuer in UPI → settles through a sponsor bank
solution.why_others_wrong: Non-banks do not hold settlement accounts with RBI for UPI; CCIL does not settle UPI; settlement is not in cash.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Through a sponsor bank, meeting NPCI's requirements for the sponsor bank arrangement

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Under RBI's Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework, 2026, which of these UPI AutoPay debits need an Additional Factor of Authentication (AFA)?
P. The first debit of ₹499 under a new monthly streaming mandate
Q. The fourth monthly debit of ₹12,000 for school fees
R. A monthly mutual fund SIP debit of ₹60,000 (not the first)
S. A monthly gym membership debit of ₹22,000 (not the first)

solution.explanation: The first transaction under any e-mandate needs AFA (it may be combined with registration), so P needs AFA. Later recurring debits are AFA-free up to ₹15,000 (Q is fine) and up to ₹1,00,000 for insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bills (R is fine). S, at ₹22,000 in an ordinary category, exceeds ₹15,000 and needs AFA.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'S only' forgets the first-transaction rule; options with R ignore the ₹1 lakh limit for mutual funds.
solution.final_answer: Option C: P and S only

All recurring transactions may be authorised without AFA up to ₹15,000/- per transaction ... Payment of insurance premiums, subscription to mutual funds, and credit card bill payments may be made without AFA up to ₹1,00,000/- per transaction

They lapse and must be cancelled by the merchant
They are converted into NACH mandates

steps: Card reissued → existing e-mandates can be mapped to the new card
solution.why_others_wrong: The framework does not make mandates lapse or convert them to NACH or UPI.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They can be mapped to the reissued card

fact_checks.claim: In case of cards, existing e-mandate(s) can be mapped to reissued cards

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about RBI's directions on due diligence of AePS touchpoint operators (ATOs):
I. If an ATO's due diligence has already been done as a Business Correspondent or sub-agent, the acquiring bank may adopt it.
II. The acquiring bank must ensure that technological integrations such as APIs are used only for enabling AePS operations.
III. The directions apply only to scheduled commercial banks, not to co-operative banks.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: Banks must do customer due diligence of ATOs before onboarding, but may adopt due diligence already done for them as BCs/sub-agents (I correct). They must put in place system-level controls so that APIs are used only for AePS operations (II correct). The circular is addressed to scheduled commercial banks including RRBs, urban co-operative banks, state and district central co-operative banks, and NPCI (III wrong).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with III are wrong; 'I only' misses II.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and II only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Payment Systems Report (December 2025), toll plazas onboarded on NETC rose from 964 in December 2021 to 1,896 in December 2025, while FASTags issued grew from 4.42 crore to 11.87 crore. Which statement is correct?

options.text: FASTags grew about 2.7 times and toll plazas about 2 times, so FASTags per plaza rose from about 46,000 to about 63,000
Toll plazas grew faster than FASTags, so FASTags per plaza fell
Both grew about 2.7 times, leaving FASTags per plaza unchanged
FASTags per plaza rose from about 4,600 to about 6,300

solution.explanation: Toll plazas: 1,896 ÷ 964 ≈ 1.97 times. FASTags: 11.87 ÷ 4.42 ≈ 2.69 times. FASTags per plaza: 4.42 crore ÷ 964 ≈ 45,900 in 2021 and 11.87 crore ÷ 1,896 ≈ 62,600 in 2025.
solution.why_others_wrong: FASTags grew faster, so the per-plaza figure rose; the 4,600/6,300 option is off by a factor of ten.
solution.final_answer: Option A: FASTags grew about 2.7 times and toll plazas about 2 times, so FASTags per plaza rose from about 46,000 to about 63,000

fact_checks.claim: The number of toll plazas onboarded increased from 964 in December 2021 to 1,896 in December 2025. FASTag issuance grew from 4.42 crore to 11.87 crore during this period

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

The Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Schedule to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007

solution.why_others_wrong: Scheduled bank status comes only from the Second Schedule to the RBI Act.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Payments Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, how does a payments bank start a 'view only' internet or mobile banking facility, compared with a 'transactional' facility?

options.text: Neither needs any approval or intimation
View-only needs RBI's prior approval; transactional needs only Board approval
View-only: with Board approval, intimating RBI within 30 days with a GAICA report; transactional: only with RBI's prior approval

solution.explanation: Banks with CBS and IPv6-enabled public-facing IT may offer view-only facilities, intimating RBI's Department of Regulation through PRAVAAH within thirty days of the Board-approved decision, along with a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) report. A transactional facility needs RBI's prior approval.
solution.why_others_wrong: The two facilities are treated differently; the last option reverses them.

Banks shall require prior approval of the Reserve Bank for launching transactional banking facility

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

options.text: Savings vehicles for unserved and underserved people, and credit to small businesses, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and the unorganised sector, through high technology–low cost operations
Financing of infrastructure projects through long-term bonds
Large-ticket corporate lending and investment banking
Payments and remittances only, without any lending

solution.explanation: SFBs aim at (i) savings vehicles primarily for unserved and underserved sections and (ii) credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and other unorganised entities, through high technology–low cost operations.
steps: Savings for underserved + small-ticket credit, low-cost technology
solution.why_others_wrong: Corporate/infrastructure finance is not their objective; payments-only is the payments bank model.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A newly licensed small finance bank commences business in October. Under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025, how is its first priority sector target set?

options.text: At 40% of ANBC for the first three years
On its opening balance sheet, applying from day one
On its first audited balance sheet as on 31 March, applying to the following year; it cannot sell PSL Certificates in the intervening period
It has no PSL target for the first five years

solution.concept: First PSL target of an SFB
solution.explanation: The first audited balance sheet as on 31 March after commencement forms the basis of the first PSL target, for the subsequent financial year. In the intervening period (commencement to that 31 March) the SFB is not allowed to sell PSLCs.
steps: Basis: first audited 31 March balance sheet
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no day-one target, no 40% transitional rate and no five-year holiday.
solution.final_answer: Option C: On its first audited balance sheet as on 31 March, applying to the following year; it cannot sell PSL Certificates in the intervening period

fact_checks.claim: The first audited balance sheet as on March 31st, post commencement of operations of the small finance bank, would form the basis for the first PSL target for the bank (for the subsequent financial year). During the 'intervening period' ... the small finance banks are not allowed to sell Priority Sector Lending Certificates

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What capital adequacy requirement applies to small finance banks under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025?

options.text: CRAR of 15%, with Tier II capped at 50% of Tier I
CRAR of at least 15% on a continuous basis, Tier I at least 7.5% of RWAs, and Tier II capped at 100% of Tier I
CRAR of 9%, as for other commercial banks
CRAR of 12%, with no separate Tier I floor

solution.explanation: SFBs must maintain minimum CRAR of 15% of RWAs continuously; Tier I capital must be at least 7.5% of RWAs; Tier II is limited to 100% of Tier I.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9% and 12% are not the SFB requirement; the Tier II cap is 100% of Tier I, not 50%.
solution.final_answer: Option B: CRAR of at least 15% on a continuous basis, Tier I at least 7.5% of RWAs, and Tier II capped at 100% of Tier I

fact_checks.claim: The small finance bank shall be required to maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 per cent of its risk weighted assets (RWA) on a continuous basis ... Tier I capital should be at least 7.5 per cent of RWAs. Tier II capital should be limited to a maximum of 100 per cent of total Tier I capital

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A small finance bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹8,000 crore, Tier I capital of ₹560 crore and Tier II capital of ₹700 crore. Applying the SFB capital norms, which statement is correct?

options.text: CRAR is 15.75%, so the bank complies
Eligible Tier II is capped at ₹560 crore, so CRAR is 14% and Tier I is 7%; both requirements are breached
CRAR is 15.75% but Tier I at 7% is short
CRAR is 14% but Tier I at 7% meets the 7% floor

solution.explanation: Tier II counts only up to 100% of Tier I: min(700, 560) = 560. CRAR = (560 + 560) ÷ 8,000 = 14% < 15%. Tier I ratio = 560 ÷ 8,000 = 7% < 7.5%. Both are breached.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.75% ignores the Tier II cap; the Tier I floor is 7.5%, not 7%.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Eligible Tier II is capped at ₹560 crore, so CRAR is 14% and Tier I is 7%; both requirements are breached

fact_checks.claim: minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 per cent ... Tier I capital should be at least 7.5 per cent of RWAs. Tier II capital should be limited to a maximum of 100 per cent of total Tier I capital

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
An NBFC that has secured borrowings backed by a floating charge on its assets converts into a small finance bank. Consider:
I. SFBs are precluded from creating floating charges on their assets.
II. The existing floating-charge borrowings may be grandfathered till maturity.
III. The assets under such a charge carry no extra risk weight.
Which of the above is/are correct under the SFB Licensing Guidelines, 2025?

solution.explanation: SFBs cannot create floating charges. For a converting NBFC/MFI, such borrowings on the balance sheet on conversion day are grandfathered till maturity, but an additional 25% risk weight is imposed on the assets on which the charge/lien was created. So III is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: SFBs are precluded from creating floating charge on their assets. For such NBFCs / MFIs ... if they have created floating charges on their assets for secured borrowings ... RBI will permit grandfathering of such borrowings till their maturity. An additional risk weight of 25 per cent will be imposed on the assets on which charge / lien has been created by the converting entity

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 9 October 2026, after reviewing liquidity conditions, RBI announced an OMO sale of government securities worth ₹25,000 crore. What is the effect of an OMO sale on banking system liquidity?

options.text: It absorbs liquidity, as buyers pay RBI for the securities
It has no effect, as it only changes ownership among banks
It injects liquidity, as RBI pays the buyers

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 19 October 2026 the Government ran a switch auction of ₹20,000 crore, exchanging securities maturing in 2027–2029 for securities maturing between 2033 and 2060. What is the main purpose of such a switch?

options.text: To inject liquidity into the banking system
To raise fresh borrowing of ₹20,000 crore
To ease near-term redemption pressure by lengthening the maturity profile of debt
To convert dated securities into Treasury Bills

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI announced that Floating Rate Bond 2034 will pay 7.26% a year for the half year 30 October 2026 to 29 April 2027. The coupon equals a base rate plus a fixed spread of 0.98%. What base rate does this imply, and how is it set?

6.28%: the repo rate on the rate-fixing day

solution.explanation: Base rate = coupon − spread = 7.26 − 0.98 = 6.28%. For FRB 2034 the base is the average of the WAY of the last three 182-day T-bill auctions from the rate-fixing day, and the coupon resets every half-year.
