solution.explanation: A (forward) proxy server is an intermediary for client requests. It can cache content, filter sites, log access and hide internal addresses from the internet.
steps: Forwards requests on behalf of clients + caching + filtering = proxy
solution.why_others_wrong: A DHCP server hands out IP settings. A mail server handles email. A database server stores and queries data.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A customer sees a padlock icon next to the address of a website that looks like her bank's login page. What does the padlock actually confirm?

options.text: That the connection between her browser and that website is encrypted (HTTPS); it does not prove the site is genuinely her bank's
That the website belongs to her bank and is safe to use
That the website has been checked by the RBI
That the site cannot contain any malware

solution.explanation: The padlock means the site uses HTTPS with a valid certificate for the address shown, so data in transit is encrypted. Phishing sites can also get certificates for their own look-alike domains, so the customer must still check the exact domain name.
steps: Padlock = encrypted connection to that domain
solution.why_others_wrong: Fraudsters can obtain certificates for fake domains, so the padlock alone proves neither ownership nor safety. The RBI does not certify websites through the padlock.
solution.final_answer: Option A: That the connection between her browser and that website is encrypted (HTTPS); it does not prove the site is genuinely her bank's

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Why must the antivirus software on branch PCs download updates every day?

options.text: To get the latest virus definitions (signatures) so that it can recognise newly discovered malware
To make the internet connection faster

solution.explanation: Signature-based antivirus compares files against a database of known malware patterns. New malware appears daily, so the database (definitions) must be updated to detect it.
steps: Updated definitions = detection of new threats
solution.why_others_wrong: Antivirus updates do not add RAM, speed up the internet or renew licences of other software.
solution.final_answer: Option B: To get the latest virus definitions (signatures) so that it can recognise newly discovered malware

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: At an airport, a traveller sees two open Wi-Fi networks: 'Airport_Free_WiFi' (genuine) and an identically named one with a stronger signal that a criminal is broadcasting from a laptop to capture users' traffic and login details. What is the criminal's access point called?

solution.explanation: An evil twin is a rogue Wi-Fi access point that copies the name of a legitimate network so that users connect to it, letting the attacker intercept or alter their traffic (a man-in-the-middle position).
steps: Fake access point with the same name = evil twin
solution.why_others_wrong: A honeypot is a decoy system set up by defenders to attract attackers. A botnet is a network of infected computers. A logic bomb is code that triggers on a condition.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank lets customers sign in with passkeys (FIDO credentials) instead of passwords. Why do passkeys resist phishing far better than passwords, even if a customer opens a perfect copy of the bank's site?

options.text: Passkeys encrypt the customer's password before sending it
Passkeys are long passwords that are hard to guess
The passkey is tied to the bank's real site and works by a public-key challenge-response, so there is no shared secret the customer could type into a fake site
Passkeys are sent by SMS for every login

solution.explanation: With a passkey, the device holds a private key for that account and service; the server stores only the public key. At sign-in the device signs a challenge, and the credential is used only with the service it was created for. There is no password to reveal, so a look-alike site gets nothing reusable.
steps: Private key stays with the user's device; server has the public key
Login = signed challenge, bound to the real site
solution.why_others_wrong: Passkeys are not passwords at all. They do not use SMS codes. They do not involve sending an encrypted password.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The passkey is tied to the bank's real site and works by a public-key challenge-response, so there is no shared secret the customer could type into a fake site

fact_checks.claim: FIDO Alliance: passkeys are phishing resistant and secure by design; they are tied to a user's account on a website or app, use public-key challenge-response, and have no shared secrets.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank redesigns its security so that a device inside the head-office LAN is no longer trusted automatically: every request to every application must be authenticated and authorised, whatever network it comes from. Which security model is this?

solution.explanation: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust is granted to users or devices based only on their network location or ownership; access is decided per request using identity, device state and policy.
steps: No trust from being 'inside' = zero trust
solution.why_others_wrong: Perimeter security trusts everything inside the firewall, which is exactly what is being removed. Obscurity relies on secrecy of design. Single sign-on is one login for many applications, not a trust model.

fact_checks.claim: NIST SP 800-207: zero trust assumes no implicit trust is granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location or on asset ownership.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Txn table. Which txn_id appears in the FIRST row of this query's result?

SELECT txn_id FROM Txn ORDER BY txn_date DESC, amount DESC;

solution.explanation: Rows are sorted by txn_date, newest first. Two rows share the latest date 2026-10-05 (T09, 7000 and T10, 2500); the second key, amount DESC, puts T09 first.
solution.why_others_wrong: T10 would be first with amount ASC. T01 is the oldest date (first with txn_date ASC). T05 has the largest amount but an older date.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Txn table. What does this query return?

SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) FROM Txn WHERE acc_no = 'A11';

solution.explanation: A11 has T01 (D, 20000), T03 (W, 1500) and T07 (W, 10000). CASE turns deposits positive and withdrawals negative: 20000 - 1500 - 10000 = 8500, the net change in A11's balance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 31,500 adds all three amounts ignoring the type. -8,500 reverses the signs. 18,500 leaves out the ATM withdrawal T07.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Txn table. Which accounts does this query return?

SELECT acc_no FROM Txn WHERE channel = 'UPI'
EXCEPT
SELECT acc_no FROM Txn WHERE channel = 'ATM';

solution.explanation: The first query gives the accounts with UPI transactions: A11, A13, A14. The second gives accounts with ATM transactions: A12, A11. EXCEPT keeps the rows of the first result that are not in the second (and removes duplicates): A13 and A14.
solution.why_others_wrong: A11 also used an ATM, so it is removed. A11 and A12 are the ATM users (the reverse difference would give only A12). A13 only forgets A14's UPI transaction T10.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Txn table. How many rows does this query return, and which txn_id does it give for account A13?

SELECT acc_no, txn_id FROM (SELECT acc_no, txn_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY acc_no ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn FROM Txn) AS t WHERE rn = 1;

options.text: 10 rows; for A13 it returns T04
5 rows; for A13 it returns T08
5 rows; for A13 it returns T04

solution.concept: Window functions: ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY
solution.explanation: PARTITION BY acc_no numbers the rows separately within each account, largest amount first. rn = 1 keeps each account's largest transaction: one row per account. There are 5 accounts (A11-A15), so 5 rows. For A13 (T04 1500, T08 800) it returns T04.
steps: One partition per acc_no: A11, A12, A13, A14, A15
solution.why_others_wrong: T08 is A13's smaller transaction. 10 rows would mean no filtering by rn. A single row (T05 or T06, the largest overall) would need ROW_NUMBER without PARTITION BY.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5 rows; for A13 it returns T04

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

solution.explanation: The subquery returns A13, A11, A14, A12, A16 and also NULLs. For acc_no X, 'X NOT IN (..., NULL)' means X <> each value AND X <> NULL; any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, so the condition is never TRUE and no row is returned. Adding WHERE ref_acc IS NOT NULL in the subquery (or using NOT EXISTS) would give the intended answer, A15.
steps: NOT IN can never be TRUE -> empty result
solution.why_others_wrong: A15 is what the analyst intended, but the NULLs prevent it. A12 does appear as ref_acc (T06). The query cannot return all accounts, because each one is compared with the same list.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A Customers table has 6 columns and 2,500 rows. In relational database terms, what is the number 2,500 called?

solution.explanation: Cardinality is the number of tuples (rows) in a relation; degree is the number of attributes (columns). Here the cardinality is 2,500 and the degree is 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: Degree is the number of columns (6). A domain is the set of allowed values of an attribute. The schema is the table's structure (name and columns).
solution.final_answer: Option C: Cardinality of the relation

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Table Teaching(student, subject, faculty) records that each faculty member teaches only one subject, and each student has one faculty member per subject. Its candidate keys are {student, subject} and {student, faculty}. The dependency faculty -> subject holds, but faculty alone is not a candidate key. The table is in 3NF. Which normal form does it violate?

options.text: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form), because the determinant 'faculty' is not a super key
First Normal Form, because it has a composite key
Second Normal Form, because subject is a non-key attribute

solution.explanation: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X is a super key. In faculty -> subject, faculty is not a super key. The table still satisfies 3NF because subject is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key), which 3NF allows but BCNF does not.
steps: faculty is not a super key
solution.why_others_wrong: A composite key does not break 1NF (atomic values do). Subject is part of a candidate key, so it is not a non-key attribute and 2NF/3NF hold. The faculty -> subject dependency does violate BCNF.
solution.final_answer: Option A: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form), because the determinant 'faculty' is not a super key

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Transaction T1 runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Loans WHERE branch = 'Pune' and gets 40. Before T1 finishes, T2 inserts a new Pune loan and commits. T1 runs the same query again and gets 41. What is this anomaly called?

solution.explanation: A phantom read occurs when a transaction re-runs a query with a search condition and finds a different set of rows because another committed transaction inserted or deleted matching rows. The SERIALIZABLE isolation level prevents it.
steps: Inserted and committed by another transaction = phantom
solution.why_others_wrong: A dirty read reads uncommitted data, but T2 had committed. A lost update overwrites another update. A deadlock is two transactions waiting for each other's locks.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the fixed-deposit register. What does =COUNTIF(B2:B9, "<>Pune") return?

solution.concept: COUNTIF with a 'not equal to' criterion
solution.explanation: <> means 'not equal to'. Pune appears 3 times among the 8 branch cells, so 8 - 3 = 5 cells are not Pune (Delhi x 3, Agra, Nagpur).
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts the Pune rows themselves. 4 forgets one non-Pune row. 8 counts every row.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the fixed-deposit register. Cell F8 contains =EDATE(C8, E8) and is formatted as a date. What does it show?

solution.explanation: EDATE(start_date, months) returns the date that is the given number of months after the start date. Row 8 is Kiran: 08-Jun-2026 plus 9 months = 08-Mar-2027, the maturity date.
solution.why_others_wrong: 08-Sep-2026 adds only 3 months. 08-Jun-2027 adds 12 months. 17-Jun-2026 adds 9 days instead of 9 months.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: EDATE returns the serial number of the date that is the indicated number of months before or after the start date.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the fixed-deposit register. What does this formula return?

=MAXIFS(D2:D9, B2:B9, "Delhi", E2:E9, "<36")

solution.explanation: MAXIFS(max_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...) returns the largest value among rows meeting all criteria. Delhi rows: Ravi 120000 (24 months), John 200000 (36), Kiran 90000 (9). Tenure < 36 excludes John. The maximum of 120000 and 90000 is 120000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200000 ignores the tenure condition (36 is not < 36). 90000 is the minimum, not the maximum. 0 would appear only if no row matched.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: MAXIFS(max_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...) returns the maximum among cells specified by the criteria.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the fixed-deposit register. In Excel 365, what does this formula return?

=ROWS(UNIQUE(B2:B9, , TRUE))

solution.explanation: UNIQUE(array, [by_col], [exactly_once]). With exactly_once = TRUE it returns only the values that occur exactly once. Pune occurs 3 times, Delhi 3, Agra 1, Nagpur 1, so the result is {Agra; Nagpur} and ROWS gives 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 is the number of distinct branches (exactly_once omitted or FALSE). 6 counts the rows of Pune and Delhi. 0 would mean every branch repeats.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: UNIQUE's exactly_once = TRUE returns all distinct rows or columns that occur exactly once; FALSE or omitted returns all distinct ones.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the fixed-deposit register. What does this formula return?

=XLOOKUP("Ravi", A2:A9, D2:D9, "None", 0, -1)

solution.explanation: XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). match_mode 0 = exact match; search_mode -1 searches from the last item upwards. 'Ravi' is in rows 3 and 5; searching from the bottom finds row 5 first, whose amount is 30000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120000 is the first Ravi (default search_mode 1). 150000 adds both deposits, which XLOOKUP never does. 'None' appears only if no Ravi exists.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]); search_mode -1 performs a reverse search starting at the last item.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In MS Word, a clerk undoes a change with Ctrl + Z and then realises the change was correct after all. Which shortcut redoes the undone action?

solution.explanation: Ctrl + Y redoes the last undone action (or repeats the last action if nothing was undone).
solution.why_others_wrong: Ctrl + R right-aligns a paragraph, Ctrl + U underlines and Ctrl + D opens the Font dialog in Word.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: Ctrl+Y - Redo the previous action, if possible.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A trainer wants to give participants printed copies of a 30-slide presentation with six small slides on each page and space to take notes. Which print layout should she choose in PowerPoint?

solution.explanation: In File > Print, the Layout list offers Handouts with 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 9 slides per page, which puts several slide images on each sheet for the audience.
steps: Several slides per sheet for audience = Handouts
solution.why_others_wrong: Full Page Slides prints one slide per page. Notes Pages prints one slide with the speaker's notes. Outline prints only the text.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Handouts (6 slides per page)

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: to print several slides per page, select one of the Handout options from the Layout list on the Print screen.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: An Excel sheet lists 3,000 loan accounts from all branches. A manager wants to see only the rows for Pune for a moment, without deleting or moving the other rows. Which feature should she use?

solution.explanation: A filter hides the rows that do not meet the chosen condition; they reappear when the filter is cleared. The data itself is not changed.
steps: Show only matching rows, temporarily = Filter
solution.why_others_wrong: Sorting reorders all rows but still shows them. Deleting removes data permanently. Merge & Center combines cells for headings.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Filter (AutoFilter) on the Branch column

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In MS Word, an officer wants the selected paragraph to line up evenly with both the left and the right margins, like a newspaper column. Which shortcut applies this alignment?

solution.explanation: Ctrl + J justifies the paragraph (adds space between words so lines reach both margins). Ctrl + E centres, Ctrl + L aligns left and Ctrl + R aligns right.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ctrl + E centres the text, Ctrl + L aligns it to the left margin only, Ctrl + R to the right only.

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: Ctrl+J - Justify the paragraph.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In a loan sheet, the manager wants every EMI-due date that has already passed to turn red automatically, and to go back to normal if the date is corrected, without anyone colouring cells by hand. Which Excel feature should be used?

solution.explanation: Conditional Formatting applies a format (fill, font colour, icons) to cells only when a rule is true, for example 'cell value is less than =TODAY()', and updates as values change.
steps: Format depends on a rule = Conditional Formatting
solution.why_others_wrong: Data Validation restricts what can be typed. Freeze Panes keeps headings visible. Format Painter copies fixed formatting once.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A clerk must be able to type only in the input cells B2:B6 of an EMI calculator; all formula cells must be protected from changes. She selects the whole sheet and clicks Protect Sheet, but now she cannot type in B2:B6 either. What should she have done first?

options.text: Removed the 'Locked' setting (Format Cells > Protection) from B2:B6, because every cell is locked by default and locking takes effect only when the sheet is protected
Hidden the formula cells before protecting the sheet
Applied Data Validation to the formula cells

solution.explanation: Every cell's Locked property is on by default, but it has no effect until the sheet is protected. To leave input cells editable, unlock them first (Format Cells > Protection > clear Locked) and then protect the sheet.
solution.why_others_wrong: Hiding formula cells does not make B2:B6 editable. CSV loses formulas and protection. Data Validation controls values, not protection.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Removed the 'Locked' setting (Format Cells > Protection) from B2:B6, because every cell is locked by default and locking takes effect only when the sheet is protected

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: by default, protecting a worksheet locks all cells so none are editable; cells must be unlocked before the sheet is protected to stay editable.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A farmer with a basic feature phone and no mobile internet wants to check his balance and send money. Which NPCI service lets him do this by dialling a short code and choosing from on-screen menus?

solution.explanation: NPCI's *99# service uses USSD, which works on the voice/signalling channel of ordinary GSM phones, so it needs neither a smartphone nor mobile data.
steps: Feature phone + no internet + dial a code = *99# USSD
solution.why_others_wrong: UPI Lite is a small-value wallet inside a UPI app. FASTag is for tolls. Internet banking needs internet access.

fact_checks.claim: NPCI's USSD-based mobile banking service (*99#) lets users do basic banking from any GSM handset without mobile internet.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Which UPI-based mobile payment app was developed by NPCI and launched on 30 December 2016?

solution.explanation: BHIM (Bharat Interface for Money) is NPCI's own UPI app, launched on 30 December 2016, for sending and receiving money directly between bank accounts.
steps: NPCI's UPI app from December 2016 = BHIM
solution.why_others_wrong: RuPay is NPCI's card network. AePS is Aadhaar-based payments at micro-ATMs. NEFT is an RBI-run funds-transfer system, not an app.

fact_checks.claim: NPCI: BHIM was launched on December 30, 2016 by the Prime Minister; it is NPCI's UPI-based app.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A customer receives a new debit card and uses it at an ATM in her town without problems, but her first online shopping payment is declined. Under the RBI's January 2020 directions on card security, what is the most likely reason?

options.text: Debit cards can never be used online in India
She must first use the card for an international payment
Online use is allowed only after six months
New cards are enabled only for domestic contact-based use (ATM and PoS); she must switch on online use through her bank's app, net banking or another channel the bank offers

solution.explanation: RBI (January 15, 2020) directed that cards be enabled at issue only for contact-based use at ATMs and PoS in India. Card-not-present (online), international and contactless use must be enabled by the customer, who can switch each channel on or off and set limits at any time.
steps: New card -> domestic contact-based use only
solution.why_others_wrong: Debit cards can be used online once enabled. There is no six-month wait. International use is a separate switch and is not needed first.
solution.final_answer: Option D: New cards are enabled only for domestic contact-based use (ATM and PoS); she must switch on online use through her bank's app, net banking or another channel the bank offers

fact_checks.claim: RBI (RBI/2019-20/142, 15 January 2020): cards shall be enabled for use only at contact-based points of usage within India at issue; issuers must provide a facility to switch on/off and set limits for online, international and contactless transactions.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A small shopkeeper displays one QR code that customers can scan to pay with apps linked to Visa, Mastercard or RuPay cards, and also with UPI apps. This interoperable QR standard, launched in India in February 2017 and developed with NPCI by the card networks, is called:

solution.explanation: BharatQR is a common QR standard developed by NPCI with Mastercard and Visa (American Express and RuPay are supported), so one code accepts payments from different card networks; it is also interoperable with UPI.
steps: One QR across card networks and UPI = BharatQR
solution.why_others_wrong: UPI Lite X is for offline UPI-Lite payments. e-RUPI is a purpose-specific prepaid voucher. NETC is the FASTag toll system.

fact_checks.claim: BharatQR was launched on 20 February 2017 as a common QR standard developed by NPCI, Mastercard and Visa, interoperable across RuPay, Mastercard, Visa and American Express and with UPI.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Each branch server is connected to a UPS so that it keeps running for a few minutes during a power cut. What does UPS stand for?

solution.explanation: A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) uses a battery to supply power instantly when the mains fails, giving time to save work and shut down safely.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A branch PC stores its data on an HDD with spinning magnetic platters. What does HDD stand for?

solution.explanation: HDD = Hard Disk Drive, a storage device that records data magnetically on rotating platters.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Merchants display QR codes for UPI payments. The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994. What does QR stand for?

solution.explanation: QR stands for Quick Response: the 2D code was developed by Denso Wave (Masahiro Hara's team) and announced in 1994 with fast reading as its aim.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.

fact_checks.claim: DENSO WAVE: QR stands for 'quick response'; the QR Code was announced in 1994.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Banks exchange some financial messages in XML, a text format with user-defined tags such as <Amount>. What does XML stand for?

solution.explanation: XML (Extensible Markup Language) is a W3C standard for structured data in text form, where users define their own tags (unlike HTML's fixed tags).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank's file server keeps working when one disk fails because its disks are combined in a RAID array. The 1988 Berkeley paper that introduced the term used 'Inexpensive' for the letter I; what does RAID stand for in today's usage?

solution.explanation: RAID first meant Redundant Arrays of Inexpensive Disks (Patterson, Gibson and Katz, 1988); the industry later changed it to Redundant Array of Independent Disks.
steps: RAID = Redundant Array of Independent (originally Inexpensive) Disks
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Redundant Array of Independent Disks

fact_checks.claim: CHM: RAID stood for Redundant Arrays of Inexpensive Disks in the 1988 paper and was later changed to Redundant Array of Independent Disks.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank's applications check employees' user names, passwords and group memberships against a central directory service using the LDAP protocol. What does LDAP stand for?

solution.explanation: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is the standard protocol for reading and updating directory services such as Active Directory, often used for central login and user lookups.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other expansions are made up.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol

fact_checks.claim: RFC 4511 is titled 'Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP): The Protocol'.
